Document Text: Date: 25/03/2025 Case reference : CAM9784London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 03/03/2025 about digital strategy.   We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice which explains how and why it applies. For the purposes of research, I would like to request the following information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000: 1. Please provide a copy of the council’s current or latest Digital Strategy. If the council does not have a Digital Strategy, please confirm this is the case. I am interested in both organisational Digital Strategy (specific to the council) and place-focused Digital Strategy (specific to the geographical footprint of the local authority). We have not formally published a standalone Digital Strategy. Instead, we have chosen to focus on embedding digital as an enabler of our broader organisational strategy, ‘We Make Camden.’ This approach ensures that digital transformation is fully integrated into our ambitions for the borough, rather than being treated as a separate initiative. Please see: https://www.camden.gov.uk/wmc 2. Please provide a copy of any digital-related strategies across the council. This includes any technology, information or data related strategies. Example strategies include Technology Strategy, IT Strategy, Applications Strategy, Cyber Strategy, Data Strategy, AI Strategy, Analytics Strategy, Information Strategy.This information is exempt. Please see the exemption notice set out below. 3. Please provide the following information in relation to the council’s most senior digital leader*: a) Job description/profile. Chief Experience and Information Officer. b) Salary range. Please use the link below for Camden’s Pay Policy Statement for 2024/25 and annual reports which include pay information for Directors: https://www.camden.gov.uk/chief-officer-pay-at-camden-council c) When the position was created. The current postholder has been in post since 2020 with the remit of the post evolving over that period. The role of Director for this area has existed for a much longer period.   d) Whether the position is currently vacant or occupied. Please see the response above. e) Title of the role the council’s most senior digital leader reports to. Executive Director Corporate Services  f) The position of the role in the organisation’s hierarchy. If the Chief Executive is Level 1 and positions reporting directly to the Chief Executive are Level 2, please confirm the level of the council’s most senior digital leader. The Chief Experience and Information Officer is Level 3. g) Confirm whether the role attends all top-management team meetings**.No, the role does not attend the council’s top-management team meetings. *The role responsible for developing, defining and leading delivery of the organisation’s digital vision and strategy. Those responsibilities should be the primary purpose of the role. Common job titles for these positions include Chief Digital Information Officer, Chief Information Officer, Chief Digital Officer, Director of Digital. **Defined as the regular meetings between the Chief Executive and their top-management/leadership team (e.g., Executive/Strategic Directors/CFO). Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 31(1)(a) – Law Enforcement We do not release information about our technology and data infrastructure or cyber-attacks, the methods or potential results of any cyber-attacks or any measures taken to mitigate or prevent cyber-attacks within our technology and data infrastructure.  Releasing this information itself could affect our cyber security. We consider disclosing this information would make the council a target of crime. Therefore, this information is exempt from disclosure under section 31 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Section 31(1)(a) says that we do not need to provide information that would be likely to prejudice the functions of law enforcement - the prevention and detection of crime.  Camden believes that releasing this information would increase the likelihood of criminals using the information to target attacks against public bodies. For example, releasing this information may make the council a more attractive target for cyber or ransomware attacks. Public Interest Test: As Section 31 is a qualified exemption we need to consider the public interest test. Factors in favour of disclosure: It would help transparency and accountability of the council.• It could show the effectiveness and resilience of our technology and data infrastructure, including cyber security measures taken to mitigate or prevent the effects of cyber-attacks.• Factors in favour of withholding:There is an inherent public interest in crime prevention.• There is public interest in avoiding the costs (financial, distress, inconvenience, publicity, regulatory) associated with any cyber or ransomware attacks.• There is public interest in preventing any threat to the integrity of council data.• There is public interest in ensuring the council can comply with its duties to take all necessary steps to safeguard data.• We believe that the balance of public interest lies in upholding the exemption and not releasing the information. Document Title: Follow on to CAM12134 - information relating to your local authority's administration of the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) under Part 8 of the CIL Regulations 2010
Document Text: Date: 07/04/2026 Ref: CAM12458 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 09/03/2026 about Follow on to CAM12134 - information relating to your local authority's administration of the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) under Part 8 of the CIL Regulations 2010. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding some of the information because it is exempted under the EIR 2004. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemption applies. Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. Using the publicly-available information to which you have directed me, I have been able to secure most of the information I sought. The attached spreadsheet summarises this, and shows the gaps in red bold type (usually as "n/a") In summary, I now only require the total value of Demand Notices issued in the four financial years 2015-16 to 2018-19. Please can you consider my request again in the light of this substantial narrowing of the request. As per my original request, data about the net amount demanded is preferable but I can accept gross amounts if you only hold gross information (that is, simply the total of all the Demand Notices you issued each year without any adjustment for notices which were subsequently superseded). I would also ask you to check your published Infrastructure Funding Statement (IFS) for 2022-23 as I suspect that it is partially incorrect. Some of the data in your 2022-23 IFS appears to be identical to the data provided in your 2021-22 report. There are a number of instances of identical data, but for present purposes the key problem is that on the 'CIL Summary' tab, the amount of CIL demanded is stated as £11,856,385 in both years (see cell B2 of both reports, attached). I suspect that this is an error in the 2022-23 report. Please, therefore, can you give me the correct figure which you should have reported at the time. Finally, I should say that your response seems to focus (on page 2) entirely on the burden associated with responding to item 3 of my request. This seems like a misunderstanding of item 3 to me. My request under item 3 is only relevant to the extent that it helps me understand your response to items 1 and 2 - and since you had no information to give me under items 1 and 2, it does not seem logical to complain that item 3 is burdensome. But so that we can dispense with this argument immediately, please now disregard item 3 of my request and I will rely on your duty to provide advice and assistance in contextualising any information that you are able to provide. I can understand that reviewing 2,500 separate records is not possible - but I am narrowing my request (see above), and to even contemplate a large manual review implies that you possess no London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk aggregated information at all in the form of spreadsheets, tables etc, created at the time for the purpose of internally managing CIL. You do not say whether you have searched for aggregated data of this type and found none. It seems entirely possible to me that you will hold, and could provide, spreadsheets or financial records from the four years noted above, even if they are not in precisely the format I sought. Dozens of CIL charging authorities, including small rural authorities who are much less sophisticated in their reporting than Camden, have been able to give me this data. Please could you double check that you do not hold at least some Demand Notice data for some or all of the four years noted above. Refusal notice: 12(4)(b) Under Regulation 12(4)(b) it would be considered manifestly unreasonable to provide a response to your request because the cost of compliance, and burden of dealing with your request, is excessive. The exception protects the Council’s ability to carry out its public functions and provides a balance between transparency and the protection of resources. We hold some information, but to see what we hold and to locate, extract, collate, and redact this data would be excessive and divert officers from their core functions and statutory obligations. While information may exist within individual case records or audit logs indicating when particular values were amended, extracting and reporting on this would require a manual review of at least 1,000 records. Based on an estimated 30 minutes per record, this equates to approximately 500 hours of officer time. Conducting work of this scale would exceed the appropriate limits and would place an unreasonable burden on the Council under the Environmental Information Regulations. This process would remove the Community Infrastructure Levy team from their daily workloads for just over 68 working days, causing delays in processing new applications, slower responses to developer queries, and potential postponement of statutory reporting obligations. These interruptions could impact project timelines and reduce the team’s ability to meet compliance requirements and support ongoing development initiatives. In addition, the Information Rights team would need significant time to complete any required redactions. This involves carefully reviewing each document to identify and remove sensitive or exempt information in line with legal requirements. Given the volume and complexity of the material, this step would substantially increase the overall time and resource commitment, further extending the timeline and compounding the impact on both teams’ core responsibilities. Therefore, we consider that the burden on the council in undertaking the work required would be unreasonable and Regulation 12(4)(b) applies. This exception is subject to a Public Interest Test and this is below. I have noted the factors for and against disclosure together with their relevant weights. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: • It would improve transparency to the general public of the Council (medium weight) • The presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations (low weight) The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: • Processing this question would be a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council (medium weight) • This question would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities (medium weight) • It would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on the provision of services to the public (medium weight) • It is not in the public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request (medium weight) It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. Document Title: the employment status of [named person]
Document Text: Date: 19 January 2026 Ref: CAM11811 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 16 December 2025, about the employment status of [named person]. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Your request: I am submitting a Freedom of Information request regarding a member of staff referenced in publicly available Camden Council committee papers. Your Hampstead District Management Committee – 4 December 2025 meeting pack lists "[named person]" as "ASB Apprentice". As this information was published by Camden Council into the public domain, I am requesting clarification of her employment status with the authority. Please provide the following information: Was [named person] employed by Camden Council at the time the meeting pack was published (December 2025)? Yes or No. What was her official job title at the time of publication? Was this role a permanent post, fixed-term contract, or apprenticeship? The start date of her employment with Camden Council in this ASB role. (I am not requesting any personal data such as home address, payroll number, HR file contents, or anything exempt under GDPR.) If she has since left Camden Council, please confirm the month and year her employment ended. (Again, no personal or sensitive HR data is requested.) This request concerns publicly facing enforcement functions. ASB, community safety, enforcement, and housing-related officers act on delegated statutory powers and therefore fall within the category of staff whose role-related information is routinely disclosable under FOIA. For clarity, I am not requesting personal data, internal HR assessments, or anything related to performance, conduct, or disciplinary history. I am requesting role-related information that the public has a legitimate interest in, especially as part of an officially published committee document. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Response The council will neither confirm nor deny if it holds the information requested: Section 40(5): requests for personal data about public authority employees Under section 40(5)(b)(i) of the Freedom of Information Act we neither confirm nor deny whether the council holds this information. Ambulance call-out data is provided to a good level of granularity by the London Ambulance Service (LAS). However, despite the overall reliability of this dataset, t here are some significant limitations and quirks that must be considered when reading the data. 2. In theory, LAS paramedics apply an alcohol ‘flag’ to all “all attendances to incidents or injuries where alcohol is determined as a factor”. Those incidents that the LAS includes in this data will therefore incorporate those call outs where the patient has themselves become so intoxicated that they required assessment or treatment, or where they have been the victim of crime whilst they or the perpetrator has been intoxicated in the view of the paramedics doing the recording. 3. However, there is known underreporting of the involvement of alcohol by paramedics (not just in London) when assessing those patients that they are called to attend. This may be due to (and not limited to) the following factors: paramedics being new to the job, a lack of appropriate training and consistency in recording, some individuals lacking attention to detail, the discretion to flag alcohol or not to flag and, most importantly, the paramedics’ primary responsibility of focusing on the patient and thus prioritising their welfare, often in chaotic situations, over the completion of forms. 4. For example, a recent study by Manca F et al (2021) Estimating the Burden of Alcohol on Ambulance Callouts through Development and Validation of an Algorithm Using Electronic Patient Records manually reviewed all ambulance attendance records for a defined period at weekends in a specific location (not London). This found that the number of alcohol-related call outs was likely to be at least 27. This was a significant increase over previous studies which typically suggested that the figure was around 10%. 5. Whilst this study’s results can’t be seamlessly transferred to LAS data and collecting practices, it is reasonable to suggest that, particularly at weekends, figures may be considerably higher than those shown in the tables below. 6. As a result, there will be a significant additional number of alcohol-related call outs where intoxication has also been a key factor than the figures given. 7. Secondly it is important to state that not all LAS alcohol-related call outs are for those patients using licensed premises in the borough (either on or off premises). There are other potential causes. For example, domestic violence where the seriousness of the assault has been magnified by alcohol consumption (responsibility always remains with the perpetrator) and the perpetrator’s alcohol has not been bought locally. Alternatively, there are those socialisers or clubbers who arrive in Camden having become intoxicated elsewhere and who may end up in an incident such as a pedestrian- vehicle collision or victim of an assault or robbery. 8. It is impossible to be more precise than the LAS attendance has been in Camden and by time and location. Ambulance call outs by hour 9. The chart below shows the number of hourly alcohol-related ambulance alcohol-related call outs to Camden during framework hours, then in hourly periods after the latest framework hour (e.g., midnight on a Saturday) and then those ‘other’ call outs 5 after the last framework hours but before the next framework hour commences again. Figure x Average number of alcohol-related callouts per hour during and after framework hours 2019 to 2022 combined. 10. For information, framework hours in Camden are currently: • Monday to Thursday 10:00am until 11:30pm (13.5 hours / 56% of 24hr day) • Friday and Saturday 10:00am until midnight (14 hours / 58% of 24hr day) • Sunday 11:00am until 10:30pm (12.5hrs / 52% of 24hr day) . 11. Overall, alcohol-related ambulance call outs are relatively low within framework hours in Camden - at less than one per hour from Monday to Thursday (average). 12. Alcohol-related ambulance call outs during framework hours on Saturday are more than double the rate of call outs during the week (at 1.6 per hour) . 13. Sunday has the highest number of ambulance alcohol-related call outs to Camden within framework hours. This is the busiest day of the week in terms of the borough’s night-time economy. 14. In the hour following the end of framework hours, alcohol -related ambulance call outs jump significantly on the weekend nights to around 4 call outs per hour. 15. However, for Monday to Thursday there are negligible alcohol- related ambulance call outs. This remains true for the six hours following the end of framework hours between Monday and Thursday. 16. This mostly likely reflects the user patterns and footfall volume of the night-time economy in terms of weekend activity. 17. Unlike during the week, at the weekend there are considerably elevated numbers of alcohol-related call-outs post-framework hours (i.e., between midnight and 5am). In the first two hours after framework hours (i.e., from midnight to 2am) there are around 4 call outs per hour. This then declines to 1.5 call outs per hour on average between 4am and 5am. 18. The other category includes the period starting five hours after the last framework hour (i.e., 3:30am Sunday, 4:30am weekdays and 5am Saturday morning / Sunday morning) and until the start of framework hours again. 19. For example, on Sunday ‘other’ covers the time from 5am to 11am. This suggests a high number of ambulance call outs during the early part of Sunday morning. This is likely to be a combination of those still out in the night-time economy till a very late hour (Camden Town for example still sees many people on the street past 5am) and potentially those who have carried on drinking at home (with alcohol that may have been bought in the borough’s 24 hr off licneces). 20. The chart below shows a time-series analysis of the same data as above. Figure x. Number of hourly ambulance call outs by day of the week and time of day , 2019 to 2022. 21. This chart also allows us to see the breakdown of alcohol-related ambulance call outs by day of week during the week. It shows a slight build-up of call-outs during the week, peaking at the end of Friday night before midnight and just after midnight Saturday morning. This pattern is then repeated for the same 11pm to 1am on Saturday / Sunday. 22. The chart shows a clear temporal pattern of a moderate rise in alcohol-related ambulance call outs during the 6am to 6pm period, but then a spike in alcohol-related call outs begins around 6pm and this is most pronounced on Friday and Saturday nights. 23. After framework hours there is a rapid drop off in alcohol-related call outs down to a consistent low point at around 6am each morning – regardless of the day of the week. Analysis by month and year 24. The chart below shows the number of alcohol-related call outs to Camden by month and year allowing the impact of the pandemic to be seen in some detail. Figure x. Trend in alcohol-related ambulance call outs by day of the week and time of day, 2019 to 2022. Figure x. Number of alcohol-related ambulance call outs by day of the week and time of day, 2019 to 2022. 2019 2020 2021 2022 Jan 118 145 56 140 Feb 119 124 85 110 Mar 170 87 111 121 Apr 122 46 130 103 May 144 76 163 170 Jun 142 82 137 113 Jul 160 127 138 111 Aug 147 132 132 138 Sep 149 97 122 145 Oct 164 103 122 112 Nov 150 114 124 124 Dec 149 87 132 98 Total 1734 1220 1452 1485 25. The headline pattern is that the pandemic lockdowns appear to have had a considerable impact on alcohol-related ambulance call outs in Camden (a significant reduction of 30% between 2020 and 2019). 26. However, alcohol was still available in off-licences and supermarkets, as well as through home delivery during the pandemic and academic research shows that overall alcohol consumption remained at similar levels* in England despite the closure of on-premises such as pubs, restaurant, bars in nightclubs, i.e. with increased home drinking making up the missing on-premises consumption (*Ref. Hardy et al, 2022, The impact of changes in COVID-19 lockdown restrictions on alcohol consumption and drinking occasion characteristics in Scotland and England in 2020: an inter rupted time-series analysis). 27. The explicit reasons for this fall in alcohol-related call outs are not known, but it may be that emergency services being overwhelmed dealing with Covid cases meant people with other problems such as those linked to alcohol were less likely to call 999. However, it is a defensible to say that when licensed premises are closed the number of alcohol-related ambulance call outs falls significantly, even when societal alcohol consumption remains the same. 28. In 2020 the chart shows there is an immediate impact on alcohol-related call outs when the country locks down on March 26 th. alcohol-related then start rising moderately in April but stay at a much lower than historical level till end of June. 29. Towards the end of June there is a sharp rise that takes call outs back up to these near historical levels seen in 2019. This coincides with the relaxing of the 2m rule on 23 rd June 2020 and the opening of pubs on 4 th July. 30. At the end of August, when it was clear that Covid had not been controlled , local lockdowns commenced and in September the ‘rule of six’ and the 10pm curfew were introduced. At that time the data above shows that there is another drop off in alcohol - related ambulance admissions. Given that alcohol-related ambulance callouts peak in Camden on weekends between 11pm and 1am, these falls , whilst not causal, are strongly associative with the restrictions imposed on the operation of on-licensed premises at that time. 31. There was a small rise in alcohol-related ambulance callouts in October 2020. However, during November England went into a second national lockdown and in December 2020 London went back into a local lockdowns (19th December, tier 4). This essentially cancelled the Christmas and New Year season for the on-licensed trade. At this time there is an accompanying fall in alcohol-related ambulance call outs in Camden. 32. On 6 th January 2021 there is the third national lockdown. This appears to have impacted alcohol-related alcohol ambulance call outs in Camden as they fall to less than 60 a month. 33. During February and March 2021 there is a notable in rise alcohol-related alcohol ambulance call outs in Camden, despite the hospitality and night-time economy remaining shuttered. This suggests that whilst the NTE has a significant impact on alcohol-related call outs (as shown by the hourly data previously) there are other contributors, e.g., drinking in public and drinking at home, which when done to excess still required paramedic attendance. 34. In April 2021 pub gardens were allowed to open in England, and on 17 th May indoor drinking in on-licence premises (excluding nightclubs, theatres etc.) were also allowed to open. This also combined with times when councils supported outdoor drinking, eating and streateries under the provisions contained in the Business and Planning Act 2020. 35. At this point – May 2021 - the number of alcohol-related alcohol ambulance call outs in Camden rises rapidly to its highest level in 2021 at around 160 a month. 36. In June, as all restrictions are lifted, there is a small fall in alcohol-related alcohol ambulance call outs and they then remain at a consistent level from June to December 2021, averaging around 120-140 call outs a month. 37. The opening of nightclubs on 19 th July 2021 appears to have had no impact on the number of alcohol-related alcohol ambulance call outs in Camden. This is also reflective to some degree of the peak time for alcohol-related calls outs – weekends between 11pm and 1am, rather than the 1am to 5am peak operational time of nightclubs in the borough. 38. Overall, in 2022, there is a notable fall across the year in alcohol related call outs in Camden compared to 2019 (120 a month versus 150 a month pre -pandemic)., There is one exception - a peak in May . 39. It is too early, and the analysis is not granular enough, to draw statically significant conclusions, but this may be the new norm. That is, there are now less alcohol-related alcohol call outs in Camden as a matter of course, and that the impact of alcohol sales and consumption has lessened their impact on the LAS, relative to when the special policy (CIAs) were last reviewed. Correlation between outlet density and ambulance call outs 40. The following chart examines any statistical correlation between the number alcohol- related alcohol ambulance call outs in Camden relative to the density of licensed outlets operating beyond framework hours. 41. (The analysis uses the medium super output area level area of geography. An MSOA is an area within a borough that on average has around 7,800 residents or 2000 households. There are 28 MSOAs in Camden). Figure x. Number of alcohol-related ambulance call outs against premises density 2019 to 2022 by MSOA 42. Overall, there appears to be a strong correlation between the density of licensed premises operating beyond framework hours and the number of alcohol -related ambulance call outs. 43. Those MSOAs with less than 100 licensed premises operating beyond framework hours (which is all but four MSOAs in Camden) tended to have less than 300 alcohol-related ambulance call outs over four years. Indeed, the median of these MSOAs is around 150 alcohol-related ambulance call outs over the period. 44. However, there are four MSOAs with significantly higher levels of alcohol-related ambulance call outs. MSOAX has around 400 licences and also has the highest number of alcohol-related ambulance call outs at 800. However, this MSOA is still beneath the line, so in absolute terms it is high in call outs but in relative terms it is below the median. 45. However, it is the two MSOA outliers above the line where the ratio of alcohol-related ambulance call outs to licensed premises are at their highest (insert MSOA names and locations). 46. However, whilst there is a clear correlation between premises density and alcohol- related ambulance call outs, the relationship is broadly proportionate. That is, the line does not follow an exponential curve but a relative one and there are few outliers. 47. The R2 number is known as the ‘coefficient of determination’ and is a result of a regression analysis performed for this CIA. In plain language, the R2 number tells us how well a pattern is explained by the variables being analysed. The closer the number towards 1, the greater the correlation between the variables. F or example, an R2 figure of 0.50 in this study would suggest that half of alcohol-related ambulance call outs are explained by the density of licences outside framework hours. 48. In this case a figure of 0.7684 means that more than 75% of the relationship between alcohol-related ambulance call outs is explained by the density of licences outside framework hours. This is a high level of correlation. Typically, statisticians would use the following table as a guide to statistical robustness (with a degree of interpretation based on what it is that is being studied). R-Squared Interpretation 0.75 - 1 Significant amount of variance explained 0.5 - 0.75 Good amount of variance explained 0.25 - 0.5 Small amount of variance explained 0 - 0.25 Little to no variance explained Summary 49. In summary, there is a strong correlation between the geographical density of licensed premises operating beyond framework hours and the number of alcohol-related ambulance callouts. 50. This pattern is reinforced by the fall in alcohol-related ambulance callouts during Covid in 2020 when on-licensed premises were closed. 51. However, the level of fall in alcohol-related ambulance callouts when on-premises in Camden were closed was a long way from 100% meaning those call outs that continued have come from those consuming alcohol from off-licences, supermarkets delivery services. 52. It should be borne in mind that, overall, the number of alcohol- related ambulance callouts per month are not high even pre-Covid (albeit they will be a significant underestimate). 53. In 2022, there appears to have been a significant and consistent fall in alcohol-related ambulance callouts in Camden. Whether this fall is permanent will be important to monitor in the context of the two special policy areas (CIAs). Document Text: Date: 3 November 2025 Ref: CAM11273 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 6 October 2025 about the number of looked after children in Camden for the period 1 January 2020 to 31 December 2024. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. 1. The number of looked-after children in your borough between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024, broken down by year. 2. The number of looked-after children in your borough reported missing between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024, broken down by month (or by year if month-level data is not held). 3. The number of looked-after children in your borough subject to Child Protection Plans (CPPs) between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024, broken down by year. a. Of those, please provide the number subject to a CPP due to concerns over child sexual exploitation (CSE). 4. The number of looked-after children in your borough where there have been safeguarding concerns or reports relating to CSE between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024, broken down by year. 5. The number of children currently subjects of concern under the Multi-Agency Sexual Exploitation (MASE) Panel in your borough. a. Of these, please provide the number where concerns relate to group-based child sexual exploitation. 6. The number of children currently subjects of concern under the Multi-Agency Criminal Exploitation (MACE) Panel in your borough. a. Of these, please provide the number where concerns relate to group-based child sexual exploitation. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 7. The number of looked-after children in your borough who have made allegations of sexual offences, broken down by year from 1 January 2020 to 31 December 2024. 8. The number of recorded cases of alleged staff misconduct in local authority- run or commissioned children’s homes between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024, broken down by: o Children’s Care home (where possible without identifying individuals; please suppress small numbers where appropriate), and o Reason for the alleged misconduct. 9. Copies of any internal reports, briefing documents, or assessments produced between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024 that specifically reference “trap houses” or abandoned properties used for crime in your borough (anonymised/redacted as necessary). 10. Whether your authority has provided training or circulated material under Operation Makesafe. If so, please provide copies of any generic training or awareness materials. 11. Copies of any policies, procedures, or guidance documents relating to the reporting of unauthorised visitors to local authority-run or commissioned children’s homes. 12. The total number of unauthorised visitors reported at local authority-run or commissioned children’s homes in your borough between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2024, broken down by year (please provide by care home only if this can be done without exceeding the FOI cost/time limit). We are withholding this information as we consider the following exemption applies. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. Where the Council reasonably estimates that responding would exceed the 18-hour limit, it is permitted to refuse the entire request without calculating the exact time or working up to the limit. The Council does not hold the data requested in question 7 in a structured or reportable format that would allow for accurate identification or reporting allegations of sexual offences. The information requested in question 9 is broad and not stored in a searchable format, as our systems do not support keyword searches for terms such as “trap houses” or “abandoned properties.” While the Community Safety team has confirmed no specific data is held on trap houses, references to cuckooed or abandoned properties used for criminal purposes may exist within various documents. In Children Services, such references may appear in briefings or reports from the past four years but are not held in a structured format that will allow for accurate identification or reporting. Retrieving this information would require a manual review of 796 individual case records. We estimate an average of 5.5 minutes per case, resulting in approximately 4,378 minutes, or 72.9 hours of officer time. Advice and Assistance For questions 7 and 9, it would be difficult to refine the request to reduce the time required to under 18 hours. A limited spot check of approximately 20-30 records may be possible - but this is unlikely to provide a representative or meaningful sample. Document Title: heating charges and Universal Credit
Document Text: Date: 20/09/2024 Case reference : CAM8481London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 06/09/2024 about heating charges and Universal Credit. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 / Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: Freedom of Information - eligible service charges - heating I am making a request for information concerning what the Council determines to be eligible services charges in respect of Universal Credit. 1. Does the Council consider the standing charge element of the heating charges to be eligible? No, the council does not consider the standing charge element of heating charges to be eligible for Universal Credit. The council follows the guidelines set out by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), particularly the Universal Credit (UC) Service Charges Guidance for Social Landlords and the Universal Credit Regulations 2013. Under these regulations, only certain service charges are eligible for support through Universal Credit. The standing charge for heating is typically considered ineligible because: It relates to the administrative cost of managing a personal energy account, which is a personal utility •expense, not a housing-related service cost. Eligible service charges under Universal Credit are those that cover costs related to the maintenance of the communal areas and fabric of the property, rather than individual utility consumption.• 2. If the Council does not consider the standing charge as eligible, what is the supporting basis for this decision? The council's decision follows the normal DWP guidelines and regulatory framework set out in the Universal Credit Regulations 2013. Specifically, these regulations state that utility costs, including standing charges for personal heating accounts, are excluded from the eligible service charges under Universal Credit. Relevant Guidelines: Universal Credit Regulations 2013 (Regulation 12): This regulation outlines which housing costs are eligible for Universal Credit support. Utility costs, including those associated with individual consumption or account management (such as standing charges), are generally ineligible. DWP's Universal Credit Service Charges Guidance for Social Landlords : This guidance reinforces that only communal service charges that benefit the property as a whole are eligible. Document Title: CCTV
Document Text: Date: 10/05/2019 Ref: FOI12714 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 02/05/2019 about CCTV . We have dealt with th is under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested . However we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt . The answers to your questions are below. We have stated wher e we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why the exemptions apply. 1. Supplier of the contract for CCTV maintenance and support Tyco , Amflex, Amey and Kier 2. How much the Council spend annually with the supplier? This is exempt under Section 43 of the Freedom of Information Act. This is because a new procurement contract for CCTV maintenance will be up for tender shortly. See the refusal notice below. 3. What is the renewal date of this contract? Variable dates as in separate contracts. Kier Amey incorporated in TFM contr act. Both end on 2nd January 2020 4. What is the duration of the contract? 9 months 5. What is the review date of this contract? October If possible the likely outcome of this review Not possible to anticipate. 6. The primary brand of the CCTV equipment. I don ’t require the model just the brand. As provided by each provider to meet output specifications. 7. The description of the services provided under this contract. Please state if this contract includes more that just CCTV services. CCTV maintenance and supp ort. Total FM Service (Hard and Soft Services) London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 8. Contact details of the employee responsible for the contract between the supplier and the organisation. Can you please provide me with their full contact details. The Council does not publish individual off icers names with respect to future procurement but follows all the required legislation applicable to public procurement including publishing notice of intention to procure in the appropriate journals . Refusal Notice Section 43(2) – The Council has withheld this information because Section 43(2) exempts information whose disclosure would, or would be likely to, prejudice the commercial interests of any person (an individual, a company, the public au thority itself or any other legal entity). The council is relying upon the higher threshold of likelihood that disclosure would have a prejudicial effect. The parties whose commercial interests are concerned are the companies listed in question 1 , and the council. The h arm that would be caused to companies listed in question 1 is that their commercial details such as profit margins and detailed business model, would be revealed , which would negatively impact their trading position and ability to secure contacts. The harm that would b e caused to the council is that our ability to achieve the best process for a new contract would be reduced as the ‘going rate’ would be disclosed. The link between the disclosure and harm is that for companies listed in question 1 , rival companies would have awarene ss of their business model and pricing structure which would allow rivals to undercut them and reduce their chances of successfully tendering, and for the council, that disclosure of the current amounts paid and prices would reduce the chances of higher re venues being achieved in the anticipated new tenders for similar areas. In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest argu ments for releasing this information are as follows:  Improving transparency in decision making.  Ensuring value for money.  To ensure accountability of the authority.  Demonstrating the council is meeting its fiduciary duties. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows:  It is not in the public interest to disclose information that would be likely to damage the commercial interests of a company, as this could lead to financial problems for the company and/or job losses.  It is not in the public interest to damage the council’s commercial interests, as this affects how it spends public money and the services it can provide to residents and other stakeholders.  It is not in the public interest to release information that could n egatively influence ongoing and future negotiations as this could have an adverse effect on value for money for the council, so for residents and other stakeholders.  Withholding the information does not prevent scrutiny of the council’s actions and decisi ons. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 11/11/2025 about councillors on our planning committee.  We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (EIR 2004). Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, I would like to request the following information: 1. A list of all councillors who are or have been members of the planning committee, for the period 2000 to the present day. 2. For each councillor, please include their start and end dates of service on the committee. 3. Please also indicate which councillor(s) served as Chair of the committee, and their corresponding dates in that role. We are not processing this request.  It would involve a disproportionate amount of time, effort and expense to the council and is excepted under the EIR 2004.  Please see the exception notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exception that applies is:regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable. We have also considered the time it will take the council to locate the information requested in the request, to extract it, collate it and then to review and redact any sensitive information that will be subject to further exceptions under the EIR 2004. If we assume 12 Planning Committee meetings a year (and some years have had more than that), we would need to check a minimum of 300 meetings over the 25 - year period to examine and collate relevant information.  Even if it only took 5 minutes to find the papers and check and record the membership at each meeting, that would be 25 hours of Officer time.  Further additional time, would need to be taken, as documents pre-2006 are not readily available electronically and would require extraction and collation form our Local History Archive at Holborn. We have considered the impact and burden that processing this request would have on the team who would have to deal with it. We have concluded that the time, effort and costs involved would place a disproportionate burden on the team and severely impact their ability to perform their normal duties. In applying this exception, the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004.  We have indicated the weight of each of these considerations. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: - it would improve the transparency for the general public of the council’s planning committee and the councillors who are or have been members (medium). • The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: - processing this request in full would be provide a large burden in terms of officer time and cost to the Council (High). • this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the council’s core business activities, (High) and: • it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s provision of services to the public (High). • it is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request (High). • It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004. We considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not. Document Text: Date: 13/10/2022 Case reference : CAM3987 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 27/09/2022 about ICT policies and strategy documents for ICT security, cyber security, information security, cloud security and users etc.  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice below which explains how and why it applies. Refusal Notice We are frequently asked for information about IT security in Camden.  The council has considered these issues carefully and we have decided that we do not release this information. This is because we consider it is exempt under section 31 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. We have explained why below. section 31(1)(a) – Law Enforcement We do not release information about what IT or related security policies and systems we have in place because we consider disclosing this information would make the council a target of crime.  Therefore, this information is exempt from disclosure under section 31 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Section 31(1)(a) says that we do not need to provide information that would be likely to prejudice the functions of law enforcement- the prevention and detection of crime. Camden believes that releasing this information would increase the likelihood of criminals using the information to target attacks against council systems. For example, knowing when we last updated a security system or policy would allow criminals to know●what vulnerabilities existed at that time and target attacks on those. It is important Camden does not do anything that would allow personal data it holds to be accessed illegally. knowing if Camden’s policies and systems do not have particular vulnerabilities will increase the chances of other more vulnerable organisations being targeted by criminals● As Section 31 is a qualified exemption we need to consider the public interest test. Factors in favour of disclosure: It would help transparency and accountability of the council● It would reassure people about whether our policies or systems are vulnerable or not● It would provide information about how effective our security systems are● Factors in favour of withholding: There is an inherent public interest in crime prevention.● There is public interest in avoiding the costs (financial, distress, inconvenience, publicity, regulatory) associated with any attacks● There is public interests in preventing any threat to the integrity of council data● There is public interest in ensuring the council can comply with its duties to take all necessary steps to safeguard data● We believe that the balance of public interest lies in upholding the exemption and not releasing the information. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Refusal Notice Regulation 12(5)(e) Under the EIR 2004 the exception under regulation 12(5)(e) applies. The regulation states: Confidentiality of commercial or industrial information where such confidentiality is provided by law to protect a legitimate economic interest – regulation 12(5)(e). A public authority can refuse to dis close information if this would adversely affect the confidentiality of commercial or industrial information. Test under 12(5)(e) of the EIRs Justification for satisfaction, related to redacted information The information is commercial or industrial in n ature; The information comprised very sensitive financial information provided by the Contractor to the Authority at a competitive bid stage of a public procurement. It has taken years of skill, technical knowledge and investment to develop this informatio n and it is of such importance that only very few individuals in the Contractor’s workforce (less than 20 out of 12,000) have access to this information to avoid it being inadvertently or deliberately leaked to competitors. It goes to the very heart of how the Contractor uniquely prices its bids in a very competitive market place. Rival bidders would keenly wish to possess such information from one of the leading companies in the sector, such as the Contractor, so as to benefit from the years of expertise w hich the Contractor has developed over the years. The information is therefore considered to be, in effect, a “trade secret”. It was therefore provided to the Authority in confidence that it would not be disclosed. It is confidential under either the common law of confidence, contract, or a statutory bar; The Authority and the Contractor agreed that the entire Contract is deemed to be confidential (under clause 46.1 of the Contract) – subject of course to FoI and EiR obligations of the Authority. The con fidentiality is protecting a legitimate economic interest; The redacted information was sensitive at the time it was submitted and given that the Contractor is currently bidding for other London/South East Contracts, is still just as relevant. Disclosure w ould significantly damage the Contractor’s legitimate economic interests because it would without doubt impact on its ability to retaining or improving market position, it would give its competitors access to commercially valuable information, all at a tim e when there are currently ongoing negotiations with other customers and potential customers. The council has consulted with the third party affected and we have taken their views into account, but the decision about what to release and withhold has bee n the council’s alone. Exceptions are subject to the public interest test where the factors in favour of releasing are weighted against those in favour of withholding. Factors in favour of releasing information  Presumption in favour of disclosure  Interest of the public on this issue  Council’s fiduciary duties to council tax payers, residents and stakeholders  Interest in openness and transparency Factors in favour of maintaining the exception  Not in public interests to cause damage to a private busines s  Not in public interest to cause damage to a council contracted service provider as this will have a negative knock on effect on the council and therefore its residents, businesses and stakeholders  The business is currently bidding for work and disclosur e of the withheld information is likely to benefit its competitors, when the business concerned does not have the same advantage, giving a non -level playing field which is not in the public interest The council’s conclusion is that the factors in favour of maintaining the exception outweigh those in favour of releasing the information. Document Title: Licensing
Document Text: Date: 06/12/2019 Ref: FOI13575 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 24/11/2019 about licensing . We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: How decisions on late licensing (or generally licensing commercial premises in Camden Council are m ade, and on what basis) There are two regimes within the Licensing Act 2003 which you are referring to. There are applications for permanent licences, and those for short one -off events. I will deta il the procedures for both. Firstly, if a venue wishes to obtain a licence to offer licensable activities, then they must seek to apply for a premises licence under the Act. To do so, an application must be lodged with the council. Copies of the applicati on must also be sent to the relevant responsible authorities. Once the application has been submitted, this starts a 28 -day consultation period. During this period, a site notice must be displayed at the premises on pale blue paper advertising the applicat ion. An advert must also be placed in the local press, and the council must have the application to view on the council website. During this 28 -day consultation period the responsible authorities and any other person have an opportunity to object to the ap plication. Any objections to application must take into account the four licensing objectives, and if opposed to the application being granted, should detail how it is believed the licensing objectives will not be upheld by the granting of the licence. The four licensing objectives are; • The prevention of crime & disorder; • The prevention of public nuisance; • Public safety • The protection of children from harm On the 29th day, if nobody has objected to the application, and the advertising requirements have been met, then the council is obliged by law to grant the licence. If relevant representations have been lodged to the application, then the council must organise a sub-committee hearing for the application to be determined at. This should be held with 20 working days of the 28 -day consultation expiry date. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk During this period, the applicant will be forwarded details of any objections, and will have an opportunity to discuss the objections with those that have lodged them. If an agreement can be reached between objectors and the applicant before the hearing, and all parties confirm this, then the hearing can be dispensed with. The licence would then be issued on the terms agreed by the parties to these discussions. If, however, agreement cannot b e reached, then the hearing will go ahead. All written evidence in relation to the application will be circulated before the hearing. All parties will be given an opportunity to speak at the hearing to further support any documentation supplied, and clarif y any points made. A panel of councillors (usually made of three members) will read all documentary evidence before the hearing, and further consider any oral evidence submitted during the hearing. Once all parties have had an opportunity to speak, the pan el of councillors will deliberate publicly on the case, and usually make a decision verbally on the day of the hearing. This will be confirmed in writing shortly thereafter. If any party feels aggrieved by the decision of the committee, then they do have t he right of appeal to the Magistrates’ Court. This appeal must be lodged within 21 days of the written decision having been issued. The other process is in relation to short events, and these notices are known as Temporary Event Notices (TENs). This legis lation has been designed to be quite light touch in how it operates. Premises may only have 15 of these in a calendar year, a single TEN may not last for more than 7 days, and may only have a total of 21 days’ worth of events in a calendar year. A TEN mus t be submitted with ten clear working days’ notice before the event is due to take place. Unlike the process above, only the police and environmental health are consulted on these notices, and are the only bodies that may object to them. The public have no right to object to such a notice. If neither body objects, then the notice is approved and may take place. If there are objections to the TEN, then a hearing must be heard no later than 24 hours before the event is due to take place. The hearing will be i n the same format as that for the premises licence, with written evidence submitted beforehand, and opportunity given to all parties to speak at the hearing. A decision will be made at the hearing. Due to the timescales there is no right to appeal this dec ision. TENs can be submitted between 9 working days and 5 clear working days of an event being due to take place. These are known as late TENs. The process is the same as the for a standard TEN, with the exception that if it is objected to the event will not be permitted to take place, and there would be no hearing to determine this. Document Text: Date: 15/07/2024 Ref: CAM7925 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 19/06/2025 about Ask for Angela campaign, promotional cost, training with costs, implementation, budget and reports . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. I’m reaching out for some information you have on the Ask for Angela campaign. 1. I request the yearly promotional cost of the campaign from 2016 - June 2024. The total promotional costs of the campaign from 2016 – June 2024 is £160. There is no yearly promotional cost. 2. I also request the yearly training cost of the campaign from 2016 - June 2024. The training cost was £5,250 + VAT for financial year 2023. There is no information about any other costs from 2016 and there is no yearly training cost. 3. I also request a breakdown of how the campaign is being implemented from 2016 - June 2024. The campaign is implemented via three different types of training: In person – At a venue with a trainer; Virtual – Online but with a trainer; E-learning – Online with no trainer. 4. I also request a breakdown of how staff members are being trained under the campaign from 2016 - June 2024. There is no data on total number of staff members from 2016 – 2023, however during this time (in 2022 and 2023) 42 venues were accredited as having completed the training. From January – June 2024, 62 staff members have been trained. 5. I also request access to any training documents or literature from the campaign from 2016 - June 2024. The presentation given is exempt from being shared due to being an accredited course and so is exempt under Section 43(2) of the Freedom of Information Act. See the refusal notice below. Further information can be found on https://www.safersounds.org.uk/ and https://www.camden.gov.uk/womens-safety#5ssfbfg4 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 6. I also request a breakdown of the budget plans of the campaign for 2025. There is no current budget plan for the campaign for 2025. 7. I also request how many local council reports have mentioned ‘Ask for Angela’ in the last year and since the campaign started in 2016. ‘Ask for Angela’ was included in one report in 2023. In total, from 2016 it has been included in 68 reports. Refusal Notice: The Council has withheld this information because Section 43(2) exempts information whose disclosure would, or would be likely to, prejudice the commercial interests of any person (an individual, a company, the public authority itself or any other legal entity). The council is relying upon the higher threshold of likelihood that disclosure would have a prejudicial effect. The parties whose commercial interests are concerned are Safer Business Network, and the council. The harm that would be caused to Safer Business Network is that there would be a potential breach of copyright by releasing their intellectual property to an unknown third party without knowing their intentions. It would cause a loss of profit and diminished market share. The harm that would be caused to the council is that our ability to achieve the best value for training would be reduced. The link between the disclosure and harm is that for Safer Business Network, the intellectual property could be copied in breach of copyright and used to compete unfairly with Safer Business Network to provide identical services. The Council pay for the materials that Safer Business Network produces. If they are made freely available online then Safer Business Network loses business as no one would buy the courses. In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: • Improving transparency in decision making. • Ensuring value for money. • To ensure accountability of the authority. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: • It is not in the public interest to disclose information that would be likely to damage the commercial interests of a company, as this could lead to financial problems for the company and/or job losses. • It is not in the public interest to damage the council’s commercial interests, as this affects how it spends public money and the services it can provide to residents and other stakeholders. • Withholding the figures does not prevent scrutiny of the council’s actions and decisions. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. Document Title: school transport for children placed in temporary accommodation
Document Text: Date: 20 March 2026 Ref: CAM12225 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 17 February 2026 about school transport for children placed in temporary accommodation. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. 1. The cost of providing school transport for children who are placed in temporary accommodation out of the local area but are still going to a school within the borough. Under section 508A of the Education Act 1996, local authorities must also promote the use of sustainable travel and transport for all children and young people of compulsory school age who travel to receive education in the local authority's area. Under section 508B and Schedule 35B of the Education Act 1996, local authorities are under a duty to provide free school transport to "eligible children". 2. In each of the last five calendar years (2025/2024/2023/2022/2021) can the council provide with the total figure it has spent in transport costs ensuring transport for children in out of area placement to their school? Can you break this figure down by type of transport (ie school bus/taxi/public transport etc or any other type of transport). We are withholding this information because the following exemption applies. Refusal - Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under Section 12 of the Freedom of Information Act on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We have considered your request carefully. However, the information you are seeking is not routinely recorded. For the purposes of home-to-school transport provision, the council does not report on whether a household is in temporary accommodation. As a result, identifying a child eligible for home-to-school transport who has been placed in temporary accommodation is a complex task, as there is no search function to determine this. Also, a child may have lived at more than one temporary accommodation address during the period covered by your request, further complicating the identification process. Where a family is relocated, any existing transport provision is arranged in collaboration with Children and Family Services and this information is not captured in a way that enables straightforward reporting from case files. To provide an accurate response, officers across five separate services would be required to generate reports for their respective areas, which would then need to be cross-referenced, manually reviewed and verified to determine whether any relevant information is held. We estimate that complying with your request would take a minimum of 38.66 hours of officer time, including: • locating the information across three data systems (6 hours) • creating a database and retrieving the records (3.5 hours) • manually reviewing approximately 1,750 Children in Need records for the 2025 calendar year to identify relevant information (29.16 hours). • undertaking further analysis on the different types of transport provided • repeating this process for each additional calendar year requested, which would significantly increase the time required. This exceeds the 18-hour appropriate limit set out by the Act. Advice and Assistance It is difficult to refine your request to a scope that could be completed within 18 hours. While we may be able to carry out a limited spot check, of a small number of files over a very short period of time - approx. 6-8 weeks, this would not provide a representative or reliable sample and therefore would be unlikely to produce information that would be meaningful. Document Text: Date: 19/07/2018 Ref: FOI11505 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 12/07/2018 about Fixed Penalty Notices . Refusal Notice Section 31 – Law Enforcement We do not release the names or businesses or addresses of empty residential properties as we consider disclosing this information would make them a target of crime. Therefore this information is exempt from di sclosure under S ection 31 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Section 31(1)(a) says that we do not need to provide information that would be likely to prejudice the functions of law enforcement - the prevention and detection of crime. Camden believes t hat releasing this information would increase the likelihood of : London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk  Empty properties being lived in by squatters. Squatting in a residential property is now a criminal offence.  Empty properties being targeted by vandals or graffiti artists and stripped of materials such as roofing, cables or piping, or otherwise vandalised or damaged.  Empty properties being targeted by criminals or terrorists for example allowing them to hide or store the proceeds of crime, or criminal or terrorist materials In the Information Tribunal Case No. EA/2011/0007 (Voyias and LB Camden), the Tribunal was satisfied that the evidence was that disclosing this information would have the effect of assisting at least some of those wishing to engage in squatting, leading to an increase in the this. Squatting in residential property is a criminal offence which shows the negative nature of squatting and crimes such as criminal damage that are often associated with it. In Voyias the Tribunal concluded that an increase in squatt ing would also lead to various categories of associated criminal activity. As a result the Tribunal found that section 31(1) (a) was engaged in that it was likely that disclosure of the disputed information would have a negative impact on the prevention of crime. Public Interest Test: As Section 31 is a qualified exemption we need to consider the public interest test. Factors in favour of disclosure :  There are general arguments in promoting transparency and accountability of public authorities.  Raising the profile of vacant properties would help encourage public engagement and debate. This was considered in the Voyias case by the Tribunal.  There is publ ic interest in avoiding the costs associated with squatting, for example repair, security and eviction costs.  The negative impact of squatting affects the surrounding community and public authorities involved, not just the individual property We belie ve that the balance of public interest lies in upholding the exemption and not releasing the information. Document Title: LADO referrals, concerns and allegations relating to nursery settings
Document Text: Date: 14 April 2026 Ref: CAM12411 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 12 March 2026 about LADO referrals, concerns and allegations relating to nursery settings. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. Please provide the following information for the last five financial years (2020- 2025), broken down by year: 1. The number of LADO referrals, concerns and allegations relating to nursery settings 2. Of these, how many allegations were recorded as substantiated 3. How many of the referrals/allegations resulted in any action recorded by the LADO (e.g., internal disciplinary action, referral to Ofsted or DBS, or police involvement). I am requesting numerical totals only, and I am not seeking any personal data. We are withholding this information as we consider the following exemption applies. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. Due to changes in the council’s recording systems, data for the period 2020/21 to 2022/23 is not held in an easily accessible format. In particular, information relating to nurseries within referral source types is not separately indexed nor routinely recorded. This can only be identified through a detailed review of individual records. Currently, council data systems do not clearly distinguish nursery settings. Information is recorded using drop-down menu options, whereby organisations with multiple London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk functions are often listed under a single name. As a result, it is not possible to reliably identify nursery provision within primary schools or other mixed-use settings. Similarly, while a “Nursery/Child Minder” category exists, a significant number of relevant referrals are recorded under broader categories such as education services, schools, or hospitals. Consequently, identifying and extracting the requested information would require a manual case-by-case review of individual records. This process is complex and would require a considerable amount of staff time and resources. We estimate that complying with your request would take approx. 25 hours and 48 minutes, comprising: • 2 hours to locate and retrieve information held across two separate data systems, and • 7 minutes per record to manually review approx. 204 referrals, including their associated free-text notes (23.8 hours) to determine whether concerns or allegations relate specifically to nursery settings. The total time required to fulfil this request would therefore exceed the appropriate time limit as set out under the Act. Advice and Assistance It would be difficult to refine your request in a way that would reduce the time required to less than 18 hours. While you may wish to consider reducing the period to those years for which data is held in existing reports and refining the scope to the broader category of education services, this is unlikely to provide a representative sample that would be meaningful.
