This report sets out the Equalities Impact Assessment (EIA) that has been carried out by the London Borough of Camden on proposals for ‘pop -up’ cycle lanes on Chalk Farm Road (between the junctions with Castlehaven Road a nd Prince of Wales Road ), which have been developed as part of the Council’s wider transport response to the Coronavirus (COVID -19) health pandemic . This assessment seeks to establish the impacts, both positive and negative, that these proposed changes wil l have on the nine protected groups defined in the Equality Act, 2010 and, where necessary, mitigate any negative impacts. These groups are: Age, Disability, Gender Reassignment, Pregnancy and Maternity, Race, Religion/Belief, Sex, and Sexual Orientation. It is pr oposed to implement the ‘pop -up’ cycle lanes on Chalk Farm Road under an Experimental Traffic Order (ETO). This accompanying EIA will be a ‘live document’ that is updated as the trial period progresses and more equalities data and comments/ feedba ck from stakeholders becomes available, both during the trial period and if a full public consultation on making the proposals permanent is held at the end of the trial period. 1.1 Context In response to the Coronaviru s (COVID -19) Pandemic, the Department for Transport has told Local Authorities to reallocate road space for significantly -increased numbers of cyclists and pedestrians. The Departmen t for Transport issued statutory guidance on 9th May 2020 (and updated on 23rd May 2020) ‘ Traffic Management Act 2004: network management in response to COVID -19’. This requires local authorities to reallocate road space to walking and cycling as quickly as possible to help encourage more people to choose alternatives to public transport when they need to travel , making healthier habits easier and helping make sure the road, bus and rail networks are ready to respond to future increases in demand. This includes: ‘Installing ‘pop -up’ cycle facilities with a minimum level of physical separation from volume traffic; for example, mandatory cycle lanes, using light segregation features such as flexible plastic wands; or quickly converting traffic lanes into temporary cycle lanes (suspending parking bays where necessary ); widening existing cycle lanes to enable cyclists to maintain distancing. Facilities should be segregated as far as possible, i.e. with physical measures separating cyclists and other traffic. Lanes indicated by road markings only are very unlikely to be sufficient to deliver the level of change needed, especially in the longer term.’ In line with this statutory guidance, a series of emergency measures have been proposed across Camden to respond to the need to facilitate the safe travel and transport needs of people in Camden, in light of C OVID -19. O n 13th May 2019 the Cabinet Member for a Camden Council Covid -19 Safer Travel in Camden response: Chalk Farm Road ‘Pop -Up’ Cycle Lane & Ferdinand Street junction improvement scheme 2 Sustainable Camden signed off the Council’s proposed approach to enabling safe travel in Camden, in light of COVID -19. The Council’s response to enabling safe travel in Camden following the COVID -19 pandemic seek s to improve road safety and help people in the borough social distance safely through providing more, safe space they can use to walk and cycle in. This response can be viewed online: http://democracy.camden.gov.uk/ieDecisionDetails.aspx?Id=2907 . The measures forming Camden’s emergency transport response includes the introduction of a strategic ‘pop -up’ cycle lane network. More information on these ‘pop -up’ cycle lanes, including a ma p of the ‘pop -up’ cy cle network, can be found on the Council’s Making Travel Safer website, here: https://www.camden.gov.uk/making -travel -safer -in- camden?inheritRedirect=true#uoqx . The ‘pop-up’ cycling changes proposed on Chalk Farm Road , assessed within this equalities impact assessment, form part of this strategic ‘pop-up’ cycle lane network. 1.2 Summary of proposals The purpose of th e proposed scheme is to make it easier and safer to cycle along Chalk Farm Road (between the junctions with Castlehaven Road and Prince of Wales Road ), this will be done through introducing the following measures, also illustrated in the scheme drawing (Appendix B of the Chalk Farm Road Decision Report): 1.2.1 Cycle lanes It is proposed to provide 1.5 metre – 2 metre wide mandatory cycle lanes, o n either side of Chalk Farm Road between Prince of Wales Road and Castlehaven Road, protected by flexible wands. The width of these cycle lanes will vary along the corridor due to restricted road width. Mandatory cycle lanes are predominantly provided on either side of the carriage -way along the entire length of the corridor, between the junctions with Castlehaven Road and Prince of Wales Road. There are however, several locations where there are breaks in the cycle lane or where there are certain times wh ere the cycle lanes is shared with other uses, this is due to limited road width and competing demand for kerb -space in these locations. These locations are: - At the southern end, in the southbound direction, the cycle lanes will stop at Hartland Road, enabling southbound cyclists to use Hartland Road, then Hawley Road to head east to continue their journeys (southbound via Camden High Street not being permissible). - On the approach to the junction with Harmood Street, the southbound cycle lane stops shor t, due to a tree. Should the scheme be made permanent, the Council would look to remove and replace the tree, in order to allow continuity of the cycle lane. - In the northbound lane outside Camden Market, opposite the junction with Hartland Road, a timed lo ading bay (10.00 -12.00 and 14.00 -16.00, Monday to S aturday) and taxi rank (8pm to 4am Monday to Friday and 10am -4pm & 9pm -4am Saturday to Sunday) will be provided within the cycle lane. - The southbound cycle lane will stop just before and after Bus Stop CD on Haverstock Hill, outside Haverstock School. The proposed measures w ould narrow the remaining carriageway to a predominant width of 3.25 metres in each direction, with the carriageway going down to 3 metres in each direction where the road width is n arrower. In some lo cations, such as close to the A delaide Road and Crogsland Road junctions a greater road width would be maintained to minimize impact on the junction capacity. If the scheme were made permanent, it is proposed to narrow the carriage way i n these locations to 3.25m or less. Tracking shows that turning movements by heavy goods vehicles, buses and rubbish collection vehicles can be 3 performed at each side road and junction, at a slow speed. 1.2.2 Pedestrian Facilities Pedestrian islands w ould be removed at the two zebra crossings on the corridor (between the junctions with Ferdinand Street and Castlehaven Road). This is proposed in order to remove the pinch point for cyclists that these islands create and to preve nt cyclists from having to merge with motor traffic at these points. This is considered the right approach as it 1) removes a potential safety risk for cyclists (caused by having to merge with motor vehicles due to limited road width) and at the same time 2) maintains pedestrians’ priority to cross at zebra crossings. The crossing distances at these two zebra crossings are 9m and 11m, which officers consider to be acceptable distances. Furthermore, sight lines for pedestrians at these crossings are good. Th ese proposals will go through a Road Safety Audit (Stages 1,2 and 3), which will further identify if there are any road safety issues with the proposed removal of the islands at the zebra crossings. An ass essment of this proposal on the protected equalitie s groups is provided in, Sections 3.2 and 4.2. New signalised crossings w ould be introduced: - Outside the Roundhouse, replacing the existing informal crossing, - A new signalised pedestrian crossing will be provided in place of the signalised junction north of the Morrisons petrol station, more detail provided in Section 1.2.4 , On Chalk Farm Road, across the southern arm of the junction with Ferdinand Street, see S ection 1.2.4 , below. A small amount of footway loss (exact locations are shown in the attached drawings) is proposed to accommodate the cycle lanes and bus boarder waiting areas, sufficient footway width for social distancing by pedestrians will be retained. 1.2.3 Bus Stops Under the proposals, b us stops w ould be moved out further into the carriageway, this would also help protect bus journey times by preventing buses having to pull in and out of the kerbside. Bus boarder areas w ould be created ( the cycle lanes w ould run between the footway and bus stops) and the cycle lane w ould be raised to the pavement level at bus stops. This is proposed at all bus stops along the corridor, apart from Bus Stop CD, where cyclists w ould merge with t raffic, due to not enough road width for a bus boarder waiting area. Bus Stop CD, outside Haverstock School, w ould be maintained but the adjacent bus lane w ould be suspended to allow adequate carriageway width and continuity of cycle lanes on both side of the road. Bus Stop CE to be relocated 100m north of its existing location on Chalk Farm Road. This is due to its current proximity to the junction with Ferdinand Street and to improve capacity at this signalised junction. 1.2.4 Signalised Junctions Chalk Farm Road/ Ferdinand Street/ Juniper Crescent Junction It is proposed to introduce improvements at the Chalk Farm Road/ Ferdinand Street/ Juniper Crescent junction as part of the proposed scheme (this w ould be done using permanent traffic signals, re placing the temporary traffic signals currently in place). These improvements are proposed to make it easier to cycle through and walk across this junction and to facilitate the approved development at the Morrisons Site on Juniper Crescent. The junction c hanges would include: - introducing two -way traffic movement on the Juniper Crescent Arm of the Junction, 4 - removing the signalised junction currently in place on the exit of the Morrisons Petrol Station service road but retaining a signalised pedestrian cros sing across Chalk Farm Road, - introducing movement for cyclists only, across the junction between Juniper Crescent and Ferdinand Street, - an early release for cyclists on all arms of the junctions, - a new signalised pedestrian crossing introduced across the s outhern arm of the Chalk Farm Road junction. - pedestrian Countdown facilities w ould be introduced on all arms of the junction, - the island on the northern Chalk Farm Road arm of the junction, which currently contains a primary signal head, w ould be removed. Officers consider that the removal of this island and the introduction of Countdown facilities on all arms of the Ferdinand Street/ Juniper Crescent/ Chalk Farm Road junction would provide a safer arrangement for pedestrians. This is because it would encou rage pedestrians to cross in a single stage rather than waiting in the middle of the road, with moving traffic on either side; and makes it clear to pedestrians how much time they have to cross the road before the lights change See Sections 3.5 and 4.4, for further assessment of these signals proposals. Junctions between Crogsland Road and Adelaide Road No changes, at th e experimental stage, w ould be made to the signalised junctions between Crogsland Road and Adelaide Road. After 12 months of the experimental scheme, we would like – if circumstances then obtaining allow this – to consult on making further changes to these junctions as part of the Council’s consi deration as to whether the whole Chalk Farm Road scheme should be made permanent. 1.2.5 Parking/ Loading Under the proposals, p arking currently provided on the footway w ould be removed and, due to limited road width, w ould be allocated to the cycle lane. The majority of the parking and loading facilities along the corridor w ouldl be removed. On all adjacent side roads some of the existing resident’s parking bays w ouldl be converted into shared residents and pay -by-phone parking. . A timed loading bay ( operating between 10.00 – 12.00 and 14.00 – 16.00) and taxi rank (8pm to 4am Monday to Friday and 10am -4pm & 9pm -4am Saturday to Sunday ) outside Camden Market (opposite Hartland Road) would be retained and the road would narrow at this point to mark a wid e cycle lane where the loading bay sits completely inside it. 1.3 What is the decision maker being asked to decide? The Direc tor of Environment and Sustainability is asked to decide whether or not to approve the implementation , under an Experimental Traffic Order, of: 1) the proposed ‘pop -up’ cycle lane on Chalk Farm Road , which forms part of the Council’s transport response to the COVID -19 Pandemic , and 2) an improved junction (including specifically for pedestrians and cyclists) at Ferdinand Street, to facilitate the Morrison’s development at Ferdinand Street/Juniper Crescent. This Equalities Impact Assessment (EIA) is an appendix to the Chalk Farm Road Decision Report and will be used to inform the Direc tor of Environment and Sustainability ’s consideration as to whether or not to authorize the propos als. This EIA shows that most impacts on protected groups w ould be positive and that protected groups would be unlikely to be significantly negatively affected by the proposed changes on Chalk Farm Road . Further detail on this assessment is provided with this report. 5 Section 2: PLANNING YOUR EQUALITY ANALYSIS Question 2: Do those from protected groups benefit or will they experience specific and disp roportionate impacts? Will the re be any di rect or indi rect discrimination? Gather relevant equality data and information to show who will be affected by this decision and how. Set this out below. Include the results of any consultation or engagement. If you have identified any information gaps set out what these are. Equality Data This section of the EIA seeks to establish the wider equalities context in which the Chalk Farm Road proposals will be situated. This is done through looking at data for each of the protected equalities groups ( Age, Disability, Gender Reassignment, Pregnancy and Maternity, Race, Religion/Belief, Sex, and Sexual Orientation ). This data comes from the National Census, 2011 and focuses on London -wide data and data for the two wards that Chalk Farm Road runs through; Haverstock Ward and Camden Town with Primrose Hill Ward . Given the nature of the current emergency, it is not considered critical to gather exhaustive information on the equality data of the local populations of these three wards, However, Table 1, on page 7 summarises the information available, from the 2011 cens us, for residents of these two wards. COVID - 19 and Protected Groups Public Transport Capacity In response to the COVID -19 pandemic, capacity on public transport in London has been significantl y reduced in order to enable social distancing, whilst travelling by bus, train or tube; only 20% of previous levels of patronage can now be catered for, leaving Londoners, with a major shortfall in transportation options. Furthermore, free travel in London for under 18s has been suspended and over-60s have to pay a fare to travel at peak times on public transport . Data specifically on the impact of COVID -19 on the travel behavior of the nine protected groups is not currentl y available. However, it is very evident that the reduction in public transport capacity has had an impact on how all Londoners travel, including those with one or more of the protected equalities characteristics. Prior to the COVID -19 pandemic a number of the protected groups were particularly reliant upon walking and public transport as a key mode of travel within London, this includes young and older people, people with disabilities, women (including pregnant women and women with small children) and peop le identifying as BAME. It can, therefore, be surmised that there will have been a shift in the ways groups previously (pre -COVID -19) reliant upon public transport are now travelling, most likely with a shift towards more of a reliance upon walking and, po tentially, cycling too. Vehicle Usage Overall, the number of vehicles using Camden’s roads is down but speeding has increased as a minority of irresponsible drivers take advantage of quieter roads. Across London, during the lockdown period, some average s peeds were recorded at 37mph on 20mph roads. Locally, areas of Camden which already suffered from speeding problems have seen speed increases of as much as 13%. TfL have estimated that if all car -owning households switched their usual public transport journeys to car, some boroughs would see a near doubling in the number of private transport journeys, causing massive congestion and pollution issues. In Camden, this would be an increase in private transport trips of over 90%, in addition to an increase in car trips originating in other boroughs. 6 Increased Walking and Cycling The reduction in public transport capacity has resulted in more people taking up walking and cycling, it is surmised that this includes an increase in walking and cycling by people characterised by one (or more) of the nine protected groups. Early modelling by TfL has revealed that as the lockdown eases the could be more than a 10-fold increase in kilometres cycled, and up to five times the amount of walking, compared to pre -COVID lev els. We have already started to see this reflected in Camden. Weekend cycle flows at the three automatic cycle count point sites, within the Borough, have recorded an average increase of 120% in cycling levels this May compared to last. Improving the ability for Londoners, including the groups protected by the Equality act, to cycle to their destination is seen as a critical part of the Covid -19 transport response by Camden Council, Transport for London and the Department of Transport. T o this end, rapid deployment of temporary protected bicycle lanes is being rolled out across London, including Chalk Farm Road . Social distancing For the sake of brevity, this analysis does not go into detail about the relative risks and/or benefits betwe en different groups in the community of facilitating social distancing (and the reduction of risk of transmitting or being infected by the virus). However, in general it is understood that COVID -19 poses a greater health threat to people of an older age, and those with pre -existing health conditions and some disabilities. It is not known whether COVID -19 has a significant negative impact on pregnant women, unborn children and young babies however, as people with these characteristics are often vulnerable to negative impacts of viral diseases, it can be supposed that the social distancing measures are likely to be of greater benefit to these individuals, relative to the general population. There is also growing evidence that people of BAME characteristics a re more susceptible to the COVID - 19 virus, even once accounting for any correlative socio -economic factors and the propensity for BAME groups to live in larger multi -aged family groups. Consultation and pre -engagement The decision taken by the Cabinet Member for a Sustainable Camden on 13th May 2020 granted permission for a revised approach to Camden’s historical consultation activities before introducing street -based measures on an experimental/trial basis, in response to the COVID -19 situation. In kee ping with this approval, the proposed changes on Chalk Farm Road will be installed on a temporary basis under an Experimental Traffic Order (ETO). In line with legal requirements, a statutory consultation will be carried out on these proposals in advance o f the ETO being drawn up. In advance of this statutory consultation, officers wrote to Ward Councillors ( Haverstock and Camden Town with Primrose Hill Wards ) and statutory consultees sharing details of the proposals and seeking their preliminary comments o n the proposed, temporary ‘pop -up’ cycle lanes on Chalk Farm Road . No comments were raised specifically relating to the nine characteristics protected by the Equality Act, 2010. The proposed rapid -response measures for Chalk Farm Road have not been the su bject of a formal consultation or engagement, and so no information of this kind is available for analysis regarding the impact of the proposed measures on characteristics of protected groups. However, as stated above, statutory consultees and Ward Counci llors have been canvassed for their views; this includes external organisations and internal consultees within Camden. Messages from the public on how Camden Council should respond within the transport setting to the social distancing requirements have bee n received on the Camden Safe Travel Commonplace website (https://camdensafetravel.commonplace.is/ ), this included individual comments requesting protected improvements on Chalk Farm Road . 7 None of the comments made about Chalk Farm Road specifically mentioned the equalities protected characteristic s. The experimental scheme will run for 18 months and stakeholders are able to comment at any time on the changes implemented. The Council would like to carry out a full public consultation after the experimental scheme has run for 12 months and will take a decision as to whether it can do this nearer the time, in light of the circumstances then prevailing. The results from th is consultation , if held, would – together with data from other sources (e.g., monitoring data - inform the Council’s consideration as to whether, at the end of the 18-month experiment, the changes should be made permanent. Should a full public consultation on the proposals be carried out, this Equalities Impact Assessment document would be updated to reflect feedback mentioning the nine protected characteristics received during the trial period and any responses and comments made in response to the equality and diversity monitoring que stions that will be asked in the public consultation questionnaire. Document Title: housing department policies regarding visits to tenants
Document Text: Date: 23/11/2022 Case reference : CAM4146 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 29/10/2022 about the housing department policies regarding visits to tenants. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: I request the following information concerning the current policies of the Housing Dept. regarding visits and check ups to tenants of the LB Camden. 1.  What are the current policies of the LB Camden's Housing Department for visits and check ups by Housing Officers and Staff and/or Patch Managers to tenants of the LB Camden? Carrying out visits is central to everyday housing practice across housing services, for example surveyors carry out visits to check the condition of a property, the private sector housing team carry out visits to make sure that private landlords are meeting their responsibilities to the their tenants and staff in housing needs teams carry out home visits to verify the detail applicants provided on their housing applications. This enquiry has asked for a response from managers in the Council’s Landlord Service so that will be the focus of this response. Camden’s landlord services are divided into different teams with specialisms which include neighbourhood housing officers working in eight neighbourhood housing teams, two rent teams, a moving homes team, welfare rights team and housing investigations team. All of these teams carry out home visits for different reasons. Visits are a necessary part of managing the Council’s housing stock effectively and because visits are essential activity, and established practice across all housing providers, it is not necessary to have one written policy setting this out. Examples of typical visits that housing management staff carry out include: ·       Visits that enable vulnerable or mobility impaired tenants to access services. ·       Welfare checks ·       Property inspections including inspections of communal areas. These often relate to fire safety concerns or other risk but may also be because there are concerns that a tenant may not be coping ·       To carry out a noise test following a complaint ·       To investigate a report of sub-letting or suspected abandonment ·       To try and engage with a tenant in rent arrears when other attempts at contact have failed In addition neighbourhood housing teams are currently exploring the possibility of a visiting programme during which housing officers will aim to visit all our tenanted homes. This will begin shortly with a small pilot on each housing officer patch to consider resident feedback and evaluate the impact on other areas of work. Guidance, which is currently in draft form, will be concluded after the pilot. 2. When were these policies made and by whom? Neighbourhood housing teams were asked to carry out a visiting programme in June 2022 by the Director of Housing. 3. I request to be supplied with a copy or copies of the relevant policies. The purpose of the scheme was included in a report to district management committees in September. The relevant section of that report is set out in the box below: Our priorities for the rest of 2022 and 2023 Alongside our pilots that will test the impact of focussed rent and voids roles on performance, landlord services will prioritise a programme in which neighbourhood housing officers (NHOs) will set out to visit every tenant. A visiting programme of this scale has not been carried out before in Camden. The purpose is to: ·       Respond to feedback from Tenants and Residents Associations that they value seeing their NHO out as a physical presence in the community ·       To inspect every council home to identify issues that increase risk to the occupiers or their neighbours ·       To engage with our tenants individually to see if there is any help the Council, or our partners, can provide. ·       To carry out a tenancy audit to ensure the people living in our homes are the tenants the property was let to. 4.  If there are no current policies, I would request confirmation of this. Not applicable. Further Information: We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Document Text: Date: 07/09/2020 Case reference : CAM353 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 14/08/2020 about payments received under Section 106 planning agreements .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end which explain how and why it applies. In accordance with the Freedom of Information Act, please can you advise of all payments received under Section 106 planning agreements: • The value of the payment • The purpose of the payment • The amount of the payment that has been spent • The amount that has been committed but not spent • The amount that has not been committed or spent • The amount that has been repaid • The reason for the repayment Please provide these details for the following years: 2017-2018 2018-2019 2019-2020 Please also provide details of any unspent money that dates back to before 2017-18.The Council will not process this request as it falls under an exception in the EIR 2004 because the cost or burden of dealing with your request is excessive. Refusal Notice The exception that applies is: regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable Guidance produced by the office of the information Commissioner states that “in assessing whether the cost, or the amount of staff time involved in responding to a request, is sufficient to render a request manifestly unreasonable the FOIA fees regulations may be a useful starting point.” We are refusing your request on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit".  This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We have calculated that it will take over 35 hours  to comply with your request because: this request is for a very large amount of financial transactional information● each transaction would need to interpreted and be provided with a full explanation● In applying this exception the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004. The public interest argument for releasing this information is:- it would improve the transparency and accountability of the Council’s dealing with these transactions● The public interest arguments for withholding the information are:- processing this request would be provide a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council● this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities, and:● it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s the provision of services to the public●It is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request● It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. We are sorry to inform you that the total cost is well above the appropriate limit for local government and in light of the balance of public interest the request can is refused under regulation 12(4)b of the EIR 2004 as outlined above. Advice and assistance Information may be able to be disclosed for a small period of time to provide a representative sample. Document Text: Date: 18/03/2025 Ref: CAM9666 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 18/02/2025 about the number of housing applicants on the housing register due to fleeing domestic abuse . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. 1. The number of housing applicants on the housing register with the council due to fleeing domestic abuse in 2024/2025, 2023/2024, and 2022/2023. a. Of these applicants, and for each year, please provide the number who were initially placed the following categories: i. Band A: Greatest need for housing ii. Band B: High need for housing iii. Band C: Medium need for housing iv. Band D: Low need for housing v. Band E: Lowest need for housing 2. The number of housing applicants on the register fleeing from domestic abuse who were housed by the council in emergency/hotel accommodation in 2024/2025, 2023/2024, and 2022/2023. 3. The number of housing applicants on the register fleeing from domestic abuse who were housed by the council in long-term accommodation in 2024/2025, 2023/2024, and 2022/2023. We are withholding this information as we consider the following exemption applies. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. Once the Council has ascertained that the appropriate limit will be reached it does not need to estimate the time that would be needed for the remainder of the request, there is no obligation on the Council to work on a request until the 18 hours limit is reached. Once it is reasonably calculated that the limit will be reached the entire request may be refused. Question 2 asks for the number of housing applicants on the housing register fleeing from domestic abuse, housed in emergency/hotel accommodation. We do not hold this information in an easily accessible format. This is because the council is undergoing a large data migration project that is affecting our capacity to access and analyse statutory homelessness support data efficiently. The migration process adds an extra layer of complexity and time to the task of retrieving data, if held. In the period July-September 2023, 633 households were identified as being in temporary accommodation. To locate the data requested in question 2 would require a council officer generate a report of households currently housed in emergency/hotel accommodation, manually read each case note to pinpoint the specific data requested. Based on a sample of 10 cases where some case notes were unclear, it took approx. 3 minutes per case to gather and analyse the data. We have calculated to provide the information for all 633 households in the quarter year would take approx. 31.65 hours. To review data for the entire year would take approx. four times as long and total in excess of 125 hours. This exceeds the 18 hours’ appropriate limit set by the Act. Advice and Assistance We hold information about the statutory housing register data. We suggest you submit questions 1 and 3 as a new request and make a new request for question 2 in a few months when the data migration is completed, and the data can be extracted more quickly. Document Title: redacted payments
Document Text: Date: 24/07/2025 Case reference : CAM10605 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 04/07/2025 about redacted payments. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 / Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: According to published data, Camden Council made over £58 million in payments to unnamed recipients in the 2024/25 financial year. Of particular concern, more than £1 million of that was categorised under Children and Learning, with both the recipient’s name and the payment purpose redacted. We understand redactions may in some cases be justified, but we note this comes in the context of: The Council’s 2022/23 accounts being disclaimed by the external auditor.• A continued failure to publish the Council’s expected anti-fraud report for 2024/25.• The audits of Camden’s 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22 financial statements have been signed off with unqualified opinions. Given the delays from previous years, there was insufficient time to conduct a full audit of the 2022/23 and 2023/24 Council accounts before the backstop dates that were issued by the government for all audits to be complete.  These audit delays were due to a range of issues and have affected most of the local government sector and the reason the government issued a backstop date.   As such, the external auditor Forvis Mazars has issued a disclaimed opinion on the Council accounts for 2022/23 and 2023/24. However, the audit of the Pension Fund accounts being more straightforward, Forvis Mazars completed a full audit for 2023/24. Due to receiving a disclaimed audit opinion in 2022/23, as expected, the auditor was unable to gain sufficient assurance on the prior year comparator data, and as such has issued a qualified opinion in 2023/24. The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) and Ministry of Housing and Local Government (MHCLG) have stated it should be made clear that local authorities should not be adversely judged that such an opinion has been issued. In plain terms, a disclaimer means that they have been unable to form an opinion. In this instance, the reason for this will be the limitation of scope imposed by statute (not by the local authority).  On 9 June, the NAO issued its guidance on rebuilding assurance - LARRIG 06. The LARRIG places emphasis on enhanced auditor risk assessments, and rebuilding assurance on carrying values of property, plant and equipment (PPE) and reserves. Additionally, it acknowledges the necessity for auditors to prioritise their resources, recognising that not all rebuilding assurance procedures can be completed within a single year.  The council is working closely with its external auditors, Forvis Mazars, to understand the impact of this guidance on rebuilding assurance and how long it would take. The LARRIG guidance issued emphasises that auditors need to consider specific circumstances for each authority following the guidance and places. Forvis Mazars is assessing this recently issued guidance and will be reporting to the committee on their planned approach to rebuilding assurance for the London borough of Camden . Camden 2024/25 Counter Fraud report is published here : 2024-25 Annual Counter Fraud Report.pdf We also note Camden’s own Data Charter, which commits the authority to transparency, accountability, and ethical use of data — especially where large sums of public money are involved. We therefore request the following: 1. Is the Council confident that none of the redacted payments in 2024/25 are fraudulent? If so, what is the evidential basis for that confidence? The Council relies on its framework of governance, risk management and internal control to minimise the risk of fraudulent activity.  Internal controls are in place in relation to payments made to third parties including checks on the validity of any third-party organisation and their payment details.    While controls are in place, no system can guarantee zero fraud. The council takes fraud extremely seriously and operates a zero-tolerance policy. It is fully committed to preventing, detecting, and investigating all instances of fraud, and will take all necessary steps to hold offenders accountable.2. On what policy or legal grounds does the Council redact the names of beneficiaries for payments over £500? Please cite any FOIA exemptions or internal guidance relied upon. The over £500 publication and the redactions in order to comply with data protection is discussed and agreed with data protection officers in Camden. Certain payments are excluded or redacted under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) and Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA)/GDPR. Exemptions Under FOIA or Local Government Transparency Code are: Councils are required to publish payments over £500 under the Local Government Transparency Code, but the code allows redactions if: It’s legally required (e.g. personal data)• It’s not in the public interest to disclose• Disclosure could cause harm• Council redactions to over £500 Payments include: 1. Personal Data (GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018) Payments to individuals (e.g. landlords, carers, foster parents, private citizens) are often redacted to protect names, addresses, or other identifying details.• Example: A housing benefit payment to a private landlord may be redacted if naming them could identify tenants.• 2. Commercial Sensitivity (FOI Act Section 43) If publishing payment details would harm a company's competitive position, councils may redact: Contract values• Supplier names (rare, but possible in sensitive procurement)• Especially common with contracts involving negotiated rates or confidential terms.• 3. Legal or Investigatory Matters Payments relating to legal claims, internal investigations, or insurance settlements may be redacted to avoid prejudicing outcomes.•4. Safeguarding / Security Payments linked to domestic abuse shelters, children’s services, or vulnerable adults may be anonymized to protect those involved.• 5. Exemptions Under FOIA or Local Government Transparency Code Councils are required to publish payments over £500 under the Local Government Transparency Code, but the code allows redactions if: It’s legally required (e.g. personal data)• It’s not in the public interest to disclose• Disclosure could cause harm• In conclusion, it is not possible to provide additional information regarding the redacted entries in the over £500 publication, as doing so would conflict with data protection obligations. 3. In relation to the £1 million+ in redacted Children and Learning payments, please provide the precise purpose of each payment — identifying the activity, service, or function funded — given that the beneficiary name is already withheld Please see the response above. Document Text: Date: 21/01/2022 Case reference : CAM2673 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 29/12/2021 about pensions Scheme investments and investment decision minutes .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answers which explains how and why they apply. Local Government Pensions Scheme: 1. A list of every company that has been invested into using the pension funds since March 2020. 2. The exact amount that has been invested into these companies since March 2020. This information is exempt. Please see the exemption notice set out below. 3. Minutes from any and all meetings related to investment decisions since March 2020. This information is already publicly available - meetings for Pension Committee are available on our website.  Please enter this link into your web browser: https://democracy.camden.gov.uk/ieListMeetings.aspx?CId=652&Year=0 Refusal Notice The exemptions that apply are: section 43: commercial interests The information is withheld because section 43(2) (Prejudicial to commercial interests) applies to it. Disclosure would have a prejudicial effect. The business of fund managers is to pick a selection of stocks and other assets to achieve a certain outcome for their clients, in this case the LBC Pension Fund. If their selection of stocks and the amounts invested were publicly available, then there would be no need for the Pension Fund or other institutional investors to use their services, and the fund managers would go out of business. As only some fund managers will be obliged by this request to make their stock selections public, then their competitors who are not so obliged will gain a competitive advantage, damaging the commercial interests of those whose stock selections were made public. In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: Improving transparency in decision making ● Ensuring value for money. ● The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: It is not in the public interest to disclose information that would be likely to damage the commercial interests of a company, as this could lead to financial problems for the company and/or job losses It is not in the public interest for commercially sensitive information about one company to be released, when information about other companies is not released, as this puts one company at a commercial disadvantage. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. section 41: information was provided in confidence This information is withheld because it is exempt under section 41. This absolute exemption applies where the information was provided to the public authority in confidence. The information was received from a third party. This information is covered by a common law duty of confidence and releasing this information would constitute a breach of confidence. In other words, if we disclosed the information the provider or a third party could take legal action. Document Text: Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 31 December 2018 and updated 06 January 2019 about planning application 2017/0911/P. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (EIR2004). Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: Response A. Our application 2017/0911/P requires a s106 affordable housing agreement, received 14 consultation responses including from the Fortune Green and West Hampstead Neighbourhood Development Forum and Councillor Lorna Russell. Q1. Can you please tell me when this application went to the Members Briefing Panel? It was scheduled to go to the panel on 02 October 2018 but did not make the schedule . Q2. If it did go to the Members Briefing Panel, please provide us with the date and the Officers Draft Committee Repo rt. Please see above and the enclosed information. Q3. If it did not go to the Members Briefing Panel; why did it not go to the Members Briefing Panel? This is because the application consisted of a scheme which would have been required to be seen at commi ttee (more than 5x units/ financial contributions - prior to changes in the scheme of delegation regarding financial contributions in 2018) and n ot under delegated approval . B: Planning Committee The Camden web site is very explicit about the types of applications that must go to committee: Planning committee: [extract from the Camden Web site] Information and Records Management Corporate Services London Borough of Camden Town Hall Judd Street London WC1H 9JE Phone: 020 7974 7857 camden.gov.uk Date: Our reference: Email: 24 January 2019 FOI12240 foi@camden.gov.uk “Applications that cannot be decided under delegated powers (that is, approximately 10 per cent of all applications) are made by members of our Planning Commit tee. These typically include applications for: [1] major developments where 10 or more new homes will be built or the floorspace will be over 1000m² [2] some minor developments where there will be an increase in floorspace [3] changes of use to businesses serving hot food, for example, restaurants, takeaways etc. [4] demolition or part demolition of listed buildings or buildings in a conservation area [5] any application which is not covered by the policies in our Local Plan [6] most applications which would involve making a legal agreement under Section 106 of the Town and Country Planning Act” Unequivocally, provisions 2 and 5 apply directly to this application. However, during the later stages of our application the case officer wrote to tell me: On 3 Oct 2017 08:39 he wrote: [Extract] "I wrote the application up for Members’ Briefing, but unfortunately due to the affordable housing contribution it has to go to committee. The next committee is on 26th October and the report will need some minor tweaks to change it from a delegated report to a committee report, but it will be ready in time." Later on 25 October 2017 at 10:37 he wrote: [Extract] "Unfortunately, we only send cases to committee that are being recommended for approval." Q4: Can you explain t his 25th of October Email please? If the application cannot be delegated and according the case officer it cannot be sent to the committee – how could it ever be decided at all? If there is another method of deciding an application I am not aware of, can y ou direct me to the relevant policy document please? We can clarify that refusals are delegated, and attach the committee terms of reference which only capture recommendations for approval under clause 3 (attached). C. Call over meeting We were informed by the case officer that the application was presented at a pre - committee “call over” meeting some time between 3rd and the 12th October 2017. Can you confirm that this meeting actually took place please?; was our application discussed and for how long, who was at the meeting and any minuets you are at liberty to provide? Document Text: Date: 11/04/2024 Case reference : CAM7197London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 29/02/2024 about data breaches.  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council will neither confirm nor deny if it holds the information requested. Please see the refusal notice below. You clarified your request by email received 13/03/2024: I can confirm I am requesting information about external cyber-attacks and attempts to breach data rather than employees committing ‘internal data breaches’. You requested: Under the Freedom of Information Act, I would like to request the following information. 1. The number of data breaches your council has been victim to in the 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023 calendar years. 2. How many people were affected by each data breach. 3. What type of data breach each one was. A data breach is when sensitive, protected or confidential data is copied, transmitted, viewed, stolen, altered or used by an individual who is unauthorised to do so. It includes: - Malware attack - Phishing attack - Brute force attack - SQL injection attack - Business Email Compromise (BEC) - Stolen information.We are often asked questions about malware, ransom ware, attacks causing data breaches, and the like. We are asked if we have had any cyber-attacks, and how many, if they have succeeded and what actions we have taken. We can be asked if we have been the victim of ransom ware, whether attacks were successful, if we paid ransoms, how often, when, to whom and for how much. We have decided that we do not tell requesters if we hold this information or not. Under Freedom Information Act this is called a ‘neither confirm nor deny’ response. We can do this under section 31 of the act.  We have explained why below. Please note that we would, however, inform the relevant data subjects if their data has been seriously compromised by a data breach. Refusal Notice section 31(3) – Law Enforcement The council believes that telling requesters if we hold information about cyber- attacks, ransom ware or related data breaches etc., will cause damage. This is because saying if we do or do not hold information would give cyber criminals insight into vulnerabilities which may, or may not, exist. This would we likely to damage our cyber security systems and plans. Therefore, we use the exemption in section 31(3). This allows us to refuse to confirm or deny if the information is held. In other words, the council is allowed to refuse to say if it holds information about this or not. When we use a neither confirm or deny response you should not assume that we do, or do not, hold any information. Section 31(3) is a qualified exemption which means we have to do a public interest test where we compare the public interest for and against disclosing. The public interest test is not about whether we should disclose any information that we might hold. It is a test of whether we should say if we hold the information or not. Factors in favour of confirming or denying if we hold relevant information. It would help transparency and accountability of the council.• It would reassure people about whether our systems are vulnerable or not.• It would provide information about how effective our security systems are.•Factors against confirming or denying if we hold relevant information. Saying if we hold information would provide information about how effective our security systems are. This would be likely to give cyber criminals insights into the strengths of the council’s cyber security and any potential weaknesses that may exist. This would increase the chances of cyberattacks. One of the reasons that cyber security measures are in place is to protect the integrity of personal and sensitive personal information so increasing the chances of an attack would have potentially serious repercussions.• If the council confirms that it holds a lot of information then this could show criminals its systems are particularly vulnerable, encouraging attacks.• If the council confirms that it holds little information this could either show it has poor reporting and recording procedures which will encourage an attack, or it could show it has robust procedures which could encourage an attack to try out criminals’ new techniques or could encourage criminals to target other councils’ systems which would increase crime elsewhere.• There is public interest in complying with our legal obligations to keep personal data secure and to act appropriately which includes keeping areas confidential where necessary.• We believe that the balance of public interest lies in upholding the exemption and not confirming or denying if we hold this information. Further Information We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Any such use will be reported to the ICO as a breach of General Data Protection Regulations and the Privacy and Electronic Communication Regulations. Document Text: Date: 09/09/2024 Ref: CAM8372 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 21/08//2024 about Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) and related matters. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response Your 2 amalgamated requests were: Request 1 I am submitting a formal request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 to obtain information concerning the culture, practices, and policies within Camden Council's Special Educational Needs (SEN) team, particularly over the past year from August 2023 to August 2024. Specifically, I request the following information: 1. **Internal Communications and Policies**: - Copies of any internal communications, directives, or policies issued within the past year that address: - The approach or strategy for interacting with parents of children with SEN. - Any specific guidance or strategies related to addressing concerns or disputes with parents, including communications that reference defamation, blame, or challenges to the credibility of parents. 2. **Complaints and Investigations**: - Details of any complaints made by parents, staff, or external professionals regarding the behaviour or conduct of Camden SEN team members, including allegations of defamation. - Records of any investigations or reviews conducted in response to these complaints, including the outcomes and any changes in policy or practice that resulted. 3. **Interactions with External Parties**: - Documentation of communications between Camden SEN team members and councilors, MPs, or external service providers that discuss or reference parents, London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . Request 2 I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 regarding the practices and communications of the Camden Special Educational Needs (SEN) department. Specifically, I am requesting the following information: 1. **Instances of Acknowledgment from August 2023-August 2024**: - Records of any instances where the Camden SEN team has formally acknowledged its own failures or shortcomings, particularly in relation to: - Delays in finalizing Education, Health, and Care Plans (EHCPs). - Failures to commission the provisions outlined in EHCPs within the specified timeframes. - Failures to meet legal deadlines, including those related to EHCPs and Tribunal processes. 2. **Communications on Accountability**: - Copies of any internal or external communications, reports, or statements where the Camden SEN team has accepted responsibility for such failures, rather than attributing these issues to parents or guardians. 3. **Policies and Procedures**: - Any policies, procedures, or guidelines within the Camden SEN team that outline how the department should handle and respond to failures in meeting legal obligations, particularly in relation to communicating with parents and addressing accountability. 4. **Complaints and Responses**: - Information on any complaints made by parents regarding the SEN team’s failure to meet its legal obligations, along with records of how these complaints were addressed, including any acknowledgments of fault or responsibility by the SEN team. The council holds the information requested but is refusing your request under section 14(1). Section 14(1) refusal notice. The council is refusing your request as it considers that it is vexatious. The council has reason to believe that you are acting together with a number of other requesters as part of a campaign to disrupt the council and particularly the SEND service by the volume of FOI requests around this subject. We have noted an increase in requests around SEND in August and early September which is greater than the normal number. We have also noted an unusual number originating from the ‘WhatDoTheyKnow’ website where it is known that requesters may use pseudonyms to hide their actual identity. There are other features in the requests such as content and style that provide evidence that this is not a coincidental increase but a campaign. A number of requests contain allegations about individual named members of staff, with accusations which are unjustifiably personal and abusive. The staff named in requests have been upset and distressed by such allegations and personal attacks. There is evidence that the requester and those acting with them are using the FOI process not to gain information but to undertake a campaign against individual council officers. In doing this, it damages the reputation of the Freedom of Information legislation itself, particularly as they are made on a public website. Handling the requests place a disproportionate burden in terms of work required to locate, collate and extract information, and in disruption to services. The large number of multiple-part requests submitted in a short space of time have the result of putting a disproportionate burden on a small number of staff in the service area who handle such tasks. This disrupts their day-to-day work and has caused anxiety due to the volume and nature of the requests. Those who are part of the campaign have also engaged in frequent emails to the service around these issues as well as complaints. The council has already required the input of senior officers to handle these matters, disrupting normal service delivery for the SEND area, legal services, and the Data Protection Advice Team. Whilst the council acknowledges that there may be some serious purpose in the concerns raised in the requests, the wording, the overlapping nature, the mingling of requests for information with complaints and allegations, show that any such serious purpose is outweighed by the vexatious nature of the requests. The council therefore believes that handling this request would cause a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption and distress that will strain council resources and get in the way of delivering mainstream services and answering legitimate requests. Therefore, the council has refused this request as vexatious. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 18/09/2024 about contracts details.   We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and/or the Environmental Information Regulations 2004  Response The council does not holds the information requested: Please provide me with the following information: Details of all contracts your authority currently holds with any of the following companies: - Celotex - Kingspan - Arconic - Arconic Architectural Products SAS - Saint-Gobain - Exova - Warringtonfire - Harley Facades - Rydon - Real Group For each contract held with any of the above, please list when the contract was awarded, its value, its purpose and when the contract is due to expire. We do not hold this information.  This is because we don’t have contracts, awarded by Procurement, with any of those companies. As some of the information not held is environmental, we have to comply with a technicality and tell you that because it is not held it is excepted under Regulation 12 (4)(a) of the EIR 2004.  The Information Commissioner does not require a public interest test where the information is not held. Further Information We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Any such use will be reported to the ICO as a breach of General Data Protection Regulations and the Privacy and Electronic Communication Regulations. Why not check our Portal Open Data Camden before making a new request as your question may already be answered by a previous FOI response or in one of our many useful and interesting datasets. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. Once the council has ascertained that the appropriate limit will be reached it does not need to estimate the time that would be needed for the remainder of the request, there is no obligation on the council to work on a request until the 18 hours limit is reached. Once it is reasonably calculated that the limit will be reached the entire request may be refused. Essential repairs allowances are offered to tenants who must decant due to essential repairs. The allowance covers the costs of carpets and curtains and are adjusted by property bedroom size and by whether the decant is temporary or permanent. Tenants under 59 years old leaving a 2-bedroom home receive £1,500 per bedroom released, plus a £500 one- off payment if moving via a mutual exchange. Under the Community Investment Programme for new housing developments, when tenants move into a new build, the developers agreed offer to the council may include provision of new large white goods such as refrigerators and washing machines. For housing applicants who have been awarded Violence/Harassment points and have moved, allowances are offered by bedroom size. • 1 Bed or Studio Flat: £110 • 2 Bed Flat: £215 • 3 Bed Flat or more: £325 Response to Q14 Information about how the council determines rent rates and policies, is already publicly available. Please enter this link into your web browser: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/direction-on-the-rent-standard-from-1-april- 2020/policy-statement-on-rents-for-social-housing. As the information is already reasonably accessible elsewhere, it is exempt under the absolute exemption in Section 21. Document Title: Co2 emissions and Trees
Document Text: Date: 27/10/2023 Ref: CAM6271 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 18/10/2023 about Co2 emissions and Trees. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) 2004. Response The council holds some of the information requested. 1. What are the estimated overall CO2 emissions in the Borough? 2. What is the trend of CO2 emissions in the Borough? Do you have figures for each of the last 20 years? Please provide the figures you have over that period. Local authority CO2 data is available on the Government website ; see the link below. It only goes back to 2005. UK local authority and regional carbon dioxide emissions national statistics: 2005 to 2019 - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk) 3. Do you have a record of the total amount of green space in the borough and how that has changed over the last 20 years? We do not have a figure for the total amount of green space as this can be defined in a number of different ways. The most recent published information regarding the amount of public open space in the borough is the 2014 Camden Open Space, Sport and Recreatio n Study via the following link: https://www.camden.gov.uk/documents/20142/15817034/CD2.5+Open+Space+Sport+Recreation +Study+2014.pdf/4ce694bd-f292-b73f-d061-d0150ea3eb5a . This identified 588.8 ha of open space provision. It includes some sites without public access, but not private gardens or some smaller green spaces. More up to date records are maintain by GiGL ( Greenspace Information for Greater London CIC - GIGL ) who hold data on the amount of green space across London, including Camden. 4. Do you have a tree planting strategy? Yes. https://www.camden.gov.uk/documents/20142/5268201/Camden+Tre e+Planting+Strategy.pdf 5. Do you have a carbon sequestration policy? 6. Document Title: the Local Authority recent response (April 2025) to the Department for Education’s SEN2 data collection
Document Text: Date: 11/07/2025 Ref: CAM10089 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 14/04/2025 about the Local Authority recent response (April 2025) to the Department for Education’s SEN2 data collection. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. A copy of your local authorities most recent response (April 2025) to the Department for Education’s SEN2 data collection. If possible, please provide the data in the format it was originally submitted (such as a spreadsheet or data file). I am specifically requesting the full dataset submitted, including the figures provided for each of the relevant fields, as part of the annual statutory return. We are withholding all of the requested information due to the highly sensitive nature of the dataset, which contains over 15,000 lines of personally identifiable data distributed across multiple data tables. This includes the names of children and young people with EHCPs, along with their date of birth, sex, ethnicity, home address postcodes and unique pupil numbers (UPNs). The structure of the dataset prevents effective anonymisation without compromising the integrity of the embedded data. The dataset covers requests, assessments, named plans, and placements. We consider the following exemptions apply. Refusal notices: Section 40(2): Personal information The council considers that to disclose the personal data requested would not be in accordance with data protection legislation and therefore we have withheld all of the information under the absolute exemption in Section 40(2). London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk The exemption states that personal data requested may be withheld when to release it would be a breach of the requirements of data protection law which is the UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018. The information withheld is personal information because it allows living individuals to be identified. The council considers that it would be a breach of the General Data Protection Regulation article 5 requirements of fairness and proportionality to publish this personal information in a FOI request. In doing this we have considered the legitimate public interest in disclosure against the interests of the data subject/s and concluded that in the circumstances disclosure would contravene the data protection requirements of fairness and proportionality particularly considering that Freedom of Information responses are public documents and published to the world and not provided just to the requester. Section 38: Health and Safety (1) Information is exempt if its disclosure under this Act would or would be likely to: (a) endanger the physical or mental health of any individual, or (b) endanger the safety of any individual. After careful consideration, we have determined that releasing postcode- level address data could pose a risk to the safety of individuals, as these are residential addresses of children, young people, and their families. Disclosure could enable identification and location of individuals, potentially leading to distress or harm. This is because Freedom of Information requests are published publicly and not limited to the original requester. Therefore, the potential impact of releasing such data into the public domain is significant. Public Interest Test As Section 38 is a qualified exemption, we are required to apply the public interest test to determine whether the information should be disclosed. Factors in favour of disclosure: • There is a genuine public interest in promoting transparency and accountability within public authorities. Disclosure of information cans support public understanding of decision-making processes and the delivery of public services. (Medium weight). Factors in favour of withholding: • The information requested includes home address postcodes of children and young people with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs). Disclosure of this data could enable individuals to be identified and located, thereby posing a significant risk to their physical and mental wellbeing. (High weight). • The individuals concerned are particularly vulnerable, and the release of such sensitive information could cause distress, anxiety, or harm. (High weight). • There is no wider public interest in the specific information requested that would outweigh the potential harm (Medium weight). We have carefully considered the balance of factors and conclude that the public interest in maintaining the exemption outweighs the public interest in disclosure. The potential harm to individuals resulting from the release of this information is substantial and would not be justified by any corresponding benefit to the public. Therefore, the information is being withheld under Section 38(1)(a) of the Act. Section 22: Information intended for future publication The information requested is held by the council however, we are applying the qualified exemption under Section 22(2) of the Act. This exemption applies because the information is intended for future publication, and it would not be reasonable to release it prior to the scheduled publication date. The Department for Education is responsible for analysing and publishing comparative summary tables for all local education authorities in England. This data is released annually in June. In applying this exemption, we have considered the public interest in both disclosing and withholding the information. Public interest arguments in favour of disclosure: • Enhancing transparency in decision-making processes. (Medium weight) • Promoting accountability of the Council. (Medium weight) • Supporting value for money in public services. (Medium weight) • Encouraging public engagement with the Council’s work. (Medium weight) Public interest arguments in favour of withholding: • The information is scheduled for publication as part of an established process, and early release would disrupt this schedule. (High weight). • Premature disclosure could pre-empt decisions that are the responsibility of the Department for Education. (High weight) We have concluded that the public interest in maintaining the exemption outweighs the interest in early disclosure. Therefore, the information will be withheld at this time. In line with our duty to provide advice and assistance, you may find the most recent published data helpful. It is available at the following link: Education, health and care plans: England 2024 - GOV.UK. Document Title: dyslexia diagnoses and assessments in Camden schools
Document Text: Date: 13/05/2025 Ref: CAM9790 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 03/03/2025 about dyslexia diagnoses and assessments in Camden schools. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: We are keen to understand the current policies and practices regarding the assessment of dyslexia amongst Local Education Authorities. As part of our ongoing efforts to support individuals with dyslexia, we aim to gather comprehensive information to better inform our advocacy and support services. 1. Do the professionals working for your LA assess and identify dyslexia? Camden Educational Psychologist Service (EPS) evaluates and identifies ‘specific learning difficulties (SpLD)’ and ‘significant literacy difficulties.’ We use these terms to describe children young people who meet the criteria for conditions such as dyslexia, dyscalculia and dysgraphia. 2. Do you provide Practice Guidance or a policy for schools which sets out expectations for identifying and supporting dyslexic children? We do not currently offer practice guidance or a formal policy for schools. Our goal is to collaborate with local schools, professionals and partners working within the sector. Through consultation, we aim to establish a shared approach, unified terminology and consistent support for all children facing literacy challenges regardless of severity across Camden settings. 3. Do you provide Practice Guidance or a policy for schools which sets out expectations for identifying and supporting children with literacy difficulties? Please see the response to questions 1 & 2 above. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 4. What terminology do you use to describe children in your schools who experience difficulties acquiring literacy skills. Recent research indicate that the term ‘dyslexia’ is often too narrowly defined to encompass all children and young people who face challenges in learning to read and write. We also recognise that there is no universally accepted definition of ‘dyslexia’ within international peer-reviewed studies. As a result, we use the term ‘significant literacy difficulties’ to describe students who meet the criteria. Our approach prioritises the early identification of all children struggling to acquire literacy and numeracy skills , ensuring that relevant assessments inform teaching approaches within a graduated intervention framework. To foster a shared understanding of SpLD, we use the following terminology during consultations, assessments, and written reports. We will use the following terms: Why have we used this term? Terms that are also used: Specific learning difficulties (SpLD) We have used this term as an umbrella term that includes severe and persistent difficulties with literacy and/or numeracy. Dyslexia Dyscalculia Dysgraphia Significant literacy difficulties When a child or young has severe and persistent difficulties learning to read and write, which remain despite intervention over time, we have used the term ‘significant literacy difficulties.’ The word significant highlights that the child’s needs are significantly above what would usually be expected for the child’s age or stage of development. Dyslexia Dysgraphia Significant numeracy difficulties When a child or young has severe and persistent difficulties learning numeracy skills, which remain despite intervention over time we have used the term ‘significant numeracy difficulties.’ Again, the child’s needs are significantly above what would usually be expected for the child’s age or stage of development. Dyscalculia 5. How do schools support children who have a confirmed diagnosis of dyslexia from an Educational Psychologist or Specialist Teacher Assessor. All educational settings should be able to identify early on, pupils who are experiencing - or at risk of experiencing - difficulties with phonological processing, early word recognition, reading and spelling. Schools may require support in developing and delivering a graduated or ‘waves’ based approach to provision. The Rose Report (2009) specifies three waves of provision to support students with SpLD. Furthermore, any direct intervention should follow the assess, plan, do, review cycle and be built upon quality first teaching. The majority of children will develop their phonological awareness and reading skills through high quality Wave 1 teaching. Wave 1: Quality First Teaching The majority of children achieve well through high quality classroom teaching. When children are being taught to read, Quality First teaching provides high quality, systematic phonic work as part of a broad and rich curriculum that engages children in a range of activities and experiences to develop their speaking and listening skills and phonological awareness. Wave 2: Small group and one -to-one interventions Some children require additional support to achieve well. This can often be provided through small group, time-limited intervention programmes delivered by a member of the school’s classroom-based support team that will advance students’ progress and help them achieve in-line with their peers.
