FOI request 1: The reply referred to point 4. ....a full and transparent options appraisal process to decide and the best heating and/or hot water for the specific site. **I would like to see a copy of that. The full options appraisal (brief below and within the Heating Policy) would apply to planned capital works projects. In this case the works were carried out as emergency boiler replacements as the site had been put onto temporary boilers after failure of the plant. No options appraisal was carried out as the internals had been renewed (rad iators / cylinders / pipework / controls) approx. 10 years earlier. This meant that the rest of the system had at least another 10 years expected life. Therefore the failed boiler house plant was replaced through the term contractor to provide service security and remove the ongoing cost of temporary boiler plant hire. 4. Conduct a full and transparent options appraisal process to decide on the best heating and/or hot water solution for the specific site. The process will happen when the district heating network/communal system is at the end of its useful life o r the system experiences multiple failures. The following aspects will be taken into consideration: • Capital cost of the works through a 30 years Net Present Value (NPV) life cycle analysis [1] • Operational and maintenance costs • Ongoing fuel costs to residents • Environmental impact – carbon emissions and NOx for air quality [1] NPV analysis is completed from the Council’s investment point of view as the owner of the network London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk • Measures to improve health and safety • Local, national and European policy, guidelines and best practice (that will also include forward look for any emerging trends or upcoming policies) • Feasibility of technology options to include: a) Retain existing system and continue with repairs and maintenance regime b) Decentralised energy networks opportunities - heat (and power, if relevant) in the locale; are there viable alternative heat sources in the area, for example adjacent organisations such as schools, hospitals, etc. which could export heat to the housing networks c) Communal boiler (conventional or condensing applications) depending on configuration of buildings being considered d) Electric heating e) Individual Ultra Low NOx boilers (conventional and storage or combination; high efficiency and condensing and the impact on existing gas and mains cold water infrastructure) f) Method of generating domestic hot water for options d – e including instantaneous generation and thermal stores g) Renewable energy technologies e.g. air source or ground source heat pumps, solar thermal; and other technologies, e.g. Combined Heat & Power (CHP) and fuel cell • Economic, Social and Environmental Matrix to conclude which technology option meets the Heating Policy objectives and delivers best value for Camden’s residents FOI request 2: Point 5 states "engage proactively with residents......at an early stage prior to statutory leaseholder consultation......". **I would like to know how and when this happened. Yours sincerely Philip Lewis Information Rights Officer 1 of 4 FINAL Heating policy_revised 2022.docxFinal Heating Policy for Council-Owned Housing – Revised 2022 Scope This policy applies to all council-owned homes and new-build council homes, covering both tenanted and leasehold dwellings, communally and individually heated properties. The policy was first approved by the Council in January 2004 and will be reviewed periodically to reflect developments in policy, technology and practice. Aims and Objectives The Council is committed to providing homes with affordable, controllable space and water heating systems that are economically maintainable, that provide value for money and align with the Council’s strategic policies and in particular We Make Camden (and future versions) and Camden’s Climate Action Plan . To achieve these aims, Camden will: Maintenance of current systems 1. Continue to improve the building’s fabric to reduce heat demand as part of a comprehensive investment approach. 2. Seek resources to finance additional energy efficiency measures, and explore renewable energy technology to ‘future proof’ energy supply. 3. Retain the existing district heating networks and expand where possible, or establish new ones as this is the most efficient way of service provision. Heat networks are also imperative for long-term strategy for heat decarbonisation. Having a central plant room will enable the transition to other alternative low carbon sources , as outlined in the Government’s Clean Growth Strategy and GLA’s London Environment Strategy 3.1. It is Council policy to refuse individual tenants and leaseholders from opting out of the communal and district heating networks, for the following reasons: • Allowing residents to opt out would lead to the communal/district heating system becoming grossly oversized and inefficient. • Some systems run in ‘series’ rather than in ‘parallel’, with t he result that changes to one dwelling can have implications ‘downpipe’. • Residual leaseholders on the communal/district system would have to pay a higher proportion of the costs associated with the maintenance of the centralised plant and infrastructure. • Regulatory and technical issues preventing installation of individual boilers. • High value of investment and long term contracts in place for large legacy networks, i.e. Somers Town Energy and Gospel Oak -Royal Free Hospital networks. 3.2. It is Council policy to refuse individual tenants and leaseholders from opting out of the bulk gas network for their heating, for the following reasons: 2 of 4 FINAL Heating policy_revised 2022.docxFinal • A new gas pipe for an individual supply to the resident would need to be installed by Cadent (formerly known as National Grid), which is not a cost effective or a practical solution. • The costs of fuel for the resident would likely be more expensive with the new supplier, because Camden buys gas in bulk (see point 18). • Breaking up the Heating Pool would have knock on effects on the fuel price for remaining users, through the reduction in bulk negotiating power. Any opt out will be a breach of tenancy/leasehold conditions. Appropriate consideration must be given to freehold properties as they have the option to be removed from the communal/district./bulk gas system. 3.3. Tenants and leaseholders will be allowed to switch their cooking supply to electricity and have their heating charges adjusted accordingly. Any requests to switch from cooking gas to electricity will not be granted until a check is carried out by Camden of the capacity of the electrical distribution cables and fuses. Upgrade of existing systems 4. Conduct a full and transparent options appraisal process to decide on the best heating and/or hot water solution for the specific site. The process will happen w hen the district heating network/communal system is at the end of its useful life or the system experiences multiple failures. The following aspects will be taken into consideration: • Capital cost of the works through a 30 years Net Present Value ( NPV) life cycle analysis 1 • Operational and maintenance costs • Ongoing fuel costs to residents • Environmental impact – carbon emissions and NOx for air quality • Measures to improve health and safety • Local, national and European policy, guidelines and best practice (that will also include forward look for any emerging trends or upcoming policies) • Feasibility of technology options to include: a) Retain existing system and continue with repairs and maintenance regime b) Decentralised energy networks opportunities - heat (and power, if relevant) in the locale; are there viable alternative heat sources in the area, for example adjacent organisations such as schools, hospitals, etc. which could export heat to the housing networks c) Communal boiler (conventional or condensing applications) depending on configuration of buildings being considered d) Electric heating e) Individual Ultra Low NOx boilers (conventional and storage or combination; high efficiency and condensing and the impact on existing gas and mains cold water infrastructure) f) Method of generating domestic hot water for options d – e including instantaneous generation and thermal stores 1 NPV analysis is completed from the Council’s investment point of view as the owner of the network 3 of 4 FINAL Heating policy_revised 2022.docxFinal g) Renewable energy technologies e.g. air source or ground source heat pumps, solar thermal; and other technologies, e.g. Combined Heat & Power (CHP) and fuel cell • Economic, Social and Environmental Matrix to conclude which technology option meets the Heating Policy objectives and delivers best value for Camden’s residents 5. Engage proactively with residents (tenants and leaseholders) on the options for heating system replacement, presenting clear analysis at an early s tage prior to statutory leaseholder consultation wherever possible. Regulations and standards compliance 6. Demand contractors’ compliance with Camden’s Design Supplement based on the CIBSE’s Code of Practice for Heat Networks and ensure all new installations are guaranteed to reach an agreed performance level. 7. Ensure all new installations are supplied with dwelling heat meters and building- level meters in accordance with Heat Network (Metering and Billing) Regulations 2014 . 8. Maintain a register of heat networks, performance and monitoring in accordance with government regulations. 9. Ensure that all heating improvements comply with current regulation and in part icular, Part L (Conservation of Fuel and Power), B, F and J of the Building Regulations. New homes and planning policy 10. Install heating systems that balance Planning policy requirements with operational resilience, cost in use, energy demand and supply, maintenance and impact on carbon reduction targets, when developing new homes. 11. Not support the installation of stand-alone CHP units in small developments (less than 50kW), where there is neither the potential nor the intention for that development to form part of a wider network – please refer to Camden’s Local Plan guidance ( http://camden.gov.uk/ccm/navigation/environment/planning- and-built- environment/planning-policy/local-development-framework/ ). The administrative burden of managing small-scale CHP electricity sales, and the low unit price available for small volumes of exported CHP electricity, means it is generally uneconomic to pursue. Furthermore, CHP proposals need to comply with maximum NOx emissions requirements specified in Draft London Plan ( https://www.london.gov.uk/what-we- do/planning/london-plan/new-london-plan/draft-new-london-plan/ ). Commissioning of heating systems 12. Require full testing and commissioning to be undertaken for all new and refurbished heating systems in compliance with the Camden Heat Networks Design Supplement. This will also include full commissioning and testing of the heat meters, communications and data received by Camden, as well as the remote access to the BMS system for ongoing monitoring. Performance monitoring 13. Monitor and measure performance of networks based on agreed performance levels to ensure value for money. This would include gas consumed and total heat delivered to properties, where metered. 4 of 4 FINAL Heating policy_revised 2022.docxFinal Data management and billing 14. Make data available from dwelling and building-level heat meters to leasehold services, rents and billing in order to ensure transparency, immediacy and accuracy in billing and charges. 15. Continue to use the charging systems that are appropriate for specific sites depending on available information. There are different types of charging systems – these are based on individual gas meters, heating pool and dwelling heat metering. Heating pool charging arrangements will remain in place for secure tenants and heating estate charges for leaseholders until dwelling heat meters are installed. 16. It is Council policy to refuse tenants and leaseholders from opting out of the bulk gas network for their heating, because Cadent (formerly known as National Grid) would need to supply a new gas pipe for an individual supply to the resident, which is not a cost effective or a practical solution. The costs of fuel for the resident would likely be more expensive with the new supplier. Breaking up the Heating Pool would have knock on effects on the fuel price for remaining users, through the reduction in bulk negotiating power. Any opt out will be a breach of tenancy/leasehold conditions. 17. Not install Pay-As-You-Go heat charging systems in order to keep the system’s administration cost to the minimum for residents. Energy procurement 18. Continue to monitor the difference in gas prices between the Council’s commercial bulk purchasing contract and London domestic gas rates in the unlikely event that residents become disadvantaged through participation in the Heating Pool, and to take advice from sector specialists to determine our gas procurement strategy. Information sharing on the heating systems 19. Notify council services including leasehold services, rents and billing, sustainability and energy management of any changes to heating systems so that the correct charges and energy management processes can be undertaken within reasonable timescales . This will include notification of additional property to heat systems, and particularly if non-residential property is added to systems in order to enable an accurate charging mechanism. 20. Consult and inform leasehold services, rents and billing, sustainability and energy management of plans for development of new homes at inception phase, throughout the course of the development and the handover process.

Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: Request 1: 1. With regards to staff names and contact details we are withholding this as we consider section 40(2) applies. We supply the names and contact details of senior staff in the top three tiers of the local authority from Assistant Dir ector and up all other staff would be classed as relatively junior positions within the council and they would have no expectation that their details would be released into the public domain For questions 2 to 6, please supply this information as a snaps hot at the end of the year for the financial years 2016/17 to 2017/18, and where possible, the most up to date snapshot available for 2018/19. 2. Total number in residential care 77 72 71 3. Total number in residential care in borough 77 70 69 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Total number in residential care out of borough 0 2 2 4. Total number in supported living 104 103 104 5. Please provide the number of adults with learning disabilities who transitioned from children’s learning disabilities services into adult’s services - in total, into adult residential care services only, and into adult supported living Services only. Children, young person disabilities service is a 0 -25 service held under the Children Social work and Safeguarding directorate. Therefore they do not au tomatically transition to adult social care when they turn 18. Our transfer policy from CYPDS to CLDS/ASC outlines that young adults will not transfer if they are still in education, which includes residential placements, this is because they will need t o be transitioned on to post educational placements/activities etc. If they are in a settled supported living/residential home then of course we would transfer to CLDS/ASC if this was the longer term plan for them. Document Title: Policies underpinning vulnerable residents
Document Text: Date: 03/11/2020 Case reference : CAM569 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 06/10/2020 about policies underpinning vulnerable residents.  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested, however we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt. The answers to your questions are below we have stated where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply.  Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why the exemptions apply. I would like to seek information regarding the policies underpinning the vulnerable residents .    The Council adheres to the legislation and statutory guidance set out in a number of pieces of legislation and statutory guidance. I have added hyperlinks to the relevant pages for ease of viewing. The Care Act 2014, the related Care and Support Statutory Guidance ● and the Mental Capacity Act 2005 are the main pieces of legislation related to Adult Social Care.● More information on how Camden applies the Care Act 2014 can be found on our website Camden Care Choices . ● Supporting People Connecting Communities, Our strategy for living and ageing well in Camden sets out how Camden supports people with disabilities and other issues that live in Camden. This is being refreshed for 2020 and a new version goes to November 2020 Cabinet. ● As part of the covid 19 response the Government introduced 'Care Act Easements' in the Coronavirus Act where local authorities could prioritise the most vulnerable when their resources were stretched. In Camden the Care Act easements were never taken up and the pressures from Covid-19 were managed within flexibilities already allowed in the Care Act 2014. Adult Social Care's privacy notice which governs the use of individual personal data can be viewed here During the national lockdown, the council stood up a Community Hub to support the clinically extremely vulnerable who had been advised to shield themselves from infection. This offer included a welfare call to Camden’s 8,200 shielding residents to ensure they had essential food supplies and what they needed to remain safe in their homes. For those who requested help, the Council provided a range of support that included delivering emergency food and other groceries parcels, prescription collections, travel to medical appointments and other support to enable the shielded to remain in their homes. For the shielded with more complex needs a multi-disciplinary team of professionals from across children’s and family support, adult social care and housing services came together to assess their case and put in place a holistic care package that met the needs presented. Alongside the community hub, Camden funded Age UK Camden to provide emergency food parcels to residents who were not shielded but were moderately vulnerable due to health conditions, and had chosen to self-isolate. We also provided funding to our local food banks and distributed bulk food donations from the London Food Alliance to other voluntary sector food providers. In addition, we supported our vulnerable rough sleeper population, moving them in to temporary hostels to keep them off the streets and safe during the first wave of the pandemic. We delivered food parcels and hot meals.  In total we delivered over 30,000 food parcels to Camden’s vulnerable residents. After the lockdown was eased and the Government paused the national Shielding Programme at the end of July, Camden continued to deliver food parcels to clinically extremely vulnerable residents on our distribution list, while supporting those with the means to buy their own food to link in to alternative ways to access food – e.g. online shopping or shopping assistance volunteers. Since August, Camden has been working closely with the voluntary sector, scaffolding local charities to provide the range of support and more that had been delivered by the council during the lockdown period. Going forward, the sector will provide food and other wraparound support to clinically extremely vulnerable and moderately vulnerable residents in Camden should they need any help to self-isolate. This community based hyper-local response is key to ensuring that vulnerable residents receive the support they need while linking them into their local community to create lasting networks and relationships. We have continued to communicate with the clinically extremely vulnerable through this period to update them on the latest Government guidance and provide advice on what additional measures they can take to protect themselves. Should the clinically extremely vulnerable need to shield again, there is a robust network of charities across Camden that would be able to provide whatever support these residents need to enable them to remain in their homes and stay physically and mentally safe. Council services will also continue to be available to support vulnerable residents as matter of course. I would also like to obtain the relevant Data Privacy materials, e.g. Data Privacy Impact Assessment, or any discussions regarding Data Privacy consideration in relation to the handling of vulnerable residents, usually conducted and compiled by the Data Protection Officer. There is only a legal requirement to undertake a DPIA where the data processing is deemed high risk.  We have not determined any of the data processing for this to be high risk and so no DPIAs were required.  However, we are in the process of updating the Camden Resident’s Index DPIA to account for some covid related work. Therefor although the council holds the information requested we are applying the qualified exemption in section 22 (2) of the Act because the information is intended for future publication and it is not reasonable to publish it ahead of planned publication.  The council will publish this information with the next four weeks. In applying this exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: Improving transparency in decision making● To ensure accountability of the authority● Encouraging resident engagement with the council● The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: There is a defined schedule for publishing this information and it would cause disruption to the council to publish ahead of this time● Early release would pre-empt a decision that should be made by the council or someone else● An announcement may be designed to prompt enquiries from the public and may be expected to result in an increase in workloads, for instance a press release. The authority has to ensure that our administrative arrangements are in place before the information is released● We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. Please note this will be published on our website when it is finalised. Please see below weblink.  https://www.camden.gov.uk/your-rights#huoq We do have a number of DPIA pre-screens- these are assessment documents that outline the work to be undertaken and assess the risks to allow a decision to be made about whether a DPIA is needed.  If you would like these please let us know and we can process a request for these.  With regards to discussion around data privacy for vulnerable residents. We are sorry but we are refusing this information under the section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit".  This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We have calculated that it will take approx. 21 hours to comply with your request because: There are 42 advice cases where we have advised on data protection matters regarding vulnerable people and to find and extract the advice given on each would exceed the appropriate limit.  The Data Protection Officer has been personally involved in some matters but many have been delegated to the Information Rights Team leader, and to in order to collate and locate all discussions would require an officer to look through hundreds of emails to retrieve the information you are seeking. Advice and Assistance Under the Act we are required to provide advice and assistance in order to help the requester obtain information, having considered the section 12 exemption above I would advise that you could request the first 5 cases received be reviewed to obtain the information you are seeking. Document Text: Date: 2 February 2026 Ref: CAM11911 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 5 January 2025 about Camden residents admitted to hospital where specified respiratory illnesses were recorded as a contributing factor. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds some of the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: For each of the last five financial years: The number of Camden residents admitted to hospital where excess cold, hypothermia, or cold-related respiratory illness was recorded as a contributing factor, where such data is held. Year period, the rate of emergency admissions for cold related or respiratory conditions in Camden has remained consistently lower than the England average. Although the Camden rate fluctuates statistically significantly from year to year, these changes are relatively small, and the overall level of admissions has remained broadly stable. There is no universally agreed definition of “cold related respiratory conditions.” In line with ONS practice, this analysis includes a wide range of respiratory conditions, most of which are not exclusively linked to cold weather. No age or demographic standardisation has been applied to related respiratory conditions. It is important to note that: • Not all admissions included will be attributable to cold weather. Many respiratory conditions occur throughout the year, including in summer. • Conversely, cold exposure may contribute to some admissions that fall outside the selected diagnostic codes. As such, the figures should be interpreted as indicative of overall respiratory and cold- related admissions rather than a definitive measure of cold-weather impacts. Last updated 1 9.06.20 Biffa Load Assessment Process for NLWA MDR Notes The following process relates to loads of Mixed Dry Recyclables (MDR) tipped at Biffa MRF by Borough RCVs and HGVs from trans fer station s (namely Oakleigh Road, Hendon, and Hornsey St) . The purpose of this procedure note is to document the agreed process for determining the contamination levels of MDR deliveries, which will be used for monthly invoicing and quarterly reporting to WasteDataFlow. The process is designed to produce a reliabl e contamination percentage for each rejected or downgraded load, whilst maintaining a safe working practices and not unduly delaying MRF operations. The contamination thresholds, as set out in the contract, are: Accepted Load = less than 15% Downgraded Loa d = between 15% and 25% (inclusive) Rejected Load = more than 25% The contract defines what items are classified as contamination. Last updated 1 9.06.20 Load Assessment Process Step Number Description Notes Photos 1 – Visual Assessment Upon tipping, a visual assessment is carried out to determine whether any part of the load looks to contain unacceptable levels of contamination. If this is the case, an assessment is made as to whether the contamination is spread throughout the load or is isolated to a specifi c section of the load. 2 – Contra Count A 2mx2m square is placed over the area of the load or part load which looks to be the most heavily contaminated. The Biffa quality operative counts the number of individual contamination items they can see (known as ‘contras’) within the square. Quality operatives do not dig into the material to count contras contained below the surface. Full black bags are counted as one contra and are not split open at this stage in the process. If the load in question is a part HGV load, a 2mx2m square will be placed on the most heavily contaminated section of the part load. If an HGV loa d is suspected to be fully rejected , then 2mx2m square counts will be carried out on two different areas of the load. Last updated 1 9.06.20 3 – Notification of potential rejection If the count results in more than 15 contras being identified within the square, this identifies that the load or part load potentially exceeds the contract contamination threshold of 15%. To determine the actual contamination level, further investigation is required, as set out in the following steps. At this stage, Biffa quality operatives send an initial notification to the Authority, identifying a potential reject or downgrade. The notification contains the weighbridge ticket, photographic evidence, a nd a rejections form which lists the key contaminants. Biffa aim to send notification of potential rejection within 60 minutes of the contra count being completed. If the load or part load is an incorrect waste type (e.g. green garden waste), this is the end of the process and no sample is taken. 4 – Mixing of Load The load or part load is mixed using a loading shovel by lifting and dropping the material at least two times, in line with the MRF Code of Practice regs. All of the load or part load will b e mixed together to extract a representative sample of the potentially rejected MDR. See 4.3.1 of the WRAP CoP guidance: http://www.wrap.org.uk/sites/files /wrap/MF%2 0Sampling%20Guidance%20April%202014.pdf Last updated 1 9.06.20 5 – Removal of Sample Once mixed, the loading shovel removed a scoop of MDR and tips it into 240 litre bins. 6 – Sorting of Sample The full 240 litre bin is weighed to ensure the sample size is at least 60kg, in line with the MRF Code of Practice regs. The load is then tipped onto sorting tables and all non-recyclable contamination is pulled out. The contamination is weighed, and the weight is divided by the total sample weight to calculate the contamination percentage to be applied to the load or part load. Last updated 1 9.06.20 7 – Notification of results Biffa quality operatives send notification of the sample results to the Authority, confirming the status of the load or part load (i.e. accepted, downgraded or rejected). The notification provides photographic evidence of the contamination and a completed sample composition form detailing the contaminants present the weights and the percentage results. Biffa aim to send notification of sampling results within 60 minutes of the sort being completed. Last updated 1 9.06.20 8 – Confirmatio n of results Authority and Borough officers have the opportunity to attend the MRF to view the rejected load(s). For 24 hours of notification of results being sent, Biffa will not move downgraded MDR into the MRF or dispose of rejected MDR without confirmation from Au thority officers that the results of the procedure are accepted. Authority officers will routinely monitor the process to ensure Biffa adhere to this agreed procedure. Authority officers will carry out spot -checks on rejected loads and will additionally attend site to view rejected loads if they determine that the sample result does not appear to match the photographic (and other) evidence provided. Borough officers may contact the Authority in relation to a specific load, which they feel has been wrongly allocated as rejected or downgraded, based on the evidence provided. In such a case, Authority officers will seek to arrange to view the load together with Borough officers. If Boroughs wish to query anything or view load(s), this should be communicated to NLWA Last updated 1 9.06.20 by 16.00 the day the notification of results is received.

Document Text: Date: 03/12/2024 Ref: CAM8919 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 04/11/2024 about temporary accommodation and related matters. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. Amalgamated request 1: 1. Do you currently provide WiFi to people in temporary accommodation in (a) council-owned sites (b) within the private rented sector or (c) B&Bs or hotels and (d) is this free of charge and (e) can you signpost me to your policy? I am assuming that households use free Wi-Fi in hotels, in private rented sector accommodation households are expected to procure their own internet broadband, but please do clarify if I am labouring under the wrong assumptions. 2. Do you (a) charge households in shared temporary accommodation for using washing facilities and (b) can you signpost me to your policy? 3. Local authorities are statutorily required to place in storage the items of homeless households. Could you please (a) signpost me to your storage policy and (b) clarify whether or not you charge for storage at any point. 4. Can you please list the locations of your storage, by local authority 5. If you place families in hotels which therefore do not have facilitates to cook meals – and therefore will have to pay for meals more frequently, do you have a policy of providing any additional support? Amalgamated request 2: 1. Of the single-person households placed by your authority currently in temporary accommodation, please provide a date for the household that was placed the earliest. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 2. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. Once the council has determined that the appropriate limit will be reached it does not need to estimate the time that would be needed for the remainder of the request . There is no obligation on the council to work on a request until the 18 hours limit is reached and when reasonably calculated the entire request may be refused. The information you are seeking for questions 1-3 of your second amalgamated request is not available. This is because the council is undergoing a large data migration project between systems, which is affecting our capacity to access and analyse data more efficiently. This migration process adds an additional layer of complexity and time to the task of retrieving the information requested, if held. In the quarterly period July-September 2023, we identified 633 households in temporary accommodation. To provide the information requested a council officer would have to manually review the notes of each case file and collate/record the information per household. Based on a sample of 10 cases where some case notes were unclear, it took approx. 3 minutes per case to gather and analyse the data. We have calculated to provide the information for all 633 case files would take approx. 31.65 hours. Document Text: Date: 04/03/2021 Case reference : CAM1216 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 18/02/2021 about Data Protection Impact assessments conducted by planning .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.  Response Please could you provide me with all Data Protection Impact assessments conducted by your planning department on personal data they process. Please note that I do not require any personal data. We do not hold this information.  This is because a Data Protection Impact Assessment is only required where the proposed data processing is considered to be high risk (poses a high risk to individuals in data protection terms).  A DPIA is not required for any processing that is not high risk. Generally planning information contains little special category data and is not considered high risk processing.  Therefore, the need for a full DPIA does not generally arise. Currently there are no planning DPIAs as none have met the threshold test to require one. The council publishes all its full DPIAs here:   https://www.camden.gov.uk/your-rights#huoq Before a new system is introduced, or a major new set of sharing for example is entered into, a DPIA pre-screen will be undertaken which allows the need for a DPIA to be assessed.  Where the DPIA pre-screen risk assessment shows the processing will be low risk a DPIA is not needed.  Where the risk assessment is high a full DPIA would be undertaken.  We also would undertake a DPIA where risks were medium/high. If you wanted to ask for DPIA pre-screens for planning you could make a request for these.  We hold data back to May 2018 when the new process began.The Information Commissioner has information about DPIAs on its website: https://ico.org.uk/for- organisations/guide-to-data-protection/guide-to-the-general-data-protection-regulation- gdpr/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments/ Further Information We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Document Text: Date: 03/03/2025 Ref: CAM9615 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 11/02/2025 about naming and numbering properties and streets within your jurisdiction. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exceptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. My understanding is that you are the authority statutorily responsible for naming and numbering properties and streets within your jurisdiction under the Towns Improvement Clauses Act 1847 and the Public Health Act 1925. This data forms a critical part of our national infrastructure, enabling economic growth, research, and innovation. Businesses rely on accurate naming and numbering data to serve customers, manage logistics, and make investment decisions. Academic researchers use it to study housing patterns, urban development, and social trends. Local organisations and charities need it to deliver their services to the community. Open access to authoritative naming and numbering data can drive efficiency in the private sector, enable evidence -based policymaking, and foster technological innovation in areas like delivery services and property technology. Given these significant public benefits, there is a clear and strong public interest in ensuring this foundational data is openly available for analysis, verification, and reuse. Please provide an up-to-date list of all current properties within the Authority’s jurisdiction, in Excel (.xlsx) or CSV (.csv) format. Where the word "assigned" is used, it is referring to what the Authority deems to be the official value for the purposes of administering its naming and numbering duties. Please include the following 9 columns: 1. "Property local authority reference": the reference the Authority uses internally to uniquely identify the property. 2. "Property name": the officially recognised name of the property. Leave blank if no name is assigned. 3. "Property number": the number of the property on its street. For example, "13", "221B" or "18-20". Leave blank if no number is assigned. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 4. "Property sub-division name": flat, apartment, unit or suite names/numbers, for example. Leave blank if the property is not a sub-division. 5. "UPRN": the Unique Property Reference Number. 6. "Street local authority reference": the reference the Authority uses internally to uniquely identify the street the property is located on. 7. "Street name": the name of the street the property is located on. For example, "High Street". Leave blank if no name is assigned. 8. "Street number": the number of the street the property is located on, such as "A12" or "B123". Non-standard numbers used internally by the Authority such as "C", "D" and "U" roads are also acceptable, but not required. Leave blank if no number is assigned. 9. "USRN": the Unique Street Reference Number of the street the property is located on. I am only requesting data assigned as part of the Authority’s statutory naming and numbering duties. I am NOT requesting additional metadata such as property ownership, land use classifications, geographical coordinates, postal addresses or property type. As far as I'm aware, the Authority does not make this data available elsewhere. Some commercial products provide access to data that is derived from the Authority's assigned names and numbers, but they have been further modified and mixed with third- party data sources, meaning I can't actually access the data I'm requesting via these products. The expensive and restrictive commercial licences also mean the data is not easily accessible or usable. Due to the existence of commercial products that use this public data, I understand the Authority may need to consider how this request could prejudice these commercial interests. The data I have requested is fundamentally required for the Authority to perform its statutory duties: there is no ambiguity that this data forms part of the public record. UPRNs and USRNs are explicitly designated as open identifiers available under the Open Government License. While GeoPlace coordinates the national system, the Authority is still performing the statutory function of assigning names and numbers, and is creating these national identifiers as part of their duties. The fact that UPRNs and USRNs are national standards reinforces their public nature; they're specifically designed to be universal reference points that enable interoperability across different systems and organisations. They're meant to be used alongside this data, which is why they were made openly available in the first place. Furthermore, the use of third-party data is not required to fulfil this request since the Authority is responsible for the assignment of all the data I'm requesting, including UPRNs and USRNs. The data also cannot be considered intellectual property since it is entirely factual. This is a commercially sensitive data set, which is owned as part of the National Land and Property Gazeteer (NLPG). See the refusal notice below. Refusal Notice: The exception that applies is regulation 12(5)(c) which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that its disclosure would adversely affect intellectual property rights. In applying this exception the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: • The Council would be providing a service in an open and transparent way. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: • The Council must carry out its work in a legal and ethical manner. • The Council should not have its trust damaged by breaking license agreements with suppliers. • It is not in the Council’s interests to damage the commercial viability of another company or organisation. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. We considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations overrides the decision to withhold and have concluded that it does not. Document Text: Date: 25/03/2024 Case reference : CAM7064London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 12/02/2024 about emails received, or sent by, members of cabinet containing the word "Gaza" .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. You clarified your request on 26/02/2024: We do not require the disclosure of emails where the cabinet member concerned was only copied 'CC' into the email. You requested: I request the following information pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act: (1) Disclosure of alll emails received by, or sent by, members of the Camden Council cabinet containing the word "Gaza" since 7 October 2003. The Council is refusing your request as vexatious.  It is not your conduct, tone or purpose that is a problem, but it is simply the fact that complying with your request will cause a disproportionate and unjustified level of disruption to Council employees.Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 14(1): vexatious request Section 14 (1) can be used by an authority when complying with the request will cause a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption to the Council. As this exemption is an absolute exemption there is no requirement to conduct a public interest test. We accept that your request is not frivolous, as is often the case with a vexatious refusal. However, we believe that any serious purpose is now outweighed by the severe disruption caused to the council in responding to the request. You are raising issues where there has been a large amount of public engagement. Considerable time and effort has already been spent in collating information.  We have identified 534 emails totalling 2144 pages of information that fall under the scope of your request. Disproportionate time would be needed to redact personal information and remove any elements of constituency or party-political information that are outside of the scope of the FOIA.  This time may be considered under the Act for the application of s14(1).  Each page will need to be checked for this information and to check and redact or remove information will take at least 2 mins per page. The time therefore to check and redact personal data would be over 71 hours. This is clearly an impossible task for the small team of FOI Officers who would do the redacting.  They already have a heavy workload and 71 hours would be nearly 2 working weeks. Advice and assistance You have recently made a number of information requests relating directly or indirectly to the situation in Gaza. Topics that are of particular public concern will generate considerable email traffic and collation based on a key word is likely to produce too many emails for us to be able to process and will be refused under s14(1) as explained above.If we receive two or more requests from the same person, or from different persons appearing to us to be acting in concert or as part of a campaign, we may take the cost of complying with any one of them to be the cost of complying with all of them jointly and refuse the requests under s12 of the Act. If a request is made for a particular specific narrow subject area and over a relatively short period of time (e.g., two weeks) it is more likely for us to be able to provide information within a reasonable and proportionate effort.  Such request may provide a snapshot that would inform you of the emails received and sent by members of the Cabinet. This request relates to education otherwise than at school (EOTAS) arranged by the local authority under section 61 of the Children and Families Act 2014. Please provide the following recorded information held by the local authority. Please provide the information for the following periods: Financial years 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 And, where available, the most recent position held in 2025 (year to date) 1. For each period, the total number of children and young people for whom the local authority arranged EOTAS provision. 2. For each period, the total gross expenditure incurred by the local authority on EOTAS provision. For the avoidance of doubt, this should include all payments made by the local authority in relation to EOTAS, including but not limited to tuition, therapy, alternative provision, online education, and any associated educational support costs. We are withholding this information as we consider the following exemption applies. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. The information requested is not held in an easily reportable format. For the five-year period a total of 7,436 Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) fall within scope of your request. Aligning this with academic year data (1 September to 31 August) would require detailed cross-referencing of datasets, significantly increasing the time and resource required to complete the request. We estimate that manually reviewing each file would take an average of 7.5 minutes. Retrieving and compiling the requested information would take a council officer approx. 929.5 hours. This significantly exceeds the statutory limit of 18 hours as set out in Section 12 of the Freedom of Information Act. Document Text: Date: 21/06/2024 Ref: CAM7861 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 05/06/2024 about cost of a repaved pavement along Regents Park Road from Chalk Farm Road to Bridge Approach . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000/Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested. this enquiry is for the cost of a repaved pavement along this road on the eastern side only. The contractor started last week. What is the cost of this contract and, who is the Camden Highways engineer in charge of the contract execution? The concrete slabs are Standard 600x600x63. No kerbstones are required. The works have been carried out due to a number of safety concerns raised by members the public. The reasons for the changing of the paving slabs is due to high levels of damage on certain slabs and extreme levels of undulation in certain areas which caused ponding along the walkway this prevented the footway from being utilized, and this presented a danger to the public The slabs were also out of alignment which presented trip hazards . The cost of the works is £20,000. The Kerbstones are going to be set aside for re-use and then re- laid. Regarding the name of the Camden Highways engineer, we are withholding this as we consider section 40(2) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 applies. We supply the names and contact details of senior staff in the top four tiers of the local authority from Heads of Service and up. All other staff would be classed as relatively junior positions within the council and they would have no expectation that their details would be released into the public domain. Further Information: We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Any such use will be reported to the ICO as a breach of General Data Protection Regulations and the Privacy and Electronic Communication Regulations. Document Text: Date: 11 December 2025 Ref: CAM11523 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 10 November 2025 about bruising in non-mobile infants. Please note that this correspondence replaces and supersedes our earlier response dated 9 December 2025. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: In September 2022 the Child Safeguarding Review Panel issued guidance asking that "all safeguarding partners review their current policies on bruising in non- mobile infants to check for consistency with the evidence base and national guidelines." Can you respond to the following freedom of information request: 1. Was there a review of your safeguarding policies after this guidance was published, when was it, and what did it conclude? London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 3. Does your policy require a s47 investigation or strategy discussion in all cases? Whilst in most cases of bruising in a non-mobile infant is significant and requires a strategy meeting to consider the threshold to explore the explanation for the bruising. A multi-agency partnership decision on whether to progress a Section 47 investigation is dependent on information shared at the strategy meeting. Please review the document ’Bruising in pre mobile babies briefing for professionals 2025,’ referenced in question 2 above. 4. This meeting will explore and assess the concern, applying and professional judgement and analysis to provide proportionate intervention. 5. Document Title: Legal costs compensation
Document Text: Date: 25/01/2021 Ref: CAM971 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 29/12/2020 about legal costs compensation. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding the information because it is exempt. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why the exemptions apply. Compensation Payments and Recording of VAT of Legal Costs by Camden Council Camden Council claimed £1,054,000 in compensation from construction firm Willmott Dixon, and eventually settled for £770,000 at some point in 2018- 2020. 1. Provide the total sum of compensation and the total sum of refunds of legal costs Camden Council paid to residents in connection with the work by Willmott Dixon. This question is refused under Section 42(1) of the Freedom of Information Act. See the refusal notice below. 2. List all the individual compensation payments, and separately all the individual refunds of legal costs Camden Council paid to residents (£-amounts only), from the highest payout down to the lowest payout. This question is refused under Section 42(1) of the Freedom of Information Act. See the refusal notice below. 3. According to Camden Council all solicitor firms providing legal advice to residents in above case had to register as suppliers before the cost of any legal fees could be refunded, “as VAT was involved”. 1. Provide a full list of all the solicitor firms that registered as suppli ers, the date they were registered, and the supplier reference number. This question is refused under Section 42(1) of the Freedom of Information Act. See the refusal notice below. 2. Provide the list of account names and account numbers in Camden Council’s accounting system, which have been used to record the refund of the legal costs and the VAT. This question is refused under Section 31 of the Freedom of Information Act . See the refusal notice below. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Refusal Notice Section 42(1): Legal Professional Privilege This information is exempt under Section 42(1) of the Act because it is protected by Legal Professional Privilege (LPP). LPP covers communications between lawyers and their clients for obtaining legal advice, or documents created by or for lawyers for the main purpose of litigation. The latter is the case with this request. Litigation privilege applies to confidential communications made for the purpose of providing or obtaining legal advice about proposed or contemplated litigation. Litigation privilege can apply to a wide variety of information, including advice, correspondence, notes, evidence or reports. The information withheld is covered by this exemption because the individual agreements have comprised of non- disclosure clauses, as well as ongoing litigation. The exemption is qualified and so is subject to a public interest test. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: • It would improve the transparency of the decision making process • It will allow the council’s decisions to be examined and held to account The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows : • There is very strong inherent public interest in maintaining LPP and allowing the council to take legal advice and prepare for litigation in a confidential way • Disclosure of the legal advice could prejudice the Council’s ability to defend or prosecute its legal interests, by unfairly exposing its legal position to challenge, or by disclosing its approach to and tactics in legal areas. Section 31(1)a: Prejudicial to law enforcement Section 31 – Law Enforcement – We do not release account information in the Council’s accounting system as we consider disclosing this information would make the Council a target of crime. Therefore this information is exempt from disclosure under Section 31 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Section 31(1)(a) says that we do not need to provide information that would be likely to prejudice the functions of law enforcement - the prevention and detection of crime. Camden believes that releasing this information would increase the likelihood of potential fraudsters using the information to commit financial crime in a way that criminals could use the details to pose as these suppliers and defraud the suppliers or the council The exemption is qualified and so is subject to a public interest test. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: • It would improve the transparency of the decision making process . • It will allow the council’s decisions to be examined and held to account . The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: • There is an inherent public interest in crime prevention. • There is a public interest in not making it easier for fraud to be committed. • It is not in the public interest to disclose information that would be likely to cause damage to a company, as this could lead to financial problems for the company and/or job losses. The council has concluded that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. We considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations overrides the decision to withhold and have concluded that it does not. Document Text: Date: 20/05/2021 Case reference : CAM1529 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 26/04/2021 about adults with learning disabilities.  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding some or all of the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply.  Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. Do you keep a register of the number of adults with learning disabilities in your local authority area? If so, how many adults in your local authority area are (at present) recorded as having learning disabilities? No we are sorry but we do not hold such a register. This information is held by each GP. What support is available for vulnerable adults (including those with learning disabilities) accessing social housing? How does your council support vulnerable adults in the process of finding suitable accommodation? Where a vulnerable adult who applies for social housing through our housing allocations scheme (Housing Act 1996 Part VI) already has a support worker, or other people working with or supporting them, such as a Social Worker, a carer or a supportive family member or friend, then their support network is welcomed to liaise with the Advisers in the Housing Placements Service. If a vulnerable adult applies for housing but needs support and does not have support then appropriate referrals and suggestions for how support can be gained are made. In some cases the Housing Placements Service will search for and place bids on available homes for people who are vulnerable and unable to do this for themselves or through existing support. How many people with learning disabilities in your local authority have been housed outside of their local authority area in the last calendar year? If it doesn’t exceed the cost limit, I would also like this information for the last three years please. Please note the information provided below is the number of people known to the Camden Learning disabilities service (CLDS) and Adult social care service (ASC)  31/03/2018 31/03/2019 31/03/2020 31/03/2021 Number known to CLDS living out of borough 130 127 136 145 Number with current ASC service out of borough   100 100 102 Number known to CLDS 734 732 738 759 How many people on the current waiting list for social housing in your local authority area have a learning disability? Section 12 We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit".  This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We are sorry but the information you are seeking is not held in a reportable format this is because we do not routinely report on this information and ion order to locate the information you are seeking would require an officer to conduct a manual trawl of files in order to ascertain where this information is held. There are currently 6373 applicants on the housing register at present, we estimate that it would take in excess of 95 hours  for an officer to look through each file at an estimated 10 minutes per file to retrieve the information you are seeking. Advice and Assistance I am unable to provide you with guidance on how to reduce your request as the volume of applicants who are on the housing register at any one time very each month. Document Text: Date: 17 November 2025 Ref: CAM11359 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 20 October 2025 about the number of applications made under section 21A of the Mental Capacity Act 2005. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. Please provide the following information for the financial years 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24: 1. The number of applications made under section 21A of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 in which your local authority has been involved (as applicant, respondent, or other party). 2. The total legal costs incurred by the authority in relation to those s21A applications (including in-house and external representation). 3. If available, a breakdown of those costs by year and/or by internal vs external legal spend. We are withholding this information as we consider the following exemption applies. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk The information requested is not held in a reportable format. While we hold some information on Deprivation of Liberty applications, not all applications or outcomes are consistently recorded in case notes, resulting in incomplete data. For 2023/24, there are 3,541 referrals to review. We estimate it would take a council officer approximately 7-8 minutes per record to manually review, extract and collate the data requested. This is because our data system cannot generate reports to answer question 1. For context, the number of referrals received is tabled below. Document Title: spend over £500
Document Text: Date: 09/04/2026 Case reference: CAM12436 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 16/03/2026 about spend over £500.  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.   Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice which explains how and why it applies: The request is: I write to request information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. This request concerns serious anomalies identified in the London Borough of Camden's published 'Spend Over £500' dataset, specifically relating to (a) large-scale withholding of payment information from the published transparency dataset, (b) payments to highway contractors misclassified under a social care expenditure category, and (c) payments to a highway contractor where the purpose description has been withheld. PART A — ANONYMOUS PAYMENTS: BENEFICIARY NAME WITHHELD Analysis of Camden's published Spend Over £500 dataset for the financial year 2025/26 reveals two entries where the beneficiary name has been withheld entirely from the published transparency data: 1. A beneficiary listed only as 'REDACTED': approximately £35,457,282 2. A beneficiary listed only as 'xxxxREDACTEDxxxx': approximately £9,232,709These two entries together represent approximately £44.7 million paid to entities whose identities Camden has withheld from its own published transparency dataset. Please provide: 1. The actual identity of the beneficiary or beneficiaries whose name has been listed as 'REDACTED' in the 2025/26 dataset, and the nature of the goods or services for which these payments were made. 2. The actual identity of the beneficiary or beneficiaries whose name has been listed as 'xxxxREDACTEDxxxx' in the 2025/26 dataset, and the nature of the goods or services for which these payments were made. 3. The specific legal basis or exemption under which the identity of each beneficiary was withheld from the published dataset. 4. Camden's policy on when beneficiary names may be redacted from the Spend Over £500 transparency dataset, and who has authority to authorise such redactions. 5. The total number and aggregate value of all payments where the beneficiary name has been redacted from the Spend Over £500 dataset in each financial year from 2019/20 to 2025/26. PART B — MATRIX SCM LIMITED: PURPOSE REDACTED The published 2025/26 dataset shows payments totalling approximately £29,614,029 to Matrix SCM Limited where the purpose field has been redacted in its entirety. Matrix SCM is a managed service provider for temporary local government staffing. Please provide: 6. The unredacted purpose description for all payments to Matrix SCM Limited where the purpose has been listed as 'REDACTED' in the Spend Over £500 dataset. 7. The specific legal basis or exemption under which the purpose of these payments was withheld from the published dataset. 8. The contract reference, contract value, contract start date and procurement method used to appoint Matrix SCM Limited. 9. Confirmation of whether the London Living Wage requirement in Camden's Pay Policy applies to workers placed through Matrix SCM Limited and the agencies it manages, and how Camden monitors compliance with this requirement. PART C — REDACTED PAYMENTS: SCALE AND POLICY Analysis of the full 2025/26 dataset reveals that approximately £76,880,680 across 11,077 individual records has been redacted from the published transparency data — either the beneficiary name, the purpose, or both. This represents approximately 9.6% of total confirmed spend for the year. Please provide: 10. Camden's complete policy governing when information may be redacted from the Spend Over £500 transparency dataset, including the categories of information that may be withheld and the legal basis for each category. 11. Who holds authority to approve redactions, and whether redaction decisions are subject to any internal review or audit. 12. Whether the scale of redactions in the Spend Over £500 dataset has been reviewed by Camden's internal audit function or the external auditor, and if so the outcome of that review. PART D — HIGHWAY CONTRACTOR PAYMENTS MISCLASSIFIED AS SOCIAL CARE Analysis of Camden's published spending data reveals that substantial payments to three highway maintenance contractors have been classified under the category 'Community Support Direct Payments for Carers' across multiple financial years. The amounts involved are as follows: a) VolkerHighways Limited: approximately £376,913 b) FM Conway Ltd: approximately £190,396 (historic) plus £170,478 in 2025/26 c) Marlborough Highways Ltd: approximately £140,151 (historic) plus £5,443 in 2025/26These firms are highway infrastructure and maintenance contractors with no connection to social care. Please provide: 13. A full explanation of why payments to these highway contractors have been classified under 'Community Support Direct Payments for Carers' in the published dataset. 14. The actual description of the goods or services for which each of these payments was made. 15. The correct budget line and expenditure category to which each payment should have been allocated. 16. Whether Camden's internal auditors have identified this classification issue, and if so what action has been taken. PART E — MARLBOROUGH HIGHWAYS: ADDITIONAL PURPOSE REDACTIONS The published dataset also contains payments to Marlborough Highways Ltd where the purpose field has been listed as 'REDACTED', totalling approximately £145,030 in prior years plus £106,949 in 2025/26. Please provide: 17. The unredacted purpose description for all payments to Marlborough Highways Ltd classified as 'REDACTED' in the dataset. 18. The specific legal basis or exemption under which this information was withheld. PART F — GENERAL CLASSIFICATION METHODOLOGY 19. What process does Camden use to assign expenditure category codes to individual payments, and what quality assurance checks are applied to ensure payments are correctly classified before publication in the Spend Over £500 dataset? 20. Has Camden conducted any review of the accuracy of payment classifications in the published dataset? If so, please provide the outcome of that review. CLARIFICATORY NOTEFor the avoidance of doubt, where Camden holds data in its financial system but asserts that it does not hold it in the specific form requested, I ask that Camden confirm this explicitly. I am aware that Camden's underlying financial system contains the unredacted information referenced in this request. If Camden's position is that any of the classifications described in Part D represent a genuine and accurate description of the goods or services provided by highway contractors, I ask that Camden confirm this explicitly and provide supporting documentation. If any part of this request is refused under an exemption, please identify the specific exemption relied upon for each refused element and confirm whether the public interest test has been applied. We are not processing this request as it would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 12: cost of compliance exceeds appropriate limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We have calculated that it will take approx. 1120 hours (minimum) to comply with your request because for Q5 alone: we do not hold this information in a readily electronically reportable format from our systems• compiling relevant data requires significant manual effort across multiple systems and years• 1120000 transactions that fall within the scope of this question would need to be examined• even if the data could be extracted and collated at an average minimum of 1000 transactions per hour •it would take 1120 hours Advice and Assistance We may be able to respond to most of the other questions within the s12 cost limits.
