Document Title: minutes and correspondence with Eventhia & Bottaccio
Document Text: Date: 08/10/2024 Case reference : CAM8574London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 19/09/2024 about minutes and correspondence with Eventhia & Bottaccio.   We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (EIR 2004). Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. Please supply copies of all minutes, correspondence, contracts and related documentation relating to discussions between officers and members of the local authority and representatives of Eventhia Limited and Bottaccio [and their agents and counsel] in relation to the use of the Old Town Hall Building. This request covers the period from 1st September 2023 to 30th September 2023. We are not processing this request as it is exempt.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 14: vexatious The above request is asking for information covering the period from 1st September 2023 to 30th September 2023. An earlier request CAM8354, from another person, asked for the period 1st July 2023 to 31st December 2023 and followed an earlier request for similar information (CAM7831).  CAM8354 was refused under s14 due to the burden or complying with the request causing a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption to the council.  The responses to these requests can be viewed by searching using the link below: https://opendata.camden.gov.uk/stories/s/Camden-Freedom-Of-Information-Response-Search/dwzc-va83/ On 13th September another request CAM8526 was received, asking for the information from 1st July 2023 to 31st July 2023.  Subsequently a further series of requests was received, CAM8556, CAM8560, CAM8569, CAM8570, CAM8574 (this request) and CAM8578 - all on the 18 or 19 September.  These requests, with a small addition, were identical to CAM8526, but each asking for the information for a different month covering August 2023 to January 2024. The request CAM8526, and the subsequent requests, were all sent by different individuals who are clearly acting in concert to circumvent the refusal of CAM8354. The burden in dealing with the new requests is increased by the addition of January 2024. Section 14 (1) can be used by an authority when complying with the request will cause a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption to the Council. As this exemption is an absolute exemption there is no requirement to conduct a public interest test. You are raising issues where there has been a large amount of correspondence, this is over double the amount than the previous request - CAM7831, which then compiled and processed amounted to a response of 444 pages. This required an extension of time, and final processing amounted to well over 20 hours of officer time. We estimate the information that falls under the scope of the current requests would amount to over 1285 pages when compiled. Disproportionate time would be needed to redact personal information and redact or remove any information that is exempt under s43(2) for commercial interests, and s42 for legal professional privilege. This time may be considered under the Act for the application of s14(1). Each page will need to be checked for this information and to check and redact or remove information will take at least 3 mins per page. The time therefore to check and redact this information would be over a minimum time of 65 hours.This is clearly an impossible task for one project officer and a small team of officers who would do the redacting and who already have a heavy workload. The council is refusing this request as vexatious under s14(1).  This is not only due to the burden of dealing with the requests taken in aggregate, but also because of the attempt to circumvent the refusal of CAM8354 which is an inappropriate and improper use of the formal FOIA procedures and will have the effect of harassing council staff. Environmental Information contained in the information requested is also excepted under the EIR 2004 as manifestly unreasonable. The exception that applies is: regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable. The request is manifestly unreasonable on the grounds that it is vexatious as outlined above. We have also considered the time it will take the council to locate the information requested in the aggregated requests above, to extract it, collate it and then to review and redact any sensitive information that will be subject to further exceptions under the EIR 2004. We have considered the impact and burden that processing this request would have on the team who would have to deal with it. We have concluded that the time, effort and costs involved would place a disproportionate burden on the team and severely impact their ability to perform their normal duties. We have calculated that it will take over an estimated minimum of 65 hours to comply with your request. In applying this exception, the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004.  We have indicated the weight of each of these considerations. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: - it would improve the transparency for the general public of the Council’s decisions and processes in dealing with the refurbishment of the Town Hall (High).•The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: - it is not the public interest to process requests that represent an inappropriate or improper use of the formal procedures and will have the effect of harassing council staff (High).• processing this request in full would be provide a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council (High).• this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities, (High) and:• it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s the provision of services to the public (High).• it is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request (High).• It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004. We considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not. What is Camden's effective response to tackle fly tipping in recurrent hotspots? I am particular concerned about ongoing issues in York Way particularly in proximity to the junction with Agar Grove, which have become particularly worse over the last months since Conway have taken possession of the site. We have a range of measures in place to tackle persistent fly -tipping, especially in recurrent hotspots like this location. York Way is currently on our priority monitoring list, and we have targeted patrols by our Community Enforcement Safety Officers. Where evidence allows, we take enforcement action which is by fixed penalty notice, with the possibility of prosecution. So far, this has led to six enforcement actions at this location – including two for fly-tipping and four for the unlawful presentation of waste. We will be liaising with Conway in how they can assist us in ongoing fly-tipping issues in this area 2. What are Camden plans to improve the presentation of this site, medium/long term? We collaborate with stakeholders to provide guidance on waste management facilities, ensuring that residents and businesses have suitable and accessible disposal options. Additionally, Community Safety Enforcement Officers partner with Monitoring Officers to conduct targeted educational campaigns, raising awareness about responsible waste disposal and fostering a culture of compliance. Waste management is also being integrated into broader urban planning initiatives to prevent fly-tipping and enhance the area's overall appearance over time. Document Text: Date: 17/12/2024 Ref: CAM9034 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 18/11/2024 about refunds the local authority has requested from care providers. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. For your last 2 financial years, I would like to request the total amount (as a single cost figure, e.g. £100,000) of clawbacks and refunds your council has requested from care providers, specifically those providing care for the elderly including residential homes, nursing homes and domiciliary care providers. Clawback amounts frequently appear on remittance advice to care providers; they instruct providers to use credit the council has with the provider as payment towards other outstanding invoices. I am hoping to use this information to understand the amount overpaid to care providers (and later reclaimed) before trying to identify the reasons behind overpayments. The exemption notice that applies is: Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk The information you are seeking is not held in a reportable format. Credits and overpayments may be processed on our financial systems for more than one reason, including a change to care or a retrospective increase in the amount paid, such as through a rate increase. Also an overpayment or ‘credit’ maybe offset against a further payment, therefore there is no reportable way the transactions can be separated. Based on one budget code area, covering a period of six months we identified 415 transactions. It took a council officer approx. 2-3 minutes to locate, extract and manually analyse each processed credit transaction. Using the average of 2.5 minutes per record we estimate it would take more than 17 hours to determine whether any contra transactions apply and the reason for the credit. To review data for the full calendar year would approximately be double the number of transactions sampled and take twice as long to analyse, approx. 34 hours. This does not include providing year 2 data or reviewing other budget codes. Document Text: Date: 03/05/2024 Case reference : CAM7518London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 18/04/2024 about the Housing Benefit Award Accuracy Initiative . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds some but not all of the information requested. We explain below what we hold and what we do not hold. We are withholding some of the information we hold because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained what exemption applies and why in the refusal notice at the end of the answers. Specifically, I am asking the following, for the most recent reporting period data is available [whether that is calendar year, financial year or other period]: - The most recent reported data we have is for the 23/24 financial year, up to 26/1/24. Copies of data outlining: a) The number of individuals flagged by the HBAAI algorithm as "high risk" to your council We do not hold this information.  This information was not included in the reported data we received from Department of Work and Pensions (DWP). b) The number of people put forward fur a Full Case Review by your council, split by risk category (e.g., high/low) We do not hold this information.  3,083 had been issued as of 26/01/24 but the DWP don’t split it into those categories.c) The outcomes (i.e. fraud, error, no change), however this is recorded. We do not hold this information.  This information was not included in the reported data we received from the DWP, although as of 26/01/24. 2,329 FCRs had been completed. d) Any equalities or demographic data outlining the makeup of the cohorts flagged as high risk, and/or subject to a full case review. We do not hold this information.  This information was not included in the reported data we received from the DWP. e) A copy of the performance data sent to the DWP for the most recent reporting period The data is sent to the DWP on the Single Housing Benefit Extract, and this contains personal data for all Housing Benefit claimants in Camden and is therefore exempt from release.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. f) A copy of any assessment or similar held of the impact of the HBAAI on your council There has been no such assessment. Document Text: Date: 30/06/2025 Ref: CAM10442 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 10/06/2025 about Temporary Accommodation Practices and Compliance. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. Temporary Accommodation Practices and Compliance 1. Planning Compliance – Use of C3 Flats or HMOs as Temporary Accommodation: a) What procedures does your local authority follow to determine whether the properties it uses for temporary accommodation, particularly flats, houses or HMOs, have the necessary planning permission for such use, given that the use would amount to Sui Generis hostel use? We use flats & houses to provide temporary accommodation for households. However, the properties must comply with our minimum property standards which makes clear that fact that all accommodation must comply with planning regulations and be health and safety compli ant. All planning permissions and health & safety certificates are checked prior to the property being allocated to a household. Camden does not use Houses in Multiple Occupation ( HMO’s) for the provision of temporary accommodation. b) How many current TA placements made by your authority are into properties that are classified under planning use Class C3 or C4? Currently, Camden accommodates 610 households in properties classed as C3 and 0 in C4. 2. Safeguards Against Unlawful Evictions: a) What safeguards does your authority have in place to ensure residents placed in C3 accommodations as temporary accommodation are protected against unlawful eviction? Prior to onboarding temporary accommodation providers, Camden undertakes a robust assessment of the provider/s, ensuring they have a proven track record of providing these services to other local authorities. We obtain references from other authorities these providers have worked with. It is accepted practice that once the accommodation is cancelled, the accommodation provider must secure vacant possession through legal means. When a booking is cancelled by Camden, the tenant and the accommodation provider are verbally advised that the Council is ceasing the booking and if the household refuses to vacate the property, the accommodation provider is advised to pursue a legal process to secure vacant possession. Document Title: Planning enforcement action against BT public payphone kiosks at Tottenham Court Road
Document Text: Date: 22/02/2021 Case reference : CAM1121 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 01/02/2021 about planning enforcement action against BT public payphone kiosks at Tottenham Court Road .  We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding some of the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answers which explain how and it they applies. …please also provide, pursuant to Freedom of Information Act 2000 and Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (where relevant), the following information: a) Copies/evidence of any complaints received by the Council in respect of the kiosks that are the subject of the PCNs issued; Complaints are made to the enforcement team in confidence and contain personal information, we specifically say on our website that any complaints made to the enforcement team will be kept confidential. Releasing the information would prejudice the effectiveness of the investigations/ enforcement process generally, including prejudice to future investigations and proceedings.  Please see the exception notice set out below. We can reveal the dates of some of the complaints made to indicate the number of issues raised: 14/04/2020, 07/02/2020, 30/01/2020, 01/03/2020, 25/10/2019, 31/05/2019, 24/05/2019, 17/05/2019, 05/10/2019, 03/05/2019 and 26/05/2019. We are currently in the process of taking formal enforcement action and the information provided with the above objections will form part of our case. We have had input from various Council'steams including the police at meetings and this information will be included in our delegated report, which they will later have an ability to appeal when the notice is served. b) The usage criteria applied by the Council in respect of the PCNs issued; Part 16 Class A to Schedule 2 of the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) Order 2015 (Part 16). Part 16 Class A, includes: “Development by or on behalf of an electronic communications code operator for the purpose of the operator’s electronic communications network in, on, over or under land controlled by that operator or in accordance with the electronic communications code, consisting of – The installation, alteration or replacement of any electronic communications apparatus….”1. This permitted development right is a conditional right. Paragraph A.2 provides: “(2) Class A development is permitted subject to the condition that – any electronic communications apparatus provided in accordance with that permission is removed from the land or building on which it is situated – (i) ….. (ii) ….as soon as reasonably practicable after it is no longer required for electronic communications purposes; and1. such land or building is restored to its condition before the development took place, or to any other condition as may be agreed in writing between the local planning authority and the developer”2. In determining whether we consider a breach of planning control has taken place we consider the following: is there telephonic equipment in the kiosk;1. If there is telephonic equipment, is the kiosk a) unmaintained, b) unusable or c) unused2. c) Copies of any documents which demonstrate the decision making process which resulted in the issue of the PCNs. These should include the minutes of any meetings and correspondence which have taken place to discuss these matters; This is an open enforcement investigation which may lead to legal action being taken. A formal enforcement action will be served and an enforcement notice will be served on those with a legal interest in the kiosk which will include justification for taking action. In addition, a separate delegated report will be prepared prior to action being taken. This report will be made available if an appeal is submitted. Releasing the information would prejudice the effectiveness of the investigations/ enforcement process generally, including prejudice to future investigations and proceedings.  Correspondence with counsel is also privileged.Please see the exception notice set out below. d) Copies of any relevant Council policies and/or internal procedures which have been implemented to assist in reaching the decision These are available online at www.camden.gov.uk/planning or on external websites: Policy London Plan 2017 A1 Managing the impact of development C5 Safety and Security C6 Access D1 Design D4 Advertisements G1 Delivery and location of growth T1 Prioritising walking, cycling and public transport Supplementary planning guidance CPG Design (2019) CPG Transport (2019) CPG Advertisements (2018) CPG Amenity (2018) Camden Streetscape Design Manual Fitzrovia Area Action Plan (2014). National Planning Policy Framework (2019) London Plan (2019)London Plan (Intend to Publish) (2019) Design of an accessible and inclusive built environment. External environment (code of practice - BS8300-1:2018 and BS-2:2018) Digital Roadside Advertising and Proposed Best Practice (commissioned by Transport for London) March 2013 TfL’s Pedestrian Comfort Guidance for London (2010) e) Copies (including drafts) of any officer's report to commence enforcement action We only have a draft report which relates to more than just BT kiosks. Releasing the information would prejudice the effectiveness of the investigations/ enforcement process generally, including prejudice to future investigations and proceedings.  Please see the exception notice set out below. f) Copies of any relevant part of the Council’s scheme of delegation authorising the decision to commence enforcement act i on. This information is already publicly available on our website.  Please enter the link into your web browser - the relevant delegation is at 101: http://democracy.camden.gov.uk/documents/s94022/Delegation%20Scheme%20- %20Supporting%20Communities%2019.10.18.pdf Refusal Notice Information has been withheld while the Council conducts an investigation that may result in legal action. The exception that applies is: regulation 12 (5)(b) which states that “a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent its disclosure would adversely affect the course of justice, the ability of a person to receive a fair trial or the ability of a public authority to conduct an inquiry of a criminal or disciplinary nature.” When applying this exeption we have to show why we believe it is in the public interest to apply the exception. We do this by balancing the arguments for and against disclosure:The public interest argument for releasing this information is:- it would improve the transparency for the general public of the Council’s decision-making processes ● The public interest arguments for withholding the information are:- disclosure of this information would have the potential to prejudice the Council’s ability to successfully take any legal or enforcement action by prematurely revealing details of the investigation. ● disclosure of this information would have the potential to prejudice the other party’s ability to successfully defend any legal or enforcement action by prematurely revealing details of the investigation ● premature disclosure may result in the public being presented with incomplete information that gives a distorted or inaccurate view of the facts of the case ● We believe that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in theregulationsand we haveconsideredwhether this overrides the publicinteresttestconclusion and have concluded that it does not. Document Title: Learning difficulties
Document Text: Date: 25th April 2018 Ref: FOI10914 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated the 28th March 2018 about Learning Difficulties. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: Under the Freedom of Information act I'm hoping to gain information on this, to identify what is being done in London to detect learning difficulties - specifically Dyslexia, as well as the amount of diagnoses which have been made. If you could provide me w ith the number of diagnoses of dyslexia in children made annually, for the past 10 years if possible (if not, the nearest amount) in which have happened in schools in your borough - alongside the amount of screenings/ testings for learning difficulties. I also want to receive information on what funding is being given to schools for learning difficulties, stating how much and where it is going. 1. In Camden we use the term Specific Learning Difficulties (SpLD, including Dyslexia) as Dyslexia is a type of learning difficulty which is specific to literacy. We find that the most helpful definition of Dyslexia is the one formulated by the British Psychological Society (1999). We therefore believe that Dyslexia can occur across all of the cognitive range and is evident when accurate and fluent word reading and/or spelling develops very incompletely or with great difficulty. This focuses on literacy learning at the ‘word level’ and implies that the problem is severe and persistent despite appropriate learning opportunities . 2. This is not a medical diagnosis for SpLD (including Dyslexia) but an assessment process involving educational psychologists (EP), working closely with education staff and parents. 3. The identification of a SPLD is usually made by an EP though there are others who also specialise in the teaching of pupils with SpLD who can do so. 4. We have 28 children and young people (CYP) with a primary need of SpLD (including Dyslexia) who have an EHC plan. These CYP have severe, long term and complex needs at a level requiring special education provision for their needs to be met. We recognise tha t there are many others with SpLD whose needs are not so significant and in these cases, our schools make provision for them, using resources delegated to them in their budgets; i.e. with SEN support without the need for an EHCP. 5. We have around 500 students being supported by schools with SEN support where primary need is recorded as SPLD. 6. We do not have detailed records of how many cases are identified annually. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 7. The identification of SpLD (including Dyslexia) is a process that involve s parents, schools and external agencies. We follow the guidance advice in the DfE Sen Code of Practice, and adhere to the ‘Plan, Do and Review’ cycle to ensure that the needs of CYP are both identified and met. This is particularly relevant in identifyin g SpLD (including Dyslexia); the difficulties must be found to persist ‘despite appropriate learning opportunities’ for a child to be identified as having ‘Dyslexia’ as the above definition states. We use the Rose Report ‘Identifying and Teaching Young People with Dyslexia (UK Department of Children Schools and Families, 2009) to guide our understanding of the wider cognitive features and behaviours that may co -occur or be part of SpLD (including Dyslexia). This report states that in addition to dif ficulties with reading and spelling, the following difficulties might occur. - Characteristics of dyslexia are difficulties with phonological awareness, verbal memory and verbal processing speed. - Dyslexia occurs across the range of intellectual abili ties. - Co-occurring difficulties may be seen in aspects of language, motor co -ordination, mental calculation, concentration and personal organisation, but these are not, by themselves markers of dyslexia. - A good indication of the severity and persistenc e of dyslexic difficulties can be gained by examining how the individual responds, or has responded to well -founded intervention 8. Mainstream schools receive funding for supporting children with learning difficulties at a number of different levels. The schools block funding that funds all pupils includes elements based on the characteristics of the school population that the school will use in providing support for any child requiring support which costs up to £6,000 per year. Over and above this the school will be able to call on high needs funding to ‘top -up’ this funding based on the needs of the child or young person. In Camden £1.3m is delegated to mainstream schools to top -up funding for the support of pupils without EHC plans. In addition there are higher needs pupils who have EHC plans which specify additional top -up. Camden staff work with schools to ensure that funding is used to maximum benefit. The emphasis is on specific targeted interventions, delivered as part of the class group o r in small group work. The role of learning support assistants being to work jointly with the class teacher and to support the pupil to take part in the lesson rather than to increase dependence on an adult or to isolate them from their class group. Document Title: Biodiversity Net Gain
Document Text: Date: 29/07/2021 Ref: CAM1910 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 19/07/2021 about Biodiversity Net Gain. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested. The answers to your questions are below. I would like to request, under the terms of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, the following information: - When is the Local Planning Authority planning to introduce Biodiversity Net Gain as a mandatory requirement for all small development projects in the LPA’s jurisdiction? Please provide a specific date and a short definition of what the LPA classes as a ‘small development project’. We will be primarily led by the detail of the legislation regarding Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) currently going through Parliament (within the Environment Bill), and any guidance and secondary legislation that supports this. At present, we are expecting BNG to be mandatory in Autumn 2023, with ‘small’ projects being defined as those less than 10 dwellings, and not including householder applications. - If a specific date has not yet been decided, does your Local Planning Authority intend to introduce a requirement for planning applications to include localised Biodiversity Net Gain plans for small development project within the 24 months following the passing of the Environment Bill? (Please define ‘Biodiversity Gain Plan’ as any document that is analogous to the type of document specified in the Environment Bill). At present, we are expecting BNG, including the provision of Net Gain Plans, to be mandatory in Autumn 2023. We understand a ‘small sites metric’ is in development which would be used to establish the net biodiversity gain on these sites. It is envisaged that ‘net gain plans’ would need to accompany planning applications but it is not yet clear whether the content/material presented in these plans would be the same for all sizes of development. - Is there any material that sets out what criteria a Biodiversity Gain Plan needs to meet in order to be accepted by the authority for a small development project? If such material exists please can it be attached to your response. If such material does not exist, please provide a brief description of what criteria a Biodiversity Gain Plan needs to meet within your LPA. (Again, please define ‘Biodiversity Gain Plan’ as any document that is analogous to the type of document specified in the Environment Bill). We are expecting guidance and secondary legislation after the Environment Bill has been ratified, some time in 2022. There may also be additional guidance from the Greater London Authority. We London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk are aware that CIEEM has produced a number of documents around BNG, and that a British Standard is due, but at the current time cannot say how these may relate to the LPAs processes for validating the relevant applications. - Who is the official at your Local Planning Authority that is tasked with ensuring that Biodiversity Net Gain is implemented for the LPA? BNG is expected to form part of the process for validating and assessing individual planning applications. As with other planning matters, the relevant case officer would make sure that national and local planning requirements are met. - Does the LPA’s approach to Net Gain require all ‘Biodiversity Gain Plans’ to be produced by an accredited ecologist? We are expecting guidance and secondary legislation after the Environment Bill has been ratified, sometime in 2022, and this should include what will be required of developers. However, we understand that the small sites process is being designed with non- ecologists in mind. However, we would always recommend an ecologist be consulted where a scheme has the potential to impact upon biodiversity. Document Title: Seven Dials Traffic Plan
Document Text: Date: 11/08/2020 Ref: CAM277 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 23/07/2020 about Seven Dials Traffic Plan. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding the information because it is excepted. We have stated where we are withholding informat ion and what exceptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why the exceptions apply. Freedom of Information Request Substantial number of residents, hotels & independent businesses oppose the Seven Dials Traffic Plan. The plan eliminates residential, loading bays and installs bollards in the area. The process has been unfair, arbitrary and grossly unjust. without any detailed resident or business stakeholder consultation. 1. Can you disclose all correspondence & emails from/between the officials, agents & employees of Shaftesbury Plc and officials & employees of London Borough of Camden for the past 12 months in relation to the seven dials area. 2. Can you disclose all written plans, maps, schedules and p roposals including drafts that have been submitted by Shaftesbury Plc and other stakeholders to Camden Council in relation to the plans as set out in the 17th July 2020 letter issued by Camden Council transport strategy service. 3. Can you confirm in writing the exact nature of Shaftesbury PLC sponsorship of the proposed seven dials Covid19 traffic plan as set out in the 17th July 2020 Camden Council letter and whether it includes monetary sponsorship. The Council will not process your request as it falls under an exception in the EIR 2004 because the cost or burden of dealing with your request is excessive. Refusal Notice The exception that applies is Regulation 12(4)(b) which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable. Guidance produced by the Information Commissioner’s Office states that “in assessing whether the cost, or the amount of staff time involved in responding to a request, is sufficient to render a request manifestly unreasonable, the FOIA fees regulations may be a London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk useful starting point.” We are refusing your request on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the req uester. In this request you have asked for “disclose all correspondence & emails from/between the officials, agents & employees of Shaftesbury Plc and officials & employees of London Borough of Camden for the past 12 months in relation to the seven dials area” There are over 30 members of staff who could or would have work ed on this. For them to search their mailboxes is likely to take at least 1 hour each person, totalling at least 30 hours work. This includes an Information Rights Officer compiling and redacting the information where necessary. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: • It would improve transparency to the general public of the Council. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: • Processing this request would be a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council. • Considering that the whole Council, especially the Transport Strategy Team and the Information Rights team, currently have an increased volume of work due to the Covid-19 pandemic. • This request would necessarily constitute a significant div ersion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities and emergency Covid- 19 work. • It would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on the provision of services to the public. • It is not in the public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request. It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. We considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations overrides the decision to withhold and have concluded that it does not. Document Title: provision of adult social care services and associated domiciliary care and residential care home fees
Document Text: Date: 13/11/2024 Ref: CAM8697 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 04/10/2024 about the provision of adult social care services and associated domiciliary care and residential care home fees . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. Please note that questions 1 to 5 exclude residential care (i.e. “care in a care home”), while questions 6 to 10 are specifically about residential care. 1. For the most recent date for which data is held, please state the total number of people in the council area that are required to pay for any aspect of their non-residential adult care (including but not limited to home care, day care, community alarms, telecare, and other community care services) . 2. How many of the people referred to in response to question 1 are currently in arrears on their care charges by at least one scheduled payment (or by one month)? This figure should *include* the cases referred to in response to question 3, as anyone in arrears by at least two payments (as per question 3) is by definition also in arrears by at least one payment (as per question 2). 3. How many of the people referred to in response to question 1 are currently in arrears on their care charges by at least two scheduled payments (or by two months)? 4. How many of the people referred to in response to question 1 are currently subject to debt management procedures as a result of non- payment of non- residential care charges e.g. automated reminders, final reminders, letter before action, referral to civil enforcement agency, county court judgement? 5. How many of the people referred to in response to question 4 have had their current debts referred to a debt collection agency (including any agency owned by the council)? London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 6. For the most recent date for which data is held, please state the total number of people in the council area that are required to pay for any aspect of their residential adult care (i.e. care in a care home). 7. How many of the people referred to in response to question 6 are currently in arrears on their care charges by at least one scheduled payment (or by one month)? This figure should *include* the cases referred to in response to question 8, as anyone in arrears by at least two payments (as per question 8) is by definition also in arrears by at least one payment (as per question 7). 8. How many of the people referred to in response to question 6 are currently in arrears on their care charges by at least two scheduled payments (or by two months)? 9. How many of the people referred to in response to question 6 are currently subject to debt management procedures as a result of non- payment of residential care charges e.g. automated reminders, final reminders, letter before action, referral to civil enforcement agency, county court judgement? 10. How many of the people referred to in response to question 9 have had their current debts referred to a debt collection agency (including any agency owned by the council)? 11. How many people did the council start court proceedings against in relation to non-payment of adult care charges (residential and/or non- residential) each year in 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 (year to date), excluding probate cases? Please provide the figures broken down by year To clarify, I'm requesting information about current adult social care service users (non-residential care users for questions 1-5; residential care users for questions 6-10). We have applied the section 12 refusal notice below. Refusal notice: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. The information for questions 2 and 3 is not held in a reportable format. This is because there is no automated way on Adult Social Care debtor cases to capture the information. On many cases we send initial correspondence seeking to engage which does not threaten to issue legal proceedings and would not amount to a Letter Before Action. To retrieve the data would require a council officer to manually review each casefile to see if a Letter Before Action has been sent. A similar review process has to be followed to identify the number of County Court Judgements obtained. We estimate it would take a council officer approx. 10 minutes per case to review each file. Some reviews may take less than 10 minutes because they have short histories whereas other files which have longer histories will require more time to complete. 30 minutes is required to collate the data. To review all 197 cases and collate the information would take approximately 33.3 hours. This time exceeds the appropriate limit set out in the Act. Advice and Assistance: We suggest the scope of your request be reduced and questions 2-10 refined to bear in mind the maximum 10 minutes per case advice mentioned earlier. Further Information: We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Any such use will be reported to the ICO as a breach of General Data Protection Regulations and the Privacy and Electronic Communication Regulations. Why not check our Portal Open Data Camden before making a new request as your question may already be answered by a previous FOI response or in one of our many useful and interesting datasets. Your Rights If you are not happy with how your response was handled you can request an Internal Review within 2 months of this letter by email to foireviews@camden.gov.uk or post: Information and Records Management Team, London Borough of Camden, Town Hall, Judd Street, London WC1H 9JE. Please quote your case reference number. If you are not satisfied with the Internal Review outcome you can complain to the Information Commissioner’s Office at casework@ico.org.uk telephone 0303 123 1113, live chat https://ico.org.uk/global/contact-us/live-chat/ or webform https://ico.org.uk/global/contact- us/. The ICO website www.ico.org.uk may be useful. Yours sincerely, Lorna Jonas-Tinson Information Rights Officer

Document Text: Date: 04/09/2023 Case reference : CAM5700 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 25/07/2023 about senior leaders home working, hybrid performance management and support for performance management . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: I am currently undertaking a business project in which I am considering the challenges of performance management in Local Authorities in a hybrid working environment. Can I please request you answer the following questions - in an email is sufficient but also attach any documentation you include in your answers or that you have had to consider surrounding this topic. You clarified your request on 13/08/2023:- 1) How many days are senior managers working from home and office for the organisation ? From CE down to HoS. Across the council, all services require colleagues to be working in our workplaces at least one day a week, this expectation applies at all levels including Chief Executive and Heads of Services. Colleagues who work directly with citizens are likely to be working in our buildings more often - and it is up to Directors to set out any additional expectations around working arrangements for their particular services. 2) Have you seen an increase or decrease in the need for performance management through HR processes since hybrid working arrangements have been put in place? Overall, there has been a decrease in formal performance management cases since 2020. 3) Are there arrangements you have introduced specifically to support performance management in a hybrid working context or existing advice arrangements that have proved particularly effective for hybrid working? Please provide documents where necessary Our “My Performance” scheme is based on the importance of regular, good quality conversations between a line manager and their staff member as being an effective framework for performance management in a virtual and in person setting whether those conversations are occurring face-to- face, through MS Teams and/or phone. Alongside this framework, we have shared online webinars such as – “Remote Working: What Have We Learnt?”, “Leading Remote Teams” and “Approaching and managing tricky conversations” and guides/resources to support managers to have effective conversations when managing remotely. We have also developed an online Managers Development Programme and managers have access to an online database of resources (Just-in-Time toolkit) that supports one to one’s and helpful conversations by signposting to relevant videos, articles, templates and exercises. Document Title: Chalcots Estate cladding work
Document Text: Date: 25/02/2021 Ref: CAM1189 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 15/02/2021 about Chalcots Estate cladding work. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding the information because it is excepted. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we are withholding information and what exceptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why the exceptions apply. Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, I request that you provide m e with the following information relating to Chalcots Estate and in particular, the original re -cladding works undertaken by Camden prior to the devastating fire at Grenfell Tower in 2017, along with remediation works approved by Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government (MHCLG) under the Social sector ACM cladding remediation fund: - 1. For the original re-cladding works, the year the contract was awarded, a general description of the works undertaken and the cost of the contract works, broken down, where applicable, as follows:- o Main contractor contract works o Preliminaries/Main Contractor Costs o Professional fees - Pre and Post Contract o Project contingency allowances o Irrecoverable VAT o Client cost o The names of the contractor and professional consultants. 2. For the remediation works, a general description of the works to be undertaken, and the cost of approved remediation works broken down, where applicable, as follows: - o Removal and reinstatement works o Preliminaries/Main Contractor Costs o Professional fees - Feasibility Stage o Professional fees - Post Tender Stage o Irrecoverable VAT o Client costs o The names of the contractor and professional consultants. This request is exempt under Regulation 12(5)(e) of the Environmental Information Regulations relating to Commercial Confidentiality. This is because the Council has recently started a tender London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk process for the procurement for the cladding works at the Chalcots Estate. See the refusal notice below. Refusal Notice Regulation 12(5)(e) - The regulation states that confidentiality of commercial or industrial information where such confidentiality is provided by law to protect a legitimate economic interest, a public authority can refuse to disclose information if this would adver sely affect the confidentiality of commercial or industrial information. The council is relying upon the higher threshold of likelihood that disclosure would have a prejudicial effect. The parties whose commercial interests are concerned are the previous contractor and the council. The harm that would be caused to the previous contractor is that their commercial details including costs and their detailed business model, would be revealed, which would negatively impact their trading position and ability to secure contacts. The harm that would be caused to the council is that our ability to achieve the best process for a new contract would be reduced as the ‘going rate’ would be disclosed. The link between the disclosure and harm is that for the previous contractor, rival companies would have awareness of their business model and pricing structure which would allow rivals to undercut them and reduce their chances of successfully tendering, and for the council, that disclosure of the current amounts paid and prices would reduce the chance of a wide selection of contractors bidding for the work. In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: • Improving transparency in decision making. • Ensuring value for money. • To ensure accountability of the authority. • Demonstrating the council is meeting its fiduciary duties. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: • It is not in the public interest to disclose information that would be likely to damage the commercial interests of a company, as this could lead to financial problems for the company and/or job losses. • It is not in the public interest to damage the council’s commercial interests, as this affects how it spends public money and the services it can provide to residents and other stakeholders. • It is not in the public interest to release information that cou ld negatively influence ongoing and future negotiations as this could have an adverse effect on value for money for the council, so for residents and other stakeholders. • Withholding the information does not prevent scrutiny of the council’s actions and decisions. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. We considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations overrides the decision to withhold and have concluded that it does not. Document Title: Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) and related matters
Document Text: Date: 11/09/2024 Ref: CAM8501 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 09/09/2024 about Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) and related matters. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response Your request was: Dear Freedom of Information Team,I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 regarding the failure of Camden Council's SEN team directors, managers, and senior staff to respond to emails from vulnerable families. Specifically, I would like to request the following information: Staff Responsibilities and Duties: What are the official duties and responsibilities of SEN directors, managers, and senior staff, particularly in relation to communication with vulnerable families and their representatives? How does failing to respond to vulnerable families and their representatives align with Camden Council’s Code of Conduct, which states that staff must provide the best service and treat residents with dignity and respect? Emails Received and Ignored: How many emails have Diane Osborne, [Named Colleague 1], Vikram Hansrani, and Vikram Hansrani's PA, [Named Colleague 2] , received from vulnerable camden families and their representatives since they started working for Camden Council? How many of these emails have they responded to, and how many have been ignored or left unanswered? What is the reason for not responding and policy to back this up? We are aware that Vikram Hansrani has ignored at least 4 highly vulnerable residents for at least six months each and we find this behaviour to be extremely unprofessional, unfair and unacceptable. Why does he wish to treat vulnerable parents of disabled children who is paid to serve like this? Why does Camden council think this behaviour is acceptable? We are aware that both Diane Osburne and [Named Colleague 1] have never replied to some residents since they started working for Camden less than a year ago. Why London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk is this behaviour accepted by Tim Aldridge as the director of children's services and the monitoring officer Andrew Maughan? We are aware that families have complained and raised concerns. We would like to know how many concerns and complaints were raised about the above named individuals not replying to emails sent to them directly since they started working for Camden council? Please state the approximatw dates they started (we are aware they've all been with camden for 1 year to less than a year except [Named Colleague 2] and we are happy to focus on [Named Colleague 2’s] emails from January 2023-September 2024 to reduce the volume of information being requested. Failure to Respond: Why have these staff members failed to respond to vulnerable families and their representatives? How does this pattern of ignoring communication contradict the council's commitment to treating residents with dignity and respect, as outlined in the Camden Council Code of Conduct? The lack of communication from Camden Council’s SEN team, particularly senior staff, sends a troubling message about the council’s approach to supporting vulnerable families. Ignoring emails from parents advocating for their disabled children suggests a disregard for the challenges these families face and undermines the council's duty to provide timely and effective support. This behaviour implies that the concerns of vulnerable families are not being prioritized, which can lead to a breakdown in trust between the council and its residents. For families already facing emotional and practical difficulties, the silence from key council figures can exacerbate feelings of frustration, isolation, and helplessness. This lack of response contradicts Camden Council’s commitment to treating residents with dignity and respect, as outlined in its Code of Conduct. It may also imply that the council is not fully committed to upholding its obligations to provide a high standard of service, especially when dealing with sensitive matters like EHCPs and support for disabled children. The impact on these families can be profound, as they rely on the council for critical support. What are council policies regarding senior staff ignoring communication? How long should residents expect to obtain a reply to emails from council staff? Please share any policies regarding these issues and disciplinary action regarding such matters. The council holds the information requested but is refusing your request under section 14(1). Section 14(1) refusal notice. The council is refusing your request as it considers that it is vexatious. The council has reason to believe that you are acting together with a number of other requesters as part of a campaign to disrupt the council and particularly the SEND service by the volume of FOI requests around this subject. We have noted an increase in requests around SEND in August and early September which is greater than the normal number. We have also noted an unusual number originating from the ‘WhatDoTheyKnow’ website where it is known that requesters may use pseudonyms to hide their actual identity. There are other features in the requests such as content and style that provide evidence that this is not a coincidental increase but a campaign. A number of requests contain allegations about individual named members of staff, with accusations which are unjustifiably personal and abusive. The staff named in requests have been upset and distressed by such allegations and personal attacks. There is evidence that the requester and those acting with them are using the FOI process not to gain information but to undertake a campaign against individual council officers. In doing this, it damages the reputation of the Freedom of Information legislation itself, particularly as they are made on a public website. Handling the requests place a disproportionate burden in terms of work required to locate, collate and extract information, and in disruption to services. The large number of multiple-part requests submitted in a short space of time have the result of putt ing a disproportionate burden on a small number of staff in the service area who handle such tasks. This disrupts their day-to-day work and has caused anxiety due to the volume and nature of the requests. Those who are part of the campaign have also engaged in frequent emails to the service around these issues as well as complaints. The council has already required the input of senior officers to handle these matters, disrupting normal service delivery for the SEND area, legal services and the Data Protection Advice Team. Whilst the council acknowledges that there may be some serious purpose in the concerns raised in the requests, the wording, the overlapping nature, the mingling of requests for information with complaints and allegations, show that any such serious purpose is outweighed by the vexatious nature of the requests. The council therefore believes that handling this request would cause a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption and distress that will strain council resources and get in the way of delivering mainstream services and answering legitimate requests. Therefore, the council has refused this request as vexatious. We have withheld some staff names under the following exemption. Section 40 (2) personal information. The request also asks for information about certain staff members who are named in the request. In addition to the request being vexatious, the council considers that to disclose the personal data requested would not be in accordance with data protection legi slation and therefore council has withheld this information under the absolute exemption in Section 40 (2). The exemption states that personal data requested may be withheld when to release it would be a breach of the requirements of data protection law which is the UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018. The information withheld is personal information because it allows living individuals to be identified. The council considers that it would be a breach of the General Data Protection Regulation article 5 requirements of fairness and proportionality to publish this personal information in a FOI request. In doing this we have considered the legitimate public interest in disclosure against the interests of the data subject/s and concluded that in the circumstances disclosure would contravene the data protection requirements of fairness and proportionality particularly considering that Freedom of Information responses are public documents and published to the world and not provided just to the requester. The council’s redaction policy states that junior staff member names, (those below Assistant Director level) unless in public facing positions, would not be released in a FOI response. Therefore, the names of junior staff members have been redacted from the request details as they would have no expectation that their details would be released into the public domain, and especially given the content of the request as we consider that to include them would be a breach of the requirements to act fairly and proportionately. Document Text: Date: 28/01/2022 Case reference : CAM2707 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 07/01/2022 about policy documents and templates on facial recognition technology. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: What I am keen to ascertain is whether the council is taking the same/similar approach to other councils and whether councils are referring schools to similar external guidance (if any).  That being the case could I ask you to confirm simply: a) Whether policy documents and templates cover all four of the areas covered – school use of children’s images, whether on school websites, on school social media pages or any other media; - facial recognition technology either by or in schools; - children’s biometric data either by or in schools; when, for data protection purposes, consent should be obtained from parents. If any are not specifically addressed ie because there are no schools in the area using FRT then it would also be helpful to have this confirmed. Our policy documents/templates cover school use of children's images including school websites, social media and other media such as newsletters. It also covers use of children’s biometric data in schools; and when for data protection purposes consent should be obtained from parents. Policies/templates do not cover facial recognition technology (FRT) as we have not been informed of any schools who we support using this technology.  b)         If all four areas are covered please can you indicate very briefly what the broad advice is to schools regarding use of facial recognition technology and biometric data -and if any external documents are referred to ie ICP, DfE could you advise which? We have not advised on FRT as schools have not requested this and we are not aware of any schools we support using the technology. Biometrics data is special category data and therefore requires 'explicit consent' from children aged 13 or above or from parents if the children is under 13. What the consent is for should be made explicitly clear and as with any consent based processing, the option to withdraw consent and how to do this should be made clear to data subjects/parents.  ICO guidance (What is special category data?) is referenced in the biometric policy/templates.  c)         If your documents do indicate at what each children’s consent should be sought rather than parents would you be able to advise what the advice is in this regard – or if your advice is to seek consent from parents would you be able to please confirm this? Document Text: Date: 27/10/2025 Ref: CAM11215 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 29/09/2025 about if the inspected work at Derby Lodge turns out to be substandard, what is Camden’s policy on how to either pursue the organizations for redress or to ask leaseholders for additional payments?. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council does not hold the information requested. Vinci have been awarded a planned works maintenance contract at Derby Lodge known as contract reference RPK1060. If the inspected work turns out to be substandard, will Camden pursue the organisations it has appointed to inspect the work or will it seek redress from Vinci? If there is no written policy on what happens in such circumstance, how does Camden make a decision on which party should bear the cost of putting matters right? The council takes into account matters such as the relevant surrounding circumstances, the specific defects, the wider context, economic considerations of pursuing action, and legal advice, as necessary. Within the contract there is a formal 12 month defects period. At the conclusion of the project now anticipated to be on 21.11.25 we will enter this period. Towards the end of that period all residents and remote leaseholders will be written to asking them to report any defective works. There will also be a joint inspection by the contractors, the chartered surveyor - who acted as the contract administrator, the project manager and the structural engineer who specified the remedial works required. These structural engineers’ recommendations were reviewed by another company of structural engineers who agreed with his findings and recommendations, and these have been previously released. Therefore there is no standard policy or recorded information on what actions it may or may not take if works are not to the necessary standards because this is information asked about a situation that is theoretical, and any decisions would be made based on the exact situation and circumstances that occurred. This type of decision making is within the professional ambit of those who would make the decision and like many areas of professional work are not reduced to writing, but form part of the relevant officers’ praxis. As the information not held is environmental we have to comply with a technicality and tell you that because it is not held it is excepted under Regulation 12 (4)(a). Document Text: Date: 20/12/2021 Case reference : CAM2594 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we do not hold the information requested and why. The Council may not hold written records to provide a response to all of my questions. Naturally, my desire is to receive the answers to the questions - it is irrelevant to me whether you utilise the FOI mechanism or provide it voluntarily as part of handling my complaint. My preference would be to avoid you or myself trawling through records to answer what seems like simple questions for Trading Standards to answer. Therefore, can I make the following suggestion. Where possible, the Trading Standards officer who considers my complaint attempts to answer the following questions. For those questions that remain unanswered, I have included a request for records that seeks to obtain the same. NB: ‘face coverings’ below refers to community face coverings and surgical face masks worn outside of healthcare activities, so not those defined as Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) or a medical device. 1. Is it true that anyone can set up a business in the UK to make or sell face coverings, without any prior requirement to demonstrate experience or knowledge of textiles or product safety laws to an independent body? If there is a legal requirement, please can you advise the relevant law and section This information is already publicly available.  Please enter this link into your web browser: here: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file /920648/Guidance-for-businesses-and-individuals-face-coverings-version-4.pdf 2. Is it true that face coverings made in the UK are not required to be independently safety tested at the point of manufacture? If there is a legal requirement, please can you advise the relevant law and section Please see response to question 1 above. 3. Is it true that businesses can import face coverings into the UK from anywhere in the world, without a requirement for the importer to evidence their experience or knowledge of textiles or product safety laws to an independent body? If there is a legal requirement, please can you advise the relevant law and section Please see response to question 1 above. 4. Is it true that UK retailers are not required to provide trading standards with evidence of the safety of the face coverings they are retailing before they are made available to the public? If there is a legal requirement, please advise the relevant law and section Please see response to question 1 above. Only if Trading Standards has not answered questions 1-4, I would be grateful to receive a copy of the records relating to one retailer and one manufacturer where they have provided evidence to Trading Standards, detailing their experience or knowledge of textiles and product safety laws. Document Title: Local land charges search
Document Text: Date: 06/10/2020 Ref: CAM494 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 17/09/2020 about local land charges search. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding some of the information because it is excepted. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we are withholding information and what exceptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why the exceptions apply. 1. Your current waiting/turnaround time for a local authority search (also known as local land charges search) enquiry to be completed. If feasible, we would like a waiting time for each type of search (LLC1, CON29, CON290). If t his is not possible, a waiting time for all search types is fine. This information is publicly available on our website at https://www.camden.gov.uk/local- land-charges 2. Data on how many of these searches you completed in these months: • August 2018 • August 2019 • August 2020 in this instance, we only need one total search figure per month stated (not figures for LLC1, CON29, CON290). If historic data is not available, then a figure just for August 2020 if fine. This question is excepted under Regulation 12(5)(e) of the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. See the refusal notice below. Refusal Notice Regulation 12(5)(e) - The regulation states that confidentiality of commercial or industrial information where such confidentiality is provided by law to protect a legitimate economic interest, a public authority can refuse to disclose information if this would adversely affect the confidentiality of commercial or industrial information. The council is relying upon the higher threshold of likelihood that disclo sure would have a prejudicial effect. The commercial interests of the Council are concerned as it carries out local authority searches for a fee. The harm that would be caused to the council is that by providing monthly search numbers, it would reveal the actual income to the Council from searches and so valuable information would be disclosed to private companies carrying out their own searches who could then undercut the Council. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as fo llows: • Improving transparency in decision making. • Ensuring value for money. • To ensure accountability of the authority. • Demonstrating the council is meeting its fiduciary duties. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows : • It is not in the public interest to damage the council’s commercial interests, as this affects how it spends public money and the services it can provide to residents and other stakeholders. • Withholding the figures does not prevent scrutiny of the council’s act ions and decisions. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. We considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations overrides the decision to withhold and have concluded that it does not. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained what exceptions applies.  Please see the refusal notice below which explains how and why they it applies. Please provide information on the following for all illegal parking reports made in 2021 and 2022: 1. All reports made by citizens to council services for illegal and dangerously parked vehicles 2. The method of each report, including phone call, webform, email, messaging service, love clean streets app, social media or any other method in use by your council 3. The location by postcode or latitude and longitude of each reported incident of illegal parking 4. The outcome of each report, broken down by investigated, attended, enforced (PCN or FPN), warning letter sent, closed without investigation, and any other classification used by your council 5. Time and date for each stage of the report, including time of initial report and time/date of each subsequent stage in the progression of each report. 6. PCNs and FPNs issued by the council’s traffic enforcement staff or parking enforcement staff, or third party contractors working on the council’s behalf that were not raised by citizen reporting methods 7. The location by postcode or latitude and longitude of each incident listed in item 6.8. Time and date for each stage of the incidents listed in item 6, including time of initial report and time/date of each subsequent stage in the progression of each report. To avoid double counting, please indicate clearly on points if 6, 7 and 8 if the initial report for the illegal parking was made by a citizen reporting method. We are not processing this request as it would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exception notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exception that applies is: regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable We have considered the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it, collate it and then to review and redact any sensitive information that will be subject to further exceptions under the EIR 2004. We have also considered the impact and burden that processing this request would have on the team who would have to deal with it. We have concluded that the time and effort involved would place a disproportionate burden on the team and severely impact their ability to perform their normal duties. We have calculated that it will take approx. 1094 hours (minimum) to comply with your request because: there is currently no database that holds this information in an easily accessible way● most of these enquires would be submitted via the parking operation email address● officers would have to go through 13,134 emails to determine each is related to the request● this would take at a conservative estimate an average of 5 minutes per email● for emails containing the requested information, running reports to locate all the necessary information to answer all the questions would likely take between 1 -2 hours per case● In applying this exception, the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004. The public interest argument for releasing this information is:- it would improve the transparency for the general public of the Council’s decisions and processes in dealing with illegal and dangerous parking reports.●The public interest arguments for withholding the information are:- processing this request in full would be provide a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council● this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities, and:● it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s the provision of services to the public● It is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request● It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004. We considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not.
