Decisions relating to the setting up of a neighbourhood assembly (Q 1 – 7) A formal commitment to produce a Community Vision - a planning framework to develop a coherent spatial strategy for the neighbourhood – was made by Cabinet as part of the decision report dated 17 July 2019. This committed the Council to develop such a vision alongside the local community and wider neighbourhood. The Community Vision, as a piece of planning guidance, will seek to set and agree priorities for the area and would have material weight in determining planning applications within the framework area. It will not directly deliver or approve development but will guide any proposed development in the area as well as setting priorities for investment. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk As the Community Vision document is intended to be adopted as a piece of supplementary planning guidance, the Cabinet Member for Investing in Communities, Culture and an Inclusive Economy will need to make a formal decision to adopt any final p lanning vision/supplementary planning document. A formal decision will also be taken prior to the commencement of a statutory consultation process on the basis of a draft document once produced. We expect a decision on whether to proceed with formal consul tation on the basis of a draft Community Vision to be made by the Cabinet Member in the late spring 2021. Following on from the July 2019 Cabinet decision, officers began designing an engagement strategy to collect feedback that would be used to help shape a Community Vision. After the success of the Climate Crisis Citizen’s Assembly held earlier in the year by the Council’s Participation team, the use of an assembly as part of this engagement strategy was seen as an exciting opportunity to add value and support this process. As such, during winter 2019 external consultants were appointed to help with selection and facilitation of such an assembly. Throughout the winter and spring plans for engagement activities were developed by officers. During this process, all ward councillors and the Cabinet member were regularly briefed and asked for their feedback. The neighbourhood assembly for Gospel Oak and Haverstock was subsequently established as one element of a wider engagement strategy. The assembly is formed of a group of 30 broadly demographically representative and randomly selected residents. This is one of the forms of engagement being used to collect feedback on a range of topics to help shape draft vision - but crucially just one form. The feedback collected from wider engagement efforts will play an equal part in the shaping of the vision to that received from the assembly. The assembly is not a formal decision making body, and any advice and recommendations given to the Council would not be binding. Since September we have held four initial sessions with the assembly as well as launching a community wide survey, where everyone is able to have a say in the vision’s development. The assembly meetings have been chaired and overseen by professional facilitat ors and have been designed to ensure that the residents are able to speak openly about the material presented without feeling pressured. Information about the topics covered, speakers as well as recordings from the sessions are publicly available on the project website ( https://gohcommunityvision.commonplace.is/schemes/proposals/neighbourhood - assembly/details ). The community survey is already seeing a high level of responses from a diverse range of residents, with over three weeks remaining (at th e time of writing). This is reflective of the fact that many residents in the local community feel passionately about their area and wish to contribute towards the shaping of a vision for the future. All of this feedback will be collected and used to develop a draft vision, prior to a formal decision being made on whether or not to progress to a formal consultation on the basis of a draft Community Vision. 8. An established standard of assemblies of this type is that a pool of potential assembly members is created through random selection, and then assembly members are selected from this pool using random stratified sampling based on demographic criteria to ensure that they are broadly representative of the wider population. Document Text: Date: 04/12/2019 Ref: FOI13485 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 07/11/2019 about Thames Water . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested . However we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we are withh olding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which exp lain how and why the exemptions apply. 1. Camden Councils contract to collect their tenants water charges on behalf of Thames Water ended on 31 st March 2019.Who terminated that contract Camden Council or Thames Water. Thames Water terminated the contract 2.Camden Council claim to have obtain legal advice which supports the council position that it was not buyi ng and reselling water from Thames Water to its tenants living in unmetered properties. Can you confirm what that legal advice was ? It is correct that Camden Council have received legal advice on this issue. As with other legal advice that advice is lega lly privileged and is exempt under Section 42 . See the refusal notice below. However in broad terms the position is that under the contract the Council collected water charges from tenants on behalf of Thames Water. Under this arrangement, the level of the charg es the Council collected was entirely set by Thames Water with no input from the Council. There was no buying and reselling of water by the Council and it was purely acting as agent for Thames Water in collecting charges. 3.Ca n you confirm that in accordance with the terms of the contract with Thames Water, Camden Council received an administration fee and not commission. This is correct. Under the contract the Council received an administration fee for acting as Thames Water’ s agent and did not receive any commission from Thames Water . 4.Camden Council state that a charge for their void properties was included in their administration charge, should this void charge have been returned to their tenants by way of a reduction in w ater charges. The Council provided billing and collection services, in return for a void allowance for empty properties to reflect both the administrative costs attached and the transfer of risk and bad debt associated with these accounts. Tenants are ch arged exactly the same as what Thames would have charged, had they been billed directly through Thames Water. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 5.Camden Council state that they paid their tenants water charges by bulk charge, this would have included tenants unpaid water charges, therefor e did Camden Council pay their tenants unpaid water charges. This is correct, the Council had paid Thames in full of all water charges, irrespective of whether the tenant had paid or not. Refusal notice S ection 42 - Legal Professional Privilege The information held for question 2 is exempt under Section 42(1) of the Freedom of Information Act because it is protected by L egal Professional Privilege (LPP) . LPP covers communications between lawyers and their clients for obtaining legal advice, or docum ents created by or for lawyers for the main purpose of litigation. Section 42 ensures that the confidential relationship between lawyer and client is protected , ensures openness between them , and safeguard s access to fully informed, realistic and frank leg al advice . The information withheld is covered by this exemption because it covers legal advice received by the Council from counsel. The exemption is qualified so is subject to a public interest test. The public interest argumen ts for releasing this information are as follows: • It would improve the transparency of the decision making process • It will allow the council’s decisions to be examined and held to account The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: • There is very strong inherent public interest in maintaining LPP and allowing the council to take legal advice in a confidential way • Disclosure of the legal advice could prejudice the Council’s ability to defend or prosecute its legal interests, by unfairly exposing its legal position to challenge, or by disclosing its approach to and tactics in legal areas. • It is in the public interest that the decisions taken by the Council are taken in a fully informed legal context The council has concluded that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. Question 2 asks for the number of individuals/households in temporary accommodation, average length of stay and household type. We do not hold the data requested in an easily accessible format. This is because the council is undergoing a large data migration project that is affecting our capacity to access and analyse data efficiently. The migration process adds an extra layer of complexity and time to the task of retrieving data, if held. In question 3 you have requested ‘current daily housing rates paid for temporary accommodation.’ We do not hold payment rates in this way. Agreements for determining the rates applied to the procurement of temporary accommodation in London are complex. The Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rate given for a household is the starting point for determining the cost of placing a household in temporary accommodation. The rates vary for each household according to the size and location of their temporary accommodation and is set nationally by the Valuation Office Agency (VOA). Camden is one of the boroughs that has committed to procure temporary accommodation at the Pan- London rates, in line with the Inter Borough Accommodation Agreement (IBAA) administered by the West London Alliance. The VOA divides London into a geography of Broad Rental Market Areas (BRMA), each having different rates for temporary accommodation that cuts across borough boundaries. The IBAA procurement agreement allows each borough to pay slightly different rates for properties in the same BRMA. In the period July-September 2023, 633 households were identified as being in temporary accommodation. To locate the data requested in question 2 and part of question 3, would require a council officer generate a report of households currently in temporary accommodation, manually read each case note to pinpoint the specific data. Based on a sample of 10 cases where some case notes were unclear, it took approx. 3 minutes per case to gather and analyse the data. We have calculated to provide the information for all 633 households in the quarter year would take approx. 31.65 hours. To review data for the entire year would take approx. four times as long and total in excess of 125 hours. This exceeds the 18 hours’ appropriate limit set by the Act. Please enter the following link into your web browser: https://opendata.camden.gov.uk/stories/s/Camden-Freedom-Of-Information-Response and search for CAM7141 and CAM7402. As the information requested is reasonably accessible elsewhere it is exempt under the absolute exemption in Section 21. We receive a number of requests for temporary accommodation and have published a standard FOI response to explain why we do not currently hold some of the information, the exemption we use and further details. The response is in the Freedom of Information FAQ dataset, the exact link is: Freedom Of Information FAQs | Open Data Portal , scroll down to ‘Temporary Accommodation Commercial FOI requests FAQs 091024.pdf.’ Section 21 as explained above applies. After viewing the above information, you may wish to submit a new request for question 1 and refine questions 2, 3 and 4 to comply with the 18-hour time limit explained above. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. This is in regards to the application 2025/1375/P). We are looking for two things: 1. any internal communication in the council regarding this application for development at the Lamorna site in the last three years. 2. any communication between the council and the applicant (including Maddox Planning and HGG London) regarding this development We are not processing this request.  It would involve a disproportionate amount of time, effort and expense to the council and is excepted under the EIR 2004.  Please see the exception notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exception that applies is:regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable. We have also considered the time it will take the council to locate the information requested in the request, to extract it, collate it and then to review and redact any sensitive information that will be subject to further exceptions under the EIR 2004. The information that falls under the scope of the current request took over 4 hours to initially collate and amounts to 909 pages when compiled. Disproportionate time would be needed to redact personal information and redact or remove information that is subject to other exceptions under EIR 2004 after consideration of the public interest involved. Each page will need to be checked for this information and to check and redact or remove excepted information will take at least 3 mins per page. The time therefore to fully process this request would require over a minimum time of 49 hours. We have considered the impact and burden that processing this request would have on the team who would have to deal with it. We have concluded that the time, effort and costs involved would place a disproportionate burden on the team and severely impact their ability to perform their normal duties. In applying this exception, the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004.  We have indicated the weight of each of these considerations. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: - it would improve the transparency for the general public of the council’s decisions and processes in dealing with the planning application 2025/1375/P. • The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: - processing this request in full would be provide a large burden in terms of officer time and cost to the Council (High). • this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the council’s core business activities, (High) and: • it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s provision of services to the public (High). • it is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request (High). • It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004. We considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not. Advice and assistance You may want to greatly reduce the time period of your request and/or consider which topics are of particular interest to you for which we could more easily search our records and result in complied information that would not take a disproportionate time to process. Document Title: ‘Trans toolkits'
Document Text: Date: 09/06/2020 Case reference : CAM58 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 22/05/2020 about ‘trans toolkits' . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: 1: Has your council ever issued a ‘trans toolkit’? We are committed to being consciously inclusive so that everyone can bring their best self to work. Our internal Inclusion Statement sets out our approach on how to do this so everyone in Camden feels included and is able to be who they are, feel valued, safe and respected by each other every day. In 2019, we launched our Statement of Commitment to Trans Equality. This acts as our organisational ‘toolkit’ to support employees who are transitioning and explicitly highlight our commitment to creating a safe and inclusive environment for these employees. We worked with our trade unions and LGBT+ staff network to develop the statement which was then also reviewed as part of our submission to the Stonewall Workplace Equality Index last year. 1.1: If so, when was it issued and where was it used? The Statement of Commitment to Trans Equality was published on the Council’s intranet in October 2019 and is used by staff and managers throughout the organisation. The statement is promoted via staff emails during Pride, intranet, manager workshops and via our LGBT+ staff network. 2: Have you ever pulled the use of a ‘trans toolkit’? 2.1: If so, when did this happen and why? N/A. We have never pulled the use of a ‘trans toolkit.’ 3: Does your council generally support trans people using the toilets they choose to inyour area (either M, F, or Gender Neutral where possible)? We offer a disabled toilet which is gender neutral as well as male and female segregated toilets on every floor of our main offices. In our Statement of Commitment to Trans Equality, we also state that “It is up to you to decide which gender toilet you wish to use when the time is right. You may choose to use the disabled toilets on the basis that they are gender neutral. But we won’t make you. It’s your choice and we’ll support you”. We have also engaged in a range of work to further support our LGBT+ colleagues. In 2019, we entered the Stonewall Equality Index for the first time to help us benchmark our employment practices and use the submission as a learning experience. As such, since the results we have updated our HR and recruitment systems to include a ‘prefer to self describe’ and ‘Mx’ reporting field to reflect different sexual orientation and gender fluid identities. We have also worked with our staff network to update our policies to ensure we are being inclusive of trans employees and using gender neutral language. Our ‘We Make Camden Proud’ campaign saw us joining 1.5 million others to march in solidarity with our LGBT+ community at London Pride 2019, running family-friendly events across the borough, sharing stories from staff from every corner of the organisation and raising more than £1,000 for local LGBT+ charity ‘The Outside Project’ from the sale of our hugely popular We Make Camden Proud rainbow lanyards. To ensure we are continually reviewing our practices, we have also signed up to become Stonewall Diversity Champions this year. Document Text: Date: 13/06/2022 Case reference : CAM3404 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 25/05/2022 about Council Tax Support claimants, working-age, receiving maximum, court summons, and further details .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answers which explains how and why it applies. 1. How many Council Tax Support claimants were there in your authority on 31st March 2022? There were 22,669 Council Tax Support claimants. 2. Of those claimants how many were:  a. Working-age There were 15,700 of working age. b. Receiving the maximum support available under your scheme 16,290 received the maximum support available. 3. How many court summons for non-payment of Council tax were issued in 2021/22?  A total of 26,213 summonses were sent for the 2021/2022 financial year. 4. Of those summonsed how many received Council Tax Support? We are not processing this request as it would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort,and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. 5. Of those summonsed and in receipt of Council Tax Support, how many were charged court costs and what was the total amount of those costs? We are not processing this request as it would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. 6. How many Council Tax Support claimants had a liability order issued against them for non- payment of council tax in 2021/22? We are not processing this request as it would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. 7. Of those Council Tax Support claimants with a liability order issued against them how many:  a. Had deduction from benefits requested in 2021/22? b. Had deduction from earnings requested in 2021/22? c. Had enforcement agents engaged to recover the debt in 2021/22? We are not processing this request as it would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. 8. What was the Minimum Payment under your Borough’s Council Tax Support scheme in 2021/22? There are no minimum payments in our Council Tax Support scheme. 9. How many residents receiving council tax support were in arrears with their council tax as 31st March 2022? We wouldn’t be able to identify purely arrears cases at 31/03/22 as our system reports are as at the date you run them which means any payments, liability adjustments done since would update the position in terms of arrears bought forward into 2022. To answer this question would therefore require a manual exercise which would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. 10. What is the total amount of council tax payable from people receiving council tax support in 2021/22? We would have to manually check the caseload of all recipients, work out the amount awarded(including any changes across the year) and net that off the charge.  This would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. 11. What is the total amount of council tax outstanding from people receiving council tax support in 2021/22? Please see above regarding manual checks.  This would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense.  Please see the exemption notice set out below. 12. How much did you spend on council tax support in 2021/22? We spent £29,306,305 on council tax support. 13. If you have a hardship fund specifically for CTS claimants in arrears:  a) what was the budget for the hardship fund in 2021/22? b) how much of the hardship fund was spent in in 2021/22? c) how many CTS claimants were made an award from this hardship fund in 2021/22? We do not have a hardship fund specifically for claimants, although legislation does allow for Council Tax to be written off.  We spent £1,223,576.06 clearing the pre 2021/22 arrears of anyone in receipt of 90% or more Council Tax Support. Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 12: cost of compliance exceeds appropriate limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit".  This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We have calculated that it will take approx. 1,629 hours (at a very conservative minimum) to comply with your request because: To answer Q4 - Q7:26,213 summonses would need to be manually checked to provide relevant information● this would take more than a minimum of 2 minutes per case to collate the information● To answer Q9 – Q11, we would need to: manually check all 22,669 benefit claimants against balances on 31/03/22● we would then need to try match them up and see what the position was historically● this information would take far more than a minimum of 2 minutes per case to collate● Advice and Assistance It would be difficult to refine the request so that it would take less than 18 hours.  We may be able to spot check a limited number of summonses or take a small a sample of cases in arrears to see how many were in receipt of benefits - but this may not provide a representative sample that would be meaningful.  Please contact me if you would like further assistance with this. Document Text: Date: 24 November 2025 Ref: CAM11214 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 29 September 2025 about services offered to homeless rough sleepers in a building-based environment. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. 1. Which of the following five essential basic services for homeless rough sleepers, resident in your borough, has an organisation, or organisations, been currently commissioned and paid by your Local Authority to provide to homeless rough sleepers, in a building-based environment. The services referenced in sections 1.2 to 1.5 are delivered as part of the council’s standard operation. 1.1 Hot Food – No. 1.2 Drinking Water – Yes. 1.3 Hot Beverages – Yes. 1.4 Hot Showers – Yes. 1.5 Laundry Facilities – Yes. 2. What is/are the full name(s) and contact details of the organisation(s) commissioned to provide the five listed essential basic services for homeless rough sleepers, resident in the borough? Refusal notice: Section 43(2): Commercial interests The information is withheld under Section 43(2) commercial interests of the Freedom of Information Act. The parties whose commercial interests are concerned are bidders in a live tender process for this contract. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Disclosure at this stage could prejudice the tender process by providing an unfair advantage to a bidder through access to additional information. The council is relying upon this higher threshold of likelihood that disclosure would have a prejudicial effect. As this is a qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. Public interest arguments in favour of disclosure: • Improving transparency in decision making. Disclosure would allow the public to better understand how the council commissions services and allocates resources, promoting confidence in its processes. (Medium weight) • Ensuring value for money. Providing this information could help demonstrate that public funds are spent effectively and competitively. (Medium weight) • Promoting accountability of the authority. Making the details available would enable residents, stakeholders and others to hold the council to account for its commissioning decisions and service delivery. (Light weight) • Demonstrating the council is meetings its fiduciary duties. (Medium weight) Factors for withholding the information are as follows: • Protecting the council’s commercial interests. Disclosure at this stage could compromise the integrity of the ongoing tender process, potentially reducing competition and harming the council’s ability to achieve best value for public funds. (medium weight) • Preventing adverse impact on future negotiations. Releasing this information prematurely could distort the procurement process and weaken the council’s negotiating position, resulting in less favourable outcomes for residents, stakeholders and service users. (medium weight) • Maintaining scrutiny without prejudice. Withholding this information does not prevent oversight of the council’s decisions, as established mechanisms remain in place to ensure accountability without exposing commercial sensitive details. (Light weight) • Staff wellbeing. Premature disclosure could lead to increased pressure or undue influence on staff involved in the procurement process, which may affect their ability to carry out duties impartially and effectively. (Medium weight). We have considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure under the Act overrides the decision to withhold the information and concluded that it does not. On balance, the public interest in maintaining the exemption outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. 3. How many days of the week has your Local Authority commissioned the service provider(s) to supply the five listed essential basic services for homeless rough sleepers, resident in the borough – and on which days of the week? Five days, Monday to Friday. 4. Have the five listed essential basic services for homeless rough sleepers been commissioned for provision throughout the year – including Bank Holidays – particularly Christmas and New Year – in other words 365 days a year? If not, state how many days a year your Local Authority has currently contracted the provider(s) to supply commissioned essential basic services for the homeless rough sleepers resident in the borough. Monday to Friday throughout the year, excluding bank holidays. Document Title: Empty Properties
Document Text: Date: 3rd March 2020 Ref: FOI13904 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated the 4th February 2020 about empty Properties . We have dealt with this under the F reedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested , howeve r we are withholding some of this information because it is exempt . The answers to your questions are below w e have state d where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which exp lain how and why the exemptions apply. 1) Please could you tell me the present total number of empty council pr operties on Rowley Way NW8 . - This question was responded to in your acknowledgement letter dated the 4th February 2020 2) Please also tell me the number of properties in the condition needed for letting. We do not provide a list of empty domestic properties. We consider this is exempt from disclosure under section 31 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 We do not release the names or businesses or addresses of empty residential properties as we cons ider disclosing this information would make them a target of crime. Therefore this information is exempt from disclosure under section 31 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Section 31(1)(a) says that we do not need to provide information that would b e likely to prejudice the functions of law enforcement - the prevention and detection of crime. Camden believes that releasing this information would increase the likelihood of :  Empty properties being lived in by squatters. Squatting in a residential pr operty is now a criminal offence.  Empty properties being targeted by vandals or graffiti artists and stripped of materials such as roofing, cables or piping, or otherwise vandalised or damaged.  Empty properties being targeted by criminals or terroris ts for example allowing them to hide or store the proceeds of crime, or criminal or terrorist materials In the Information Tribunal Case No. EA/2011/0007 (Voyias and LB Camden), the Tribunal was satisfied that the evidence was that disclosing this inform ation would have the effect of assisting at least some of those wishing to engage in squatting, leading to an increase in the this. Squatting in residential property is a criminal offence which shows the negative nature of squatting and crimes such as crim inal damage that are often associated with it. In Voyias the Tribunal concluded that an increase in squatting would also lead to various categories of associated criminal activity. As a result the Tribunal found that section 31(1) (a) was engaged in that i t was likely that disclosure of the disputed information would have a negative impact on the prevention of crime. Information and Records Management Law and Governance Directorate London Borough of Camden Town Hall Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Public Interest Test: As Section 31 is a qualified exemption we need to consider the public interest test. Factors in favour of disclosure  There are general arguments in promoting transparency and accountability of public authorities.  Raising the profile of vacant properties would help encourag e public engagement and debate.  Factors in favour of withholding  There is an inherent pub lic interest in crime prevention. This was considered in the Voyias case by the Tribunal.  There is public interest in avoiding the costs associated with squatting, for example repair, security and eviction costs.  The negative impact of squatting affe cts the surrounding community and public authorities involved, not just the individual property We believe that the balance of public interest lies in upholding the exemption and not releasing the information. This decision was upheld in Voyias and recen tly by the ICO in a decision notice in the case of Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea. Advice and Assistance We know that some requesters will have genuine reasons for asking for this information. However releasing information under the Freedom of I nformation Act is providing it to the whole world not just the individual requester and we cannot take an individual requester’s reasons for asking into account. You might find that the council’s Empt y Property page is useful: https://www.camden.gov.uk /housing#section -1 The council also publis hes the current list of council owned properties available for sale or rent on our website, some of which may be empty. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 16/07/2020 about children with an Education Health Care Plan. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.   Response 1.The number of children on an education, health and care plan (EHCP) in the local authority area as of March 1 who required a risk assessment, including but not exclusive to whether they could attend school, during the coronavirus crisis. 2.The total number of risk assessments the council has collected about pupils, including both ones conducted by the school and reported back to the council and those undertaken by the council, depending on the local approach, between March 1 and today (July 16) 3. If it was concluded in the risk assessment that a child was not able to go to school, the reason why. 4.The number of risk assessments that decided a child could attend school. We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit".  This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We are sorry but the information you are seeking is not held in a reportable format this is because we do not report on this information. In order to locate the information you are seeking would require an officer to conduct a manual trawl and read in excess of 1,399 files to ascertain where this information is held. We estimate that to do this would take approximately 130 hours to complete Advice and Assistance When we refuse a request under Section 12 we have to provide the requester with advice and assistance on how to refine their request so it would fall within the 18 hours limit.  We have considered carefully how we can do this and we have concluded  that in this case this is not possible. This is because d ue to the time it would require to go through each file and read each risk assessment and the reason which  in some cases may not be clear this would not provide uniform responses as each case would be so unique. In addition the risk assessments would have changed over time so a child where it was considered safer to access on line learning in March , may have been attending on site education in May or June  either due to personal circumstances or changes in guidance. We do not have the capacity to clarify or track the changes for each individual pupil . The exception that applies is: regulation 12(3) which states “ the information requested includes personal data of which the applicant is not the data subject, the personal data shall not be disclosed otherwise than in accordance with regulation 13. ” regulation 13(1) states: “(1) To the extent that the information requested includes personal data of which the applicant is not the data subject and as respects which either the first or second condition below is satisfied, a public authority shall not disclose the personal data. (2) The first condition is — (a) in a case where the information falls within any of paragraphs (a) to (d) of the definition of “data” in section 1(1) of the Data Protection Act 1998, that the disclosure of the information to a member of the public otherwi se than under these Regulations would contravene — (i) any of the data protection principles; ” London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. The name and contact details of the requester have also been redacted. TWENTY CREDITON HILL FREEHOLD COMPANY AND 20 CREDITON HILL LIMITED20 CREDITON HILL, LONDON NW6 1HP Mr copy to:Building Control Ms Tulip Siddiq, MPPlace Management House of CommonsSupporting Communities London SW1A OAALondon Borough of Camden5 Pancras SquareLondon N1C 4AG Enforcement No: 14/DS/00777 March 2018Dear Mr RE: The London Building Acts (Amendment) Act 1939Part VII - Dangerous and neglected structuresFurther to my email dated 18 January 2018 and follow up call requesting an onsite meeting neither of which you responded to, our appointed independent Civil & Structural Engineer and certain owners of 20 Crediton Hill have spent a phenomenal amount of time dealing with the dangerous wall between our property at 20 Crediton Hill and the GDST (“the Girls Day School Trust”)/HCC (“the Hampstead Cricket Club”). All of this has been necessary because Camden/you issued a Dangerous Structure Notice to Twenty Crediton Hill Freehold Company without checking ownership and responsibility for the wall, instead responding to allegations from the GDST whose tenant the HCC was a major contributor over decades to the wall failure. This should have been abundantly evident to you when you conducted a site visit last December.I urgently request that you rescind the Notice you served on Twenty Crediton Hill Freehold Company on 11 January 2018 and instead serve the Notice on the GDST/HCC as a significant cause of the wall failure is due to the HCC excavating a path and exposing the foundations of the wall, building a pavilion and extensions including drainage in extremely close proximity to the wall and to the neglect of tree and vegetation maintenance over many years by the HCC.I am copying this letter/email to our local MP, Ms Tulip Siddiq.Ownership of wall I reconfirm that the wall is not on the Title Plan or Register for Twenty Crediton Hill Freehold Company Limited. The wall appears to be on “no man’s land”, a hitherto unregistered strip of land which was acquired by the GDST/HCC in 2017 following over a century of occupation by the HCC. It was a public path or right of way together with a banked verge abutting the boundary wall. The GDST wrote to us in April 2014 stating that “the boundary surveyor’s report about the ownership of the wall reaches the conclusion that the wall does not run along the boundary between our properties, but appears to lie on a narrow strip of unregistered land that was once a banked verge. It is not clear who owns the land as it does not appear to form part of our respective titles. This means that repair obligations are also unclear.”The 13.2 metres long, approximately 1 metre high (low) mass concrete wall built in front of the original brick boundary wall was erected there by persons unknown but in all probability by the HCC many years ago as only the HCC had access to that area at all times. The mass concrete wall is built on the hitherto unregistered land that was acquired by the GDST in 2017. Therefore it would appear that the GDST now owns the mass concrete wall.Wall condition report from Structural Engineer (extract from report) 2.24 To summarise, the wall backing number 20 Crediton Hill amounts to: (working from the southern boundary with number 18 Crediton Hill)In 230 mm thick brickwork,( + piers), 1.8metres length at 3.2 metres height; clearly dangerousIn 230 “ “ , 6.8 metres length at 2.8 metres height; clearly dangerousIn mass concrete, a separate low wall in front of the boundary brick wall , 5.0 metres length at 0.8 metres height; clearly dangerous In mass concrete, a separate low wall in front of the boundary brick wall 8.2 metres length at 0.7 metres height; rotated badly In total an overall combined length of boundary around 21.8 metres Responsibility for the wall We fully recognise that the wall must be made safe. It retains land on our side and is occupied by the GDST/HCC on the other side. We do not know who built the 8.6m brick boundary wall and when it was built. The only part of the wall that was visible from and accessible by the owners of 20 Crediton Hill was the top 850mm to 1m of the 8.6m wall on the southern boundary of 20 Crediton Hill. It was agreed with 20 Crediton Hill residents in 2014 that the GDST would remove the top section of that wall as an interim safety measure. However nothing was done by the GDST and grounds staff and others continued to access the grounds by the unsafe wall.Despite our requests to the GDST/HCC to expand the exclusion zone around the 8.6 metre long brick wall while a resolution is being worked on, they have taken no action thus far to further protect grounds staff from accessing that area other than give verbal warnings. In checking the wall recently, we found further deep cracks hidden behind embedded ivy thus heightening the risk of collapse. Without admission of any liability whatsoever on our side, we instructed our garden contractor to remove the top 800mm x 8.6 metres of the full length of that high brick wall that was visible and accessible from 20 Crediton Hill’s garden. By doing so the immediate danger of the aforesaid portion of that high brick boundary wall moving further or collapsing has been eliminated. This is because, although we do not consider it to be our responsibility, we feel that safety comes first and we will do what we can from our side. As noted above, in 2017 the GDST acquired ownership of the land on which the 13.2m mass concrete wall is built in front of the original boundary wall and accordingly acquired responsibility for that section of the wall.WITHOUT ADMITTING ANY LIABILITY WHATSOEVER, I have been pressing our adjoining owner, the GDST, to see if a shared approach (together the GDST, the HCC and 20 Crediton Hill residents) could be agreed. In 2014 as well as instigating some remedial work to the wall the GDST were advocating a joint approach to the problem.Damage to the wall The HCC has built pavilion extensions in extremely close proximity to the wall behind our garden and also excavated a land back that backed on to and supported the wall without putting in alternative support measures. Our independent Civil and Structural Engineer has found that a significant cause of the wall failure was and is due to actions (or lack of) by the HCC. The GDST/HCC allowed trees and vegetation on the banked verge behind No 20’s garden to grow uncontrolled further contributing to destabilising the wall. Accordingly we consider that the repairs to be done to the damaged wall should be undertaken by the GDST/HCC.Remedial actions taken by the owners of 20 Crediton Hill Without admission of any liability of any kind on our side whatsover, we instructed our garden contractor to remove the top 800mm high section of the high brick wall over its full length of 8 metres of the wall which was visible and accessible from 20 Crediton Hill’s garden. This was because, although we do not consider it to be our responsibility, we feel that safety comes first and we will do what we can from our side. We do not accept liability for the damage to that wall. In parallel with our ongoing investigations into the dangerous wall structure, as agreed with you in our initial telephone call in January, we commissioned the services of an independent Civil and Structural Engineer to prepare alternative designs for making safe the various sections of the dangerous wall. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 03/10/2024 about section 106 agreements.   We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding some of the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice which explains how and why it applies. Freedom of Information request - Repayment of S106 Contributions Do you have an excel sheet of unexpended/unused/unspent s106 contributions as the particular clawback of 5/7/10 years has expired? Perhaps we could start there? In essence I am asking the following; 1. Do you have an excel sheet of unexpended/unused/unspent s106 contributions as the particular clawback of 5/7/10 years has expired? No, we do not have this kind of spreadsheet. 2.  If you hold data for the last 10 years, please can you confirm the amounts that may be sat in your accounts that can no longer be used dependant on the clawback from January 1st 2014 to the present 2024? This information is excepted under the EIR 2004.  Please see the exception notice set out below.Refusal Notice The exception that applies is: regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable . We have considered the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it, collate it and then to review and redact any sensitive information that will be subject to further exceptions under the EIR 2004. We have also considered the impact and burden that processing this request would have on the teams who would have to deal with it. We have concluded that the time, effort and costs involved would place a disproportionate burden on the team and severely impact their ability to perform their normal duties. We have calculated that it will take over an estimated 2,500 hours (minimum) to comply with your request. This is because: it would require examining over 5000 records with our finance and spending services.• it will take an average of 30 minutes (minimum) to examine each record to find and collate the information requested.• In applying this exception, the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: - it would improve the transparency for the general public of the Council’s decisions and processes in dealing with s106 agreements.• The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: - processing this request in full would be provide a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council.• this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities, and:• it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s the provision of services to •the public. it is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request.• It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004. We considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not. Advice and Assistance It would be difficult to refine the request so that it would not be unreasonable.  We may be able to spot check a limited number of agreements for very short defined time periods, but this is unlikely to provide a representative sample that would be meaningful. If you have a query on an individual section 106 agreement then it should be possible to provide an answer on when the funds have been spent or allocated if you can quote the planning permission number. Document Title: Camden Climate Bonds
Document Text: Date: 23/11/2021 Ref: CAM2428 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 08/11/2021 about Camden Climate Bonds. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exceptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. This is an Environmental Information Regulations request for information regarding Camden's plans to issue "Camden Climate Bonds". I would like to request the following information: From 8th May 2021 to the 8th November 2021, please provide all correspondence and communications referencing Camden Climate Bonds or related terms, including "climate bonds", "climate bond", "green bonds" and "green bond". I define “correspondence and communications” as including (but not limited to) the following: - Emails (and their attachments) - Letters - Memos - Briefings - Research documents - Policy documents - Notes taken during telephone conversations - Minutes taken during meetings/invitations This request is exempt under Regulation 12(4)(d) and Regulation 12(4)(e) of the Environmental Information Regulations. See the refusal notice below. Refusal Notice: Regulation 12(4)(d) – The regulation relates to material which is still in the course of completion, to unfinished documents or to incomplete data. Regulation 12(4)(e) - The regulation states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request involves the disclosure of internal communications. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk The correspondence requested shows early stage thinking on a financial product that the authority will ultimately launch. The proposal has not yet been fully formed. When it is, we aim to launch this proposal and raise money from the public. By making the early stage thinking public would impact the launch of this product and ultimately the policy goal for the council, to raise more funding to pay for climate-related projects. In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withho lding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: • Improving transparency in decision making. • Ensuring value for money. • To ensure accountability of the authority. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: • It is not in the public interest to damage the council’s commercial interests, as this affects how it spends public money and the services it can provide to residents and other stakeholders. • The Council has a right to a “private thinking space” to discuss proposals of projects internally and protect the information discussed, which may be related to , and affect, future work undertaken by the Council. • The Council needs a safe space to develop ideas, debate current issues, and reach decisions without external interference and distraction. • It is not in the public interest to distract from the work the Council is doing to reduce its CO2 emissions by 2030. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. We considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations overrides the decision to withhold and have concluded that it does not. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 6. What Is their email and phone number Refusal notice: The exemption that applies is: Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. However, we are withholding the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemption applies. Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. 1. All internal Quality Assurance and Improvement Programme (QAIP or QAIE) reports produced or commissioned by Camden Council’s Internal Audit function since 1 January 2022. This includes all self -assessments, external assessments, drafts, responses, and asso ciated materials. Please include any documents referencing QAIP/QAIE Sections 424 and 425, and all documentation related to the Global Internal Audit Standards (GAIS), including updates, minutes, reviews, commentary, and implementation actions. It is not essential to the scope of the request and may therefore be disreg arded. The remainder of the request stands: I am seeking all QAIP or QAIE -related documentation from 1 January 2022 onwards, including materials referencing the Public Sector Internal Audit Standards (PSIAS) and the Global Internal Audit Standards (GAIS), and their implementation. 2. All documents and communications relating to the effectiveness review of the Audit and Corporate Governance Committee (AGCC) for the financial years 2022/23 and 2023/24. This includes evaluations, self -assessments, officer comments, scoring frameworks, implementation plans, and benchmarking data. 3. All documentation explaining the rationale behind the “moderate assurance” Head of Internal Audit opinion for 2024/25, including the criteria used, internal definitions, supporting context, and any remedial or improvement plans. 4. All action plans, implementation documents, and officer responses relating to any identified non - conformance or partial conformance with GAIS or QAIP standards, whether referenced in internal audit reports, AGCC minutes, or internal records. 5. Any documentation or correspondence concerning internal benchmarking or comparative review of Camden’s QAIP or AGCC performance against other local authorities or equivalent bodies. You clarified: Please provide internal benchmarking or comparative documentation from 1 January 2022 to the present, not limited to 2024/25. 6. Any internal audit risk assessments or resource reviews that reference the impact of staffing levels (including vacant senior posts) on audit delivery or GAIS compliance. You clarified: Please provide all relevant documentation and risk assessments from 1 January 2022 to the present which reference staffing levels and their impact on internal audit delivery or conformance with GAIS or PSIAS. 7. All documentation, spreadsheets, and working papers used to support the statement made at the July 2025 AGCC meeting (around one hour into the recording) that the Council had “built in £100 million” in internal resources into treasury modelling, providi ng borrowing headroom. Please include any associated modelling showing how many years of headroom this represents, how this relates to reserve policy and the under -borrowing strategy, and any materials concerning high -interest debt. 8. All internal correspondence or documentation (including emails, notes, or directives) relating to the decision to transfer or reclassify my audit queries made under Section 26 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act as Freedom of Information requests. This includes any communications involving the FOI team, Monitoring Officer, Section 151 Officer, Director of Finance, or others involved. If no written instruction exists, please confirm who made the decision and on what basis. 9. All correspondence, email trails, forwarding instructions, or related materials referencing FOI request CAM10525, or any other reference used to process or reclassify my statutory audit queries. This includes anything that might identify which officer o r councillor was responsible for diverting my correspondence to the FOI process. 10. Please confirm whether the Chair of the Audit and Corporate Governance Committee received or was made aware of my audit concerns, and provide any summaries, briefings, or materials shared with the Chair. I note these concerns were not raised under “Any Other Business that the Chair Considers Urgent”. We are not processing this request as it would require a disproportionate amount of time, effort, and expense. Please see the exemption notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 12: cost of compliance exceeds appropriate limit We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We have calculated that it will take approx. 66 hours (minimum) to comply with your request because: For question 1 (time estimate 8 hours) : • Each PSIAS assessment contains a number of standards with a whole body of supporting documentation • The GIAS conformance assessment took the form of a project, starting in the summer 2024 and running to spring 2025. This was a substantial undertaking with a significant number of documents involve d (organised into five domains, 15 principles, and 52 standards) For question 2 (time estimate 2 hours): • In 2023 -24 a training session was held to support the 2023 -24 effectiveness review with a subsequent report to the ACGC in summer 2024. • Pulling together detailed documentation (outside of the public report) will be needed For question 3 (time estimate 9 hours) • Core documentation - 24/25 audit plan , ~ 40 Internal Audit reviews and ~ 20 follow up reviews • 24/25 Internal Audit advice to auditees, 24/25 risk deep dives , Principal risk and assurance map and Governance self -assessment as included within the AGS Information for question 4 would be included in the response to question 1. For question 5 (time estimate 6 hours): • A number of sources will need to be analysed : • Joint governance group (JGG) held quarterly, and detailed minutes are produced. ; • London Audit Group do not produce minutes but outputs are shared For question 6 (time estimate 3 hours): • GIAS compliance aspects would be covered with a response to question 1. • Additionally a resource assessment is undertaken each year as part of the annual planning process For question 7 (time estimate 24 hours) • is a complex question to answer, as it involves consolidat ing modelling done by multiple teams • the time estimate above is just for one alone - 12 hours or more (Chair recently changed for ACGC) Advice and Assistance For question 1: • Internal Audit Annual Reports as presented to the Audit and Corporate Governance Committee (ACGC ) every summer (June -July) are on the Council’s democracy website: • Browse meetings - Document Title: Anti-racism training
Document Text: Date: 05/07/2021 Case reference : CAM1767 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 21/06/2021 about anti-racism training .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding some of the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply.  Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. Re: anti-racism training contract https://order-order.com/2021/06/21/camden-council-spends-93000-on-woke-training-whilst-cutting-library- staff/ 1) What was the tendering process for selecting this company? We went through an extensive tendering process for this work and advertised the contract Anti-Racism learning offer for the London Borough of Camden on 10 December 2020 on Contracts Finder. We completed the procurement process in March 2020. For a contract of less that £100k we were not required to carry out a full tender process in this way but we wanted to be as transparent as possible and ensure a range of providers were able to bid for the work. There were two key stages in the tender process: Stage 1: Providers interested in bidding for this work were asked to complete a written submission form explaining their approach to delivering the learning offer, methodology, capability and skills. This formed 45% of the overall procurement score.● Stage 2: Following a shortlisting process, providers were then be asked to complete a virtual interview and deliver a short taster session demonstrating their approach and capability to facilitate the learning offer. This formed the remaining 55% of the overall procurement score.● The contract was awarded to In Diverse Company , with a total value of £93,000. With over 4,800 staff, this makes the cost per head less than £20 per person. We have also ensured that the programme includes a train-the-trainer element, so that Camden staff are able to continue delivering the training, beyond the contract with In Diverse Company. 2) Can you publish the training materials which were used? This information is exempt.  Please see the exemption notices below. 3) Who decided to authorise this when frontline service cuts are been made? This training was agreed by the Council as part of a programme of work that supports us to be an organisation where everyone feels able to be themselves, regardless of their background and/or cultural identity. We are determined to support our diverse communities and our anti-racism training is helping our staff to challenge all forms of racism inside and outside of work. This is a crucial part of our effort to becoming an anti-racist organisation. Refusal Notice The exemptions that apply are: section 41: information provided in confidence This information is withheld because it is exempt under Section 41.  This absolute exemption applies where the information was provided to the public authority in confidence.  The information was received from a third party (In Diverse Company). Under the terms of the contract we are not able to publish the training materials.  Our agreement with ‘In Diverse Company’ means we have an ongoing licence to use the materials but are not permitted to pass them on to any other party. Releasing this information would constitute a breach of confidence.  In other words, if we disclosed the information the provider or a third party could take the council to court. section 43(2): commercial interests This exemption applies because release of the information would have a prejudicial effect on the commercial interests of the course provider and is also likely to have a prejudicial effect on the commercial interests of Council. The course provider would suffer by having is syllabus and charges exposed to its competitors and the Council would find its negotiating position compromised when seeking to engage course providers.In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: Improving transparency in decision making● Ensuring value for money and accountability of the authority● The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: It is not in the public interest to disclose information that would be likely to damage the commercial interests of a company, as this could lead to financial problems for the company and/or job losses● It is not in the public interest to damage the council’s commercial interests, as this affects how it spends public money and the services it can provide to residents● It is not in the public interest for commercially sensitive information about one company to be released, when information about other companies is not released, as this puts one company at a commercial disadvantage.● It is not in the public interest to release information that could negatively influence ongoing and future negotiations as this could have an adverse effect on value for money for the council and so for residents● We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public st in disclosing it. Document Title: “Losses and special payments” in our 2019/20 financial accounts
Document Text: Date: 04/09/2020 Case reference : CAM350 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 14/08/2020 about “losses and special payments”in our 2019/20 financial accounts .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and/or the Environmental Information Regulations 2004  Response The council does not holds the information requested: In your nancial accounts for the financial year 2019/20 do you have a section for “losses and special payments”? 1. If so how much money was accounted for in the 2019/2020 financial year as being "losses and special payments”? (Please note l am aware that the loss may have occurred many years earlier but I am interested in items which were accounted for in the last financial year, irrespective or when the loss took place.) 2. Please detail the three largest single amounts within this total, giving a cost for each loss and a detailed description of the claim and the reason for the loss. If you do NOT have a losses and special payments section you use the explanation below for what should be included in losses and special payments. Definition for what are Losses and Special Payments. Categories of Loss: • Loss of cash – due to theft, fraud, arson, neglect of duty or gross careless, overpayment of salary, fees and allowances and other causes including accidents. • Fruitless payments – a fruitless payment can’t be avoided because the recipient is entitled to it, even though the public authority will get nothing in return. In assessing a fruitless payment, there will always be a degree of blame. For example, payment for travel tickets or accommodation that has been wrongly booked. • Bad debts – an individual debtor is a case, not every single invoice. • Damage to buildings, fittings, furniture and equipment – examples of losses under this category are: losses by fire (other than arson) and losses by weather damage, or accident beyond the control of any responsible person. Categories of Special Payment • Compensation payments made under legal obligation – clear liability under a Court Order or legally binding arbitration award. This includes compensation for injuries to persons, damage to property and unfair dismissal. • Extra contractual payments to contractors – these are payments which are not legally due under the original contract but where there appears to be an obligation which the courts may uphold. • Ex-gratia payments – these are payments the public authority is not obliged to make or for which there is no legal liability. Examples of ex-gratia payments are: o Loss of personal effects, clinical negligence/personal injury, and settlement on termination of employment,  extra statutory or extra regulationary payments and maladministration cases. o Special Severance Payments – these are paid to employees, contractors and others outside of normal statutory or contractual requirements when leaving employment in public service whether they resign, are dismissed or reach an agreed termination of contract We do not hold this information.  There is nothing in the draft statement of the accounts specifically for losses and special payments. Document Title: current rent rates on the commercial properties between 18 to 34 Camden Road
Document Text: Date: 28/05/2024 Ref: CAM7649 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 03/05/2024 about current rent rates on the commercial properties between 18 to 34 Camden Road . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However we are withholding the information because it is exempt. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why the exemptions apply. Could I please request the current rent rates on the commercial properties between 18 to 34 Camden Road, NW1 9DP. I am interested to know what the neighbouring business are paying in rent to the council. This request is exempt under Section 43(2) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. See the refusal notice below. Refusal Notice: Section 43(2) – The Council has withheld this information because Section 43(2) exempts information whose disclosure would, or would be likely to, prejudice the commercial interests of any person (an individual, a company, the public authority itself or any other legal entity). The council is relying upon the higher threshold of likelihood that disclosure would have a prejudicial effect on the Council. The harm that would be caused to the Council are as follows. The properties concerned are not just 18 – 34 Camden Road. The Council also owns 16, 38, 40 in that parade, as well as 7 – 15 odd numbers opposite. To clarify, we do not own numbers 22 or 24. In the properties requested there are a number of outstanding lease events (such as outstanding rent review or lease to be renewed) and the basis of negotiation does not relate to the global rent, but a devaluation of the area on a basis known as ITZA (In Terms of Zone A) and if a third party misconstrues it, it distorts the discussions for the tenants of the location. Also this does not show whether any tenant has any upper parts, or has undertaken an extension, or has any favourable/disadvantageous lease terms, all of which have an impact. Where we undertake negotiations, we undertake a devaluation of the evidence and ensure that information discussed is on an appropriate basis London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Furthermore, these are fixed costs to a business which could enable a competitor to know an element that a business is paying, which links through to Commercial Activity . It should be noted that Freedom of Information requests are open to the world, as they are published on the Council’s Open Data Portal. In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: • Improving transparency in decision making. • Ensuring value for money. • To ensure accountability of the authority. • Demonstrating the council is meeting its fiduciary duties. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: • It is not in the public interest to damage the council’s commercial interests, as this affects how it spends public money and the services it can provide to residents and other stakeholders. • It is not in the public interest to release information that could negatively influence ongoing and future negotiations as this could have an adverse effect on value for money for the council, so for residents and other stakeholders. • Withholding the information does not prevent scrutiny of the council’s actions and decisions. We considered whether the presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations overrides the decision to withhold and have concluded that it does not. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. In this instance we are unable to offer any further advice on this request. Document Title: Audited LA maintained schools
Document Text: Date: 2 7th November 2018 Ref: FOI12058 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for inf ormation dated the 12th November 2018 about audited LA maintained schools . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested , however we are withholding some of the information becaus e it is exempt . The answers to your questions are below w e have stated where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which exp lain how and why the exemptions apply. 1. Please can you provide a date for the last time each LA maintained school in your area was last audited by the council. Failing this, please could you tell me how many schools have not been audited since November 2013 (five years ago). – Please see answer below Q2 2. Also, for each of the last three years, please can you tell me how many schools were audited, and roughly what percentage of the your schools this made up. – I can confirm that London Borough of Camden holds the information you requested. All Schools are au dited on a cyclical basis, and on average each school is subject to an audit review every 5 to 7 years. However, our approach remains flexible and all schools due to be audited are subject to a risk assessment to ensure that we utilise our resources effect ively. Our Annual Internal Audit Report, which is presented to the Audit & Corporate Governance Committee at every June meeting, contains a summary of the number of school audits completed in year. These annual reports are available on the Council’s demo cracy pages. As an example, our June 2018 report can be found within the agenda pack found here: http://democracy.camden.gov.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=117&MId=766 7&Ver=4 As the information requested is already reasonably accessible elsewhere it is exempt under the absolute exemption in Section 21 . 3. For each of these years, if possible, please provide the name of the school audited, and the number of recommendatio ns made (please break this down into low/medium/high recs) – Please see answer below Q4 4. For each of these years, please also provide details of the recommendations. And please provide any details you have on action taken in relation to the recs. This informatio n is withheld because section 33 (1)(a) (prejudice to audit functions ) applies to it. The council is relying upon the higher threshold that disclosure would have a prejudicial effect. Information and Records Management Law and Governance Directorate London Borough of Camden Town Hall Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk We have considered the harm that would be caused if this inform ation were disclosed and concluded that as this information has been provided in confidence and with the expectation that it is to be used for the purposes of internal management and accountability including free and frank discussions, there has been no ex pectation that this information would ever be made public. In our view disclosure would have an impact on the willingness of school managers and staff to provide the most candid and at times negative information regarding their own school, its management a nd its practices. We have taken into account that disclosing this information does increase transparency and account ability of the schools involved, However to disclose the schools who were audited and the recommendations made we feel would be detrimental to th e future working relationship between the Council and these schools as information provided by the schools would come with the expectation that this information would be protected by confidentiality. The public interest arguments for releasing this infor mation are as follows:  Improving transparency in decision making  To ensure accountability of the authority  Promoting accountability and transparency in the use of public funds by public bodies and that work delivers value for money. The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows:  ensuring that auditors can effectively carry out their duties  Protecting the integrity of the audit. We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. 5. Please include a figure for the number of investigations that were opened as a result of an audit report, and the outcome of an investigation. Plus whether the investigation was published in the public domain. – Please see answ er below Q6. 6. Do you publish the findings of your school audits in the public domain?
