Document Text: Date: 17/02/2025 Case reference : CAM9539London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 30/01/2025 about major developments.  We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. FOI Request: Section 106 Agreements 1. The number of major housing developments (10 or more dwellings) in your jurisdiction which were completed between the years 2021-2025 inclusive which had a Section 106 (Town and Country Planning Act 1990) planning obligation. 35 developments of 10 or more dwellings were completed in this period. 2. Of these completed developments, the number which changed the stipulations of their S106 obligations, or did not provide them, by the time of completion.    3. For these, please provide the following: a. The name of the development, the developer name, and original planning permission reference. b. The obligations the developer agreed to as part of the Section 106 to the council upon initial planning permission being granted. c. A summary of the final delivery (including built property or financial contributions) provided by the developer to fulfil the Section 106 agreement, upon completion of the building contract. d. Any reasons given by the developer for any difference between the initial agreement and final delivery. e. If any developer did not provide anything by way of fulfilment of the Section 106 agreement, please summarise any further action taken by the council, including but not limited to litigation, requiring a replacement contribution of any kind, such as a financial contribution, discontinuing the building project, etc We are not processing questions 2 and 3 of this request as it is excepted.  Please see the exception notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exception that applies is: regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable. We have also considered the time it will take the council to locate the information requested in the request, to extract it, collate it and then to review and redact any sensitive information that will be subject to further exceptions under the EIR 2004. Whilst the Council monitors the implementation of developments we do not hold or publish a collated comprehensive record of where the stipulations have been changed or not complied with by the time of completion. To answer this question 2 would involve reviewing and reporting on all the clause records for the 35 cases to assess change or compliance. Assuming 7 clauses per development the task will involve reviewing approximately 245 clauses. A review is likely to require consultation with officers in the various services involved in the implementation of these schemes, e.g. enforcement, environmental health, transport, housing, legal and finance officers. This will take an estimated average minimum combined officer time of 30 mins per clause and so is likely to take more than 120 hours. Similarly, to provide an answer to question 3 for all of the cases will take longer than the 30 mins per clause quoted in the answer to question 2 above and the total time is likely to be in excess of 200 hours. We have considered the impact and burden that processing this request would have on the team who would have to deal with it. We have concluded that the time, effort and costs involved would place a disproportionate burden on the team and severely impact their ability to perform their normal duties. In applying this exception, the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004.  We have indicated the weight of each of these considerations. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: - it would improve the transparency for the general public of the Council’s decisions and processes in dealing with this major housing developments (Medium).• The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: - processing this request in full would be provide a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council (High).• this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities, (High) and:• it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s provision of services to the public (High).• it is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request (High).• It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004. We considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not.Advice and assistance The reference numbers of the 35 developments is are below. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 17/12/2021 about  food safety and Hygiene. Am I correct in saying that scores are allocated based on compliance to Food Safety and Hygiene (England) Regulations 2013? Do the food information contraventions also factor into this score? (This wasn't clear since they aren't subdivided into the three scoring areas) Yes The Food Hygiene Rating (FHR) is for Food Safety matters so could include some allergen issues (such as cross-contamination), although the majority of labeling regulations fall under Food Standards legislation. The items in the letter previously provided are listed under the 3 main scoring areas for FHR purposes (they also form part of the Food Establishment Intervention Rating Scheme). 2. Do you have a checklist of all operational violations that you consider in assessing compliance? Officers check items required in the Food Hygiene (England) Regulations 2013 (as amended) together with all other relevant food legislation as they apply to each premises inspected. 3. Lastly, can you tell me how violations affect the scores? Is there a ratio between scores and operational violations? (For example, a score of 0=No violations or a score of 30=15 violations) Officers score the business after the inspection depending what they find at that time. This scoring is in line with the Food Law Code of Practice (the Food Establishment Intervention Rating Scheme in particular), the Food Law Practice Guidance, the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme Brand Standard, and other relevant guidance as appropriate. As a brief (non-complete) summary, it is the effect of the contravention not merely the presence/absence or number of contraventions. Resource does not currently exist within the council to facilitate daily opening and closing, and so this would need to be agreed with a community organisation or local bu siness. Potential anti -social behaviour - The space has been designed to minimise potential anti -social behaviour, including that from rough sleepers, drug users and excessive noise. The design uses principles which aim to encourage a level of human a ctivity that is appropriate to the location, and promote a sense of community ownership, reducing opportunities for criminal and anti - social behaviour. The community will be encouraged to report any issues that do occur so that they can be logged and inve stigated as appropriate. The Camden StreetSafe app can be used to report concerns around anti -social street activity such as begging, street drinking, public drug use, an d rough sleeping. If fly -tipping occurs this can be reported using the Clean Camden app or website . They manage a large tree population throughout the borough, the majority of which are open, within the public realm on highways or wit hin parks and open spaces. The roots will be protected during construction, and a permeable material used around the base of the tree to ensure water can permeate through to reach the roots. Damage caused by the tree - Camden owned trees are managed by th e council ’s tree team. Amongst other tasks they organise cyclical inspections of the council's tree stock to have trees pruned back from surrounding buildings. The tree in Oriel Place has been scheduled for some pruning work. If there is damage occurring t o a building in relation to the tree, owners should contact their building insurers who will then contact the Council’s insurers. Commercialisation of the space - The community requested that the space be flexible, with opportunities for small scale commun ity events, and pop up stalls etc. Currently an annual Santa’s Grotto is held in the space, and it is this kind of event that the community wished to encourage more of. Requests for use of the space would require approval, which would involve careful cons ideration over what is an acceptable use of this public space. In response to local residents concerns we are reviewing the need for a power supp ly here. If a power supply is included in the final scheme, any use would require approval, which would involve careful consideration over what is an acceptable use of this public space. Light pollution - The lighting will be directed downwards using blackout shields to the roof of the lantern, preventing unacceptable levels of light to neighbouring properties. CCTV should be provided - The proximity of local r esidencies and windows would limit the angles of view of any cameras due to the need to position cameras away from windows to avoid privacy issues. The units on this network have the heating scale B1 which is Full Heating -52 Weeks-Night Setback- Heating, Hot Water & Cooking or B2 if there is no cooking gas supply. 1-26 Tiptree itself has 24x 1 bed units and 2 bedsits/studios (0 beds). 1. How much does each resident in Tiptree pay for heating? 2. How much do residents pay for heating depending on the number of rooms in their flat? The resident charge depends on whether they are leaseholders or tenants and the number of bedrooms in the flat. For 2022/23 the heating scales (charges) were per week, charged with the Rent. tenant 0-bed Heating/Hot water - £7.04 / £2.20 tenant 1-bed Heating/Hot Water - £9.19 / £3.30 For leaseholders the fuel cost is apportioned based on the heating scales for the unit. The apportionment is calculated by adding all the heating scales for the network and divided by the heating scale for the individual unit. For 2022/23 the Heating fuel cost for HY4141 was £57,137.88 (excluding indirect and overheads) leaseholder 0-bed unit apportionment - 1.2227% - £698.65 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . Document Text: Date: 19/02/2026 Ref: CAM11907 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 05/01/2026 about the number of complaints received by the council relating to excess cold, damp and mould, inadequate heating or insulation. We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds some of the information requested. However, we are withholding the information because it is excepted under the EIR 2004. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies. Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why they apply. please provide the following information for each of the last five financial years: 1. The number of complaints received by the council relating to: a) excess cold b) damp and mould c) inadequate heating or insulation 2. The number of properties (both council-owned and private rented) assessed as failing the Housing Health and Safety Rating System due to excess cold. 3. The number of enforcement actions taken against private landlords relating to cold, damp, or heating deficiencies, including: a) improvement notices b) prohibition orders c) civil penalties or prosecutions. 4. If possible, please provide data broken down by ward. Refusal Notice S12(4)(b) Under Regulation 12(4)(b) it would be considered manifestly unreasonable to provide a response to your request because the cost of compliance, and burden of dealing with your request, is excessive. The exception protects the Council’s ability to carry out its public functions and provides a balance between transparency and the protection of resources. We hold some information, but to see what we hold and to locate, extract, collate, and redact this data would be excessive and divert officers from their core functions and statutory obligations. Redirecting the Private Sector Housing manager and their team for an extended period would create substantial operational disruption. Their continued involvement is critical to the effective London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk delivery of core statutory functions, ongoing casework, and key strategic priorities. Removing this capacity would delay essential services, reduce responsiveness to residents, and undermine progress on planned initiatives and regulatory commitments. Regarding question 3, we are unable to provide figures for notices served relating to heating deficiencies in the Private Sector Housing service, as this would entail searching through each notice one by one which would exceed 18 hours. There are 188 notices served, from 2020-2025. We estimate that it would take 15 mins per notice to locate, find the details of the schedule and read it to identify whether insulation or inadequate heating are mentioned = 47 hours. Therefore, we consider that the burden on the council in undertaking the work required would be unreasonable and Regulation 12(4)(b) applies. This exception is subject to a Public Interest Test and this is below. I have noted the factors for and against disclosure together with their relevant weights. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: • It would improve transparency to the general public of the Council (medium weight) • The presumption in favour of disclosure in the regulations (low weight) The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: • Processing this question would be a large burden in terms of Officer time and cost to the Council. (heavy weight) • Answering these questions would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the Council’s core business activities. (heavy weight) • It would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on the provision of services to the public (heavy weight) • It is not in the public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request (medium weight) It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. Document Text: Date: 08/07/2024 Case reference : CAM7957London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 24/06/2024 about 2022/0528/P - O2 Centre indemnity agreement.  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice below which explains how and why it applies. Re: CAM7724 - 2022/0528/P - O2 Centre Points A - C are being dealt with at Internal Review.  Point D is a new request: In relation to request 1 set out in our letter dated 15 May 2024, we are interested to know whether the Council and Landsec have entered into an indemnity or similar agreement, or whether such an agreement remains in draft. We are not interested in any part of any completed agreement that includes financial information and any such information can be redacted. We appreciate that a document still in draft is unlikely to be disclosable. Please confirm the position, namely whether such an agreement is completed and in draft, and if the latter please disclose the same redacted as necessary. No indemnity agreement has been entered into and there is no draft that it would be appropriate to disclose. Please see the exception notice set out below. Refusal NoticeThe exception that applies is: Regulation 12(4)d the request relates to material which is still in the course of completion, to unfinished documents or to incomplete data. A first draft of an indemnity agreement was prepared by Eversheds, but it has not yet been taken any further (and it will not be taken any further until the programme is drawn up and we commit to proceed).  As things stand, it remains an initial draft which requires further detailed negotiation between the parties and is not in a form that would be appropriate to disclose. In applying this exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. The public interest arguments for releasing this information are as follows: improving transparency about the redevelopment of the O2 Centre• to ensure accountability of the authorities dealings with the redevelopment• The public interest arguments for withholding the information are as follows: the draft is purely an initial draft and is unlikely to reflect the final document until taken further• releasing an initial draft which requires further detailed negotiation and verification will result in inaccurate or misleading information being made public• this will cause confusion and may result in unwarranted controversy or publicity• We have decided that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004 and we have considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not. Document Title: the number of people assessed as destitute due to them or their family’s immigration status
Document Text: Date: 30 December 2025 Ref: CAM11667 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 27 November 2025 about the number of people assessed as destitute due to them or their family’s immigration status. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. How many people have been assessed as "destitute due to the family's immigration status" by the local authority after a failed asylum claim or leave to remain claim? How much is the cost for housing those people? How much are the monthly subsistence costs provided to those people? Please could you provide this data for the past 5 years (2021 – 2025) broken down by year. We are withholding this information as we consider the following exemption applies. Refusal - Section 12: Cost of Compliance Exceeds the Appropriate Limit We are refusing your request under Section 12 of the Freedom of Information Act on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. The ICO Section 12 guidance is that once a public authority has calculated that over 18 hours will be required to locate, extract and collate the information required, it may refuse the entire request without calculating the exact time or working up to the limit. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk For questions 1 and 2, the requested information is not held in an easily accessible format. Over the specified five year period, a total of 9,700 children were referred to Children’s Services. We estimate that manually reviewing, extracting and collating the relevant information would take approximately 3 minutes per record. This is because the MOSAIC system used by Children’s Services does not provide a straightforward mechanism for identifying cases of destitution due to a family's immigration status and lacks keyword search functionality to determine whether ‘destitute’ or related terms were recorded. Based on this, we have calculated that fulfilling the request would require approx.485 hours of officer time, which significantly exceeds the appropriate limit set out under Section 12 of the Freedom of Information Act. Advice and Assistance Given the calculations provided, it is not possible to refine the request sufficiently to bring it within the 18-hour appropriate limit. While we could undertake a spot check of a small number of records for a specific date, this approach would be unlikely to produce a representative or meaningful sample of data. Document Text: Date: 06/08/2021 Case reference : CAM1919 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 18/07/2021 about signs banning vehicles from streets including Netherhall Gardens . We have dealt with this under Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: Earlier in 2021, Camden banned vehicles from certain streets during some weekday hours, including Netherhall Gardens.   Original signage had wording and also mentiond that electric vehicles were prohibited.  This has now been replaced by much less detailed signs showing only the red circle cymbol and hours of operation.   1. Why has the signage been changed? The signage has been changed so that the “Except electric vehicles” legend has been removed. This has been amended as the council awaits approval from the department for transport to use that legend on this type of sign.   2. Has the exception for electric vehicles been removed ?   The exception for electric vehicles has not been removed. 3. I am not aware of any traffic order being approved which would allow this change. If electric vehicles are still not prohibited then this new signage is invalid and incorrectly prohbits vehicles which are permitted access - that would be an unlawful prohibition. The traffic order for this location lays out the parameters of the prohibition as well as the full list of exemptions which apply. There is no requirement to list on signage the full list of exemptions. The current signage without the “Except electric vehicles” legend is not invalid and is provided forwithin the Traffic Signs Regulations and General Directions, which we have to follow. 4. Can you please provide statistics on the number of PCNs issued in the periods before and after the signs were changed. We have not issued any penalty charge notices for Netherhall Gardens since March. 5. If the goal is to reduce congestion (and not raise revenue) then I believe the new signage will be less effective as many people will not know what the red cicle symbol means. Do you have a view on that effect? The red prohibition sign is one that is prescribed by law for this prohibition and has remained constant through the sign change. It is clearly stated within the Highway Code as well as the Traffic Signs Regulations and General Directions that this means “No Motor Vehicles”. Removing a single legend indicating an exemption should not undermine the core messaging of the signage now displayed. Document Title: Rosemary House area designated for emergency services
Document Text: Date: 12/06/2025 Ref: CAM10130 Updated Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 13/05/2025 about Rosemary House area designated for emergency services. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. There is an area directly outside my block where the refuse bins are kept (Rosemary House, Leighton Road, NW5 2UX), which many years ago we were told is designated for emergency services use only and no one is allowed to park there. Please could you tell me: 1. Is this area truly for emergency services only? If so, for how long has it been a designated space? No, there are no parking restrictions on this area. That is because t his estate is not currently subject to the Traffic Management Act (TMA) 2004 enforcement. That means that any implied ‘restrictions’ on the housing estate land, whether signed or marked are advisory only and have no force in law. The Council currently cannot enforce these but welcome details of cars that are parking where they shouldn’t so we can consider what further action we could take. 2. Have there ever been and/or are there any current plans to clearly mark out this specific area as being for emergency vehicles only (e.g floor markings and signs)? Not in this way, but if a Traffic Management Order is made then restrictions could be made. 3. What are the penalties for cars/vans parking in that space if it is strictly for emergency vehicles only? There are currently no restrictions in place that can be enforced, so there are no penalties. 4. What regulations does Camden Council have regarding the 24/7 unobstructed provision of space for emergency vehicles inside Willingham Close estate, specifically the area directly outside Rosemary House where the refuse bins are? There are currently no restrictions in place that can be enforced, because there is no Traffic Management Order in place. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 5. Does Camden Council have legal obligations to ensure 24/7 unobstructed emergency vehicle access to designated areas, including this specific space outside Rosemary House where the refuse bins are? None of the markings on estates, other than the few that have been included in a TMO, and which have Traffic Signs Regulations and General Directions (TSRGD) compliant signing, currently have any force in law. 6. Can Camden Council provide records of any agreements or formal communications between Camden Council and emergency services (such as the London Fire Brigade) regarding the 24/7 protection of designated spaces for emergency services? There is nothing held by the council around this specific issue. 7. Are there any internal policies or external legal requirements Camden Council has in place that they must follow to ensure that emergency vehicle spaces are kept clear at all times for emergency use only? Can you provide relevant documentation of these policies? There is nothing held by the council around this specific issue. 8. Have there been any past complaints or incidents involving blocked access to the emergency services space outside Rosemary House where the refuse bins are, and how were these complaints handled? What actions were taken to resolve any such incidents? There has been one complaint about this issue in the past 2 years, in April 2025. It was resolved through advice being given to the complainant. 9. Is Camden Council aware of the potential violation of emergency vehicle space due to unauthorised parking in this designated area? What steps have been taken or are planned to address this issue and ensure the space remains available 24/7 for emergency vehicles only? There is no formal designation of parking- any signs and spaces are advisory only and so there cannot be violations as such. Council has recently completed the first phase of a programme to introduce Traffic Management Orders (TMOs) across a number of estates, providing us with the legal powers needed to enforce against dangerous and inconsiderate parking. This has already been implemented on nine estates. This is an option for the future for this estate. 10. Does Camden Council have any plans to implement a Traffic Management Order (TMO) for the area inside Willingham Close estate opposite Rosemary House, to enhance enforcement of parking restrictions? If not, can you explain why this estate has not been included in the TMO rollout, especially given recent and past reports with photographic evidence of cars parking illegally in a space for emergency vehicles? There are no current specific plans, but the council will shortly prioritise the locations for Phase 2 of this programme and eventually aims to have a TMO for all estates. 11. Can Camden Council provide any documentation or records of communications with enforcement contractors (e.g., NSL) regarding the monitoring and enforcement of parking restrictions at Rosemary House? If not, why not? There is nothing held, but as there is no TMO in place there can be no enforcement by NSL and so communication would not be expected. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding some of the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answer which explain how and why it applies. I would like to know the average payments made following the sale of 32 Lawn Rd & 1 Fleet Rd, London NW3, to Fairview Homes. The information is also commercially sensitive and if publicised could impact on the future negotiating position the parties in similar transactions. Disclosure would have an adverse effect on other similar transactions carried out by the council. In applying this qualified exemption, we have had to balance the public interest in withholding the information against the interest in favour of disclosure. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: I am writing to make a Freedom of Information request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, for information regarding the IT infrastructure and data storage systems used by your organisation. Please provide the following details: 1. What data storage vendors do you currently use for your primary storage? We use Nutanix. 2. How large in Terabytes is your primary storage? (>50TB, 50-200TB, 200-500TB, 500-1PB, 1PB<?) Our primary storage is 200-500TB. 3. How many physical servers do you have? We have11 physical servers. 4. Do you use containerized applications anywhere within your IT infrastructure?No, we do not. 5. Do you use Kubernetes anywhere within your IT infrastructure? No, we do not. 6. Who do you use for your infrastructure and backup storage software? We use Rubrik with additional Azure Storage. 7. How large is your backup storage in Terabytes? It is 170TBs on local appliance and Archived data at 317TBs on Azure Blob to date. 8. What data do you use your backup storage for? We use our backup storage to retain and protect information in accordance with the published data retention schedule. This data includes databases, virtual machines, and files. 9. When is your backup storage due for refresh? Refresh is estimated to be in 2027. 10. Do you use the public Cloud (AWS/Microsoft Azure/Google Cloud)? Yes, we do. 11. If you use Public Cloud, what applications are you using it for? We use Azure and AWS services as part of its infrastructure. Azure: Blob Storage, Azure Files, Impulse, Data Research Platform. AWS: Public website and Parking Platform. 12. How large in terabytes is your public cloud estate? It is 50TBs.13. Do you use Azure VMware Solution? No, we do not. 14. When is your primary data storage due for a refresh/review? It will be in 2028. 15. Which VAR (value-added resellers) do you purchase IT infrastructure through? (E.g., CDW/Softcat/MTI/Telefonica Tech, etc.) Please see the reference contracts database published online. 16. Which frameworks does your procurement use? Please see the response above. 17. Does the Estates department have a budget to purchase devices and IT separate to central IT for CCTV? We do not have a budget to purchase devices and IT separate to central IT for CCTV but we do have a separate budget to maintain CCTV assets 18. What is the annual budget for Estates/Facilities? This information is already publicly available.  Please enter the link below into your web browser: https://www.camden.gov.uk/documents/d/guest/2024-25-budget-book-final-1 19. What % of the estates budget is associated with IT systems for the management and running of the building and facilities (e.g., CCTV systems)? We do not hold this information.  Please see the response to Q17 above. Document Text: Date: 22/12/2020 Case reference : CAM904 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 14/12/2020 about applications considered under discretionary self-isolation support and numbers granted or rejected . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds some of the information requested. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we do not hold the information requested and why. Collectively, councils were given £40 million in self-isolation support. That £40 million was made up of two pots: 'programme costs' which is a £25 million pot and not discretionary. The second is a £15 million pot and is discretionary. For the purposes of this FoI, I am interested in the discretionary pot only. Can you please answer the following: A) How many applications have been considered under the discretionary pot b) how many have been granted and c) how many have been rejected. a) We have received a total of 440 requests for a payment but we do not separate them in to discretionary or non-discretionary requests b) We have made 126 discretionary awards c) We have rejected 180 applications If you have already run out of discretionary funding d) how long did the discretionary funding pot last. Please provide both a date when it ran out and the number of days from between when you had the funding and when it ran out (I appreciate that councils may have received funding at different times). We have not run out of discretionary funding. If you haven't yet run out of discretionary funding e) how long do you anticipate it lasting. We anticipate it lasting a further 4 to 6 weeks. Finally, if you have already spent the discretionary funding, f) have you spent more from your own budget and if so g) by how much? If you haven't yet spent all your discretionary funding - and bearing in mind the Government has said that councils will not be able to recoup on discretionary overspend – h) have you or do you plan to allocate additional funding to support local residents? We do not hold this information.  This is because no decision has been taken yet. Document Title: West Kentish Town Estate
Document Text: Date: 12/03/2026 Case reference: CAM12224 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 18/02/2026 about West Kentish Town Estate.  We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (EIR 2004). Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end of the answer which explains how and why it applies. A ballot of residents of West Kentish Town Estate was undertaken by the TRA in 2023.  This ballot was based on a Landlord Offer, published in 2020. At Page 21 this Landlord Offer says “Camden is committed to ensuring that residents have a continuing opportunity to feedback and have their voice heard on schemes – this includes opportunities to say whether they think schemes should proceed.” At page 8: “There will be ongoing consultation after this [yes] decision, ensuring that residents remain involved in the ongoing design and delivery process.” The purpose of my request is to ascertain whether there has been any documented consultation with estate residents after the ballot was completed in 2023.  I am not requesting information related to the statutory consultation of the planning application related to the estate (reference 2025/2667/P), that is when support or objections for the plans can be submitted to the planning officer, rather any consultation occurring in the interim of the ballot concluding and the aforementioned application being submitted.Further to the above, can you please provide all external and internal correspondence, reports, findings, etc, regarding consultation of residents, including outcomes of any consultation after 2023. We are not processing this request.  It would involve a disproportionate amount of time, effort and expense to the council and is excepted under the EIR 2004.  Please see the exception notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exception that applies is: regulation 12(4)b which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is manifestly unreasonable. We have considered the time it will take the council to locate the information requested in the request, to extract it, collate it and then to review and redact any sensitive information that will be subject to further exceptions under the EIR 2004. We have two Community Liaison Advisors, a Multidisciplinary team of master planners working on the scheme and preparing the Planning Application including a comms agency.  We held numerous events in the specified period.  We would have many thousands of emails, correspondence, meetings, reports and findings to search through to recover and collate relevant information.  This information would then have to be to remove or redact information that is excepted under the EIR 2004. We have considered the impact and burden that processing this request would have on the team who would have to deal with it. We have concluded that the time, effort and costs involved would place a disproportionate burden on the team and severely impact their ability to perform their normal duties. In applying this exception, the Council has also considered the balance of the public interest in line with the EIR 2004.  We have indicated the weight of each of these considerations. The public interest argument for releasing this information is: - it would improve the transparency for the general public of the council’s decisions and processes in dealing with the <insert>. •The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: - processing this request in full would be provide a large burden in terms of officer time and cost to the Council (High). • this would necessarily constitute a significant diversion of resources away from the council’s core business activities, (High) and: • it would consequently have a proportionally detrimental impact on it’s provision of services to the public (High). • it is not in the public interest public interest that the Council neglect its provision of services to the public to focus on one information request (High). • It is felt that in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information. There is a presumption in favour of disclosure in the EIR 2004. We considered whether this overrides the public interest test conclusion and have concluded that it does not. Advice and assistance The 2020 ballot was a GLA requirement and administered by external electoral services.  The ‘TRA’ and the ‘ballot’ they held is not recognised by Camden and has no official role. We can provide the ‘Statement of Community Involvement’ supporting the Planning Application (2025/2667/P approved in December).  This details all the engagements efforts since 2015, including the requested “reports, findings, etc, regarding consultation of residents, including outcomes of any consultation after 2023”.  Statutory consultation only occurs after the Planning Application is submitted (July 2025). The council continues to be committed to involving all residents in the redevelopment throughout construction.  Building new homes and a neighbourhood that all are involved in ensures successful communities Further Information We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. A key driver for the project was the delivery of high‐quality new homes to meet the housing needs of existing estate residents and improve the quality and layout of open space on the estate. Although the scheme overall will build only six additional new council homes the council rented floor space will be increased by a third because the new homes are significantly larger. The scheme will also deliver new Camden Living homes let at below market rents. Feedback from residents living in the completed new homes has been extremely positive. Three blocks on the Regent’s Park estate demolished as part of High Speed 2 related works around Euston despite Council opposition. The blocks comprised 182 homes comprising 136 council rent homes and 46 leasehold properties. Document Title: general duties of Councillor Lotis Bautista
Document Text: Date: 11/09/2024 Ref: CAM8503 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 09/09/2024 about general duties of Councillor Lotis Bautista. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response Your request was: I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 regarding Councillor Lotis Bautista in her role as Chair of the Children, Schools, and Families Scrutiny Committee. Specifically, I would like to request the following information: 1. Emails Received and Responded To: - How many emails has Councillor Lotis Bautista received since taking her new post as Chair of the Children, Schools, and Families Scrutiny Committee? - How many of those emails has she responded to? - How many emails has she ignored or not replied to? - What is the official reason for not responding to emails from residents, particularly those from distressed, vulnerable parents of disabled children? 2. Role and Responsibilities of Councillor Lotis Bautista: - Please provide a detailed description of Councillor Lotis Bautista’s official role as Chair of the Children, Schools, and Families Scrutiny Committee. - Why has she not responded to vulnerable parents of disabled children who have contacted her by email? I am aware of several families including myself who she has completely ignored since taking her new role. I find it concerning that a public official would fail to address the concerns of residents, especially those contacting her about sensitive matters. Councillor Lotis Bautista, as the Chair of the Children, Schools, and Families Scrutiny Committee, has a crucial role in overseeing the performance and policies related to children's services, education, and family support within Camden. Her responsibilities include ensuring that services provided to families, especially those involving vulnerable children, are effective, responsive, and meet statutory London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk obligations. As a public official, she is accountable for representing and addressing the concerns of her constituents, including vulnerable parents of disabled children. Ignoring residents, especially those facing distressing circumstances, goes against the principles of public service and accountability. Elected officials like Councillor Bautista have a duty to engage with the public, address their concerns, and provide support or guidance where needed. Failing to respond to vulnerable families undermines trust in the system and can prevent these families from accessing critical services or help. It is essential that councillors actively listen to and engage with their communities, ensuring that all voices, particularly those in need, are heard and supported. The council holds the information requested but is refusing your request under section 14(1). Section 14(1) refusal notice. The council is refusing your request as it considers that it is vexatious. The council has reason to believe that you are acting together with a number of other requesters as part of a campaign to disrupt the council and particularly the SEND service by the volume of FOI requests around this subject. We have noted an increase in requests around SEND in August and early September which is greater than the normal number. We have also noted an unusual number originating from the ‘WhatDoTheyKnow’ website where it is known that requesters may use pseudonyms to hide their actual identity. There are other features in the requests such as content and style that provide evidence that this is not a coincidental increase but a campaign. A number of requests contain allegations about individual named members of staff, with accusations which are unjustifiably personal and abusive. The staff named in requests have been upset and distressed by such allegations and personal attacks. There is evidence that the requester and those acting with them are using the FOI process not to gain information but to undertake a campaign against individual council officers. In doing this, it damages the reputation of the Freedom of Information legislation itself, particularly as they are made on a public website. Handling the requests place a disproportionate burden in terms of work required to locate, collate and extract information, and in disruption to services. The large number of multiple-part requests submitted in a short space of time have the result of putt ing a disproportionate burden on a small number of staff in the service area who handle such tasks. This disrupts their day-to-day work and has caused anxiety due to the volume and nature of the requests. Those who are part of the campaign have also engaged in frequent emails to the service around these issues as well as complaints. The council has already required the input of senior officers to handle these matters, disrupting normal service delivery for the SEND area, legal services and the Data Protection Advice Team. Whilst the council acknowledges that there may be some serious purpose in the concerns raised in the requests, the wording, the overlapping nature, the mingling of requests for information with complaints and allegations, show that any such serious purpose is outweighed by the vexatious nature of the requests. The council therefore believes that handling this request would cause a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption and distress that will strain council resources and get in the way of delivering mainstream services and answering legitimate reques ts. Therefore, the council has refused this request as vexatious. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding the information because it is excepted as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exception applies.  Please see the refusal notice at the end which explains how and why it applies. I would like to make a request for any internal communications about the recently proposed planning reforms among/to/from Camden's Cabinet, particularly regarding the proposed changes to Section 106 Refusal Notice The exception that applies is: regulation 12 (c) which states that a public authority may refuse to disclose information to the extent that the request for information is formulated in too general a manner and the public authority has complied with regulation 9 Under Regulation 9 (2) of the Environmental Information Regulations (EIR), a public authority need not comply with a request that is formulated in too general a manner but is required to ask the applicant to provide more particulars in relation to the request. The request is rather vague and broad.  It also gives no time frame or explanation of what recently proposed planning reforms are of particular interest. To further assist you we suggest that we could search the inboxes of cabinet members using the terms “planning” / “reform” / “106.” We would surmise that your request concerns recent planning reforms published in July 2020 so we would not search back beyond this date and would look for any correspondence between cabinet members or between cabinet members and officers. The collection and recovery policy takes account of the need to maintain collection rates, the changing circumstances and needs of our residents and the problems associated with an Inner London Borough. Our working procedures are fully documented and regularly updated and we are committed to ensuring that our staff are polite, well trained and knowledgeable. 1. Our aims and objectives and how we achieve them 1.1 To issue documents in a timely manner and to the correct person(s). To assist us we:  issue enquiry forms to gather information  our inspectors will make visits to properties  use external records, such as the land registry, telephone directories, other Councils and Government Agencies, tracing agencies and bailiffs.  use internal records such as benefit records, the electoral register and any other databases as allowed for in the Local Government Finance Act or other relevant legislation 1.2 To ensure that the amount of the charge is correct. To help us we will:  encourage customers to apply for any relevant discount or exemption  carry out regular reviews of discounts and exemptions  work together with the Council’s planning section and the Valuation Office Agency to ensure property bands are up to date.  answer all enquiries fully and within the Council's targets 1.3 To ensure that all our documents are clear, concise, informative and produced in the most cost effective manner. To help us we will:  Avoid using jargon 3 of 12  make bills/leaflets/letters/forms available in various languages and Braille as appropriate  ensure that letters and forms are produced and posted in the most cost effective and efficient way 1.4 To make it as easy as possible for our customers to pay we will ensure that:  we offer various methods of payment, including on-line and telephone payments systems available 24/7  we will use discretion when considering repayment arrangements in some exceptional circumstances  our telephone lines at the Town Hall are open 8am to 5pm  customers can visit the Town Hall between 9am to 5pm  we will make appointments to see customers outside normal working hours, and make home visits where a customer is unable to contact us any other way. 1.5 To ensure that we have well-trained and knowledgeable staff. To help us we will  keep all our procedures well documented  train our staff and give regular feedback via supervision sessions and personal development  monitor performance and carry out quality checks  we will ensure that our staff are kept updated on welfare benefits changes and issues and that they promote the uptake of housing and council tax benefit 1.6 To ensure that we liaise with Advice Agencies to give our customers the best information and assistance. To help us we will:  meet with various Agencies, for example Law Centres and Citizens Advice Bureaux  review this policy when appropriate, ensuring that it acknowledges any changes in legislation or Council policy towards customers  deal with specific cases as referred to us, working together to ensure the best outcome 2. Issuing bills and adjustment notices  We issue our annual bills in mid March prior to the financial year 1 April to 31 March  When a customer tells us that they have occupied a property we will send a bill and give the statutory number of instalments  When a customer tells us that they have vacated we will issue a closing bill and process any refund pro rata to the rest of the year  Where there is a change in circumstances or an amendment to the amount due or the instalment amounts we will issue an adjusted bill, or if there is an overpayment and no further debt is due, a refund. 4 of 12 3. Paying the annual bill by instalments 3.1 The rules for paying by instalments are set out in the Administration and Enforcement Regulations. These say that when a bill is issued before the 30 April of the financial year for which the Tax is due, then the bill will be payable by 10 uninterrupted monthly instalments, and the Council can decide those dates (this is known as the statutory scheme). 3.2 However, the Council can also make an agreement with the taxpayer to pay by more or less than the statutory 10 payments. We therefore also offer weekly and fortnightly instalment schemes. The costs of running these schemes is much higher compared to direct debit or monthly instalments, but we recognise that a small proportion of our customers find it easier to budget by paying this way. They are less likely to fall into arrears and therefore ultimately we save money by not having to chase late or non-payments. We also offer quarterly, half yearly and annual schemes, which may be more convenient for some customers. 3.3 By offering these different schemes it means that our customers are given more flexibility than the statutory scheme allows and we are able to meet the needs of all our customers more effectively. There are no extra costs charged to the customer for these different schemes. 3.4 Details of the amounts and the dates that each instalment is due are set out on the annual bill. We have selected the 1 st of April to 1st January along with most other Councils, as our payment dates for the statutory scheme because this means that we can take prompt action within the same month if an instalment is missed. This ensures that the tax is collected promptly and our costs of collection are kept to a minimum. The costs of late payment ultimately rebound on all our taxpayers. 4. Payment by direct debit 4.1 This is our preferred method of payment. We are able to offer various payment dates over 10 or 12 months, on the 7 th, 15th, 21st or last day of each month. We can set up a direct debit over the phone. It is widely accepted as being the most efficient form of payment. The costs to the Council of processing a direct debit payment are much lower than other forms payment. This method is also very secure and, once set up by the taxpayer, it means there is no chance of payment not being made because the taxpayer has forgotten to pay, or mislaid the instalment booklet. Because of the savings we make it means that we can offer those customers 12 payments, payable at the end of the month if requested, giving an extra 2 months over which to spread the payments. 5. Other ways to pay 5.1 Our customers can pay in a variety of other ways than by direct debit. We will accept any of the following: 5 of 12  Cash – in person at our cashiers office in the Town Hall between 9am to 5pm Monday to Friday.  Cheque – by post to the Town Hall, or in person at our cashiers office  Debit/Credit card – in person at our cashiers. Or over the telephone, or on-line 24 hrs a day  Bank – over the bank counter  Post Office – over the counter  Pay point – at your local retailer by cash or cheque  Online through your bank – the customer can set up their own recurring payments but must quote the Council’s correct banking details which appear on the back of the bill 5.2 There may be charges payable at the point of making a payment for some of these methods. These will be detailed on the back of your bill. 5.3 The Council may from time to time add to, restrict, or withdraw some of the ways to pay at its discretion, but will always give reasonable prior notice. 5.4 In order to avoid delays and incorrect allocation of payments it is very important that the customer quotes the correct Council Tax reference number in all cases. 5.5 The methods and types of payment we offer are clearly explained on our bills and on the web site. When a customer declines to take up direct debit, we will send an instalment payment book. If a customer mislays their book we can issue a replacement, free of charge. 5.6 The Council may withdraw the issue of payment books at its discretion, but will always give reasonable prior notice. 6. Bills issued for part of the year 6.1 When a first bill is sent out later than 30 April, for example when someone moves in part way through the financial year, then the paym ent period will be shorter and there will be fewer instalments. 7. Council tax benefit 7.1 When a customer is in arrears and contacts us because they are unable to pay, we will encourage them to apply for council tax benefit if they have not already done so. 7.2 If a new application for council tax benefit is made, or a customer’s circumstances have changed which may result in a change to benefit, we will continue to collect the instalments as they appeared on the last bill. If benefit is awarded, we will reduce the remaining instalments, or if the account is overpaid for the year, issue a refund. 7.3 The reason we do not suspend collection pending the outcome of the application, is because we cannot be certain how much, if any, benefit will awarded and arrears could accrue. The Council’s benefit service will make every effort to calculate benefit without delay, providing information regarding 6 of 12 circumstances is supplied promptly. 7.4 If an award of council tax benefit is delayed by work being behind, we will withdraw from any recovery action taken in respect of debt accruing after the benefit application was made. 8. Issuing reminders and final notices 8.1 The instalment date of the 1 st of the month reflects our commitment to maximise income at the lowest cost. It is important that payments are received by the due date in order to achieve this goal. A number of our customers do not pay by the due dates. Whilst we acknowledge that late or non payment happens for many different reasons we will try to collect all overdue payments diligently, whatever the payment method. 8.2 It is the customer's responsibility to make sure that instalments are paid on time. We will always send a reminder or a final notice before sending a summons. Some of our customers dispute receipt of reminders and finals, but this is not an excuse for missing payments and cannot be used as a reason for non-payment. Whilst it cannot be proven that any of the notices we send has been received the law requires us to prove only that a notice has been sent. We fulfil this obligation by having a special posting procedure, which is secure and supported by the relevant documentation. The law supports the principle that if we can prove postage then we have acted reasonably and we have fulfilled our responsibility as far as it is possible 8.3 We follow a regular recovery timetable, and reminders and final notices are sent monthly. We can amend this timetable, adding to or removing dates as required. This enables us to manage workloads, resources and collection requirements more effectively.  If a payment is not received by the due date we will issue a reminder. We will ask the customer to pay the missed instalment within 14 days after the date on the reminder. We also ask the customer to ensure that future payments are made by the due dates.  If the missed instalment is received by the given date we will not take any further action; but if it remains unpaid then we will cancel the instalments and issue a summons without further notice for the full year's tax. (Case Example 1, Appendix 1)  If the instalment is received by the given date, but another instalment is not paid, then we will send a second reminder. If the missed instalment is received by the given date we will not take any further action; but if it remains unpaid then we will cancel the instalments and issue a summons without further notice for the full year's tax.  If the account is brought up to date but falls behind for a 3 rd time then we will issue a final notice, which cancels the instalments immediately, followed by a summons for the full year's tax within 7 days. In order to avoid a summons, the final notice must be paid in full. 7 of 12 8.4 This means that we will issue a maximum of 2 reminders during any financial year. A reminder will ask for the missing instalment(s) to be paid. (Case Example 2,Appendix 1) and advise customers of the consequences of not paying as requested. 9. What sort of payment do we expect at this stage? 9.1 If a taxpayer receives a reminder then we will expect payment by the due date given on the notice. If the taxpayer cannot pay the missed instalment(s) then we may make a short-term arrangement for the amount to be paid later in the month or with the next instalment. 10 Special payment arrangements 10.1 In some very exceptional circumstances, such as cases of extreme hardship, and depending on the information available to us, we may agree to spread the amount over a longer period. We will confirm any such arrangement in writing. If these arrangements are not paid then we will tell the customer and cancel them and recovery will resume from the point prior to the arrangement. 10.2 When we make a special payment arrangement we look at the individual circumstances of the taxpayer, for example whether they are on benefit, what type, whether they live alone or there are other family members present in the household. In discussing an affordable amount we will also consider whether there is more than 1 year's charge outstanding, vulnerability, those on a low income, whether there is a health problem or if the customer satisfies us that they cannot pay as requested for some other compelling reason. 10.3 Some cases are referred to us by the advice agencies. When making any payment arrangements we will take account of the information being provided and the problems experienced by some sections of the community. 10.4 We will be firm that payment arrangements will only be accepted if payment is made by direct debit, unless the customer does not have a suitable type of bank account. 10.5 Although we will attempt to collect the tax in the year that it is due, we accept that some customers will not be able to do this. We will therefore endeavour to ensure that we strike a balance between the affordability of repayments and the period that we expect payment in, whilst making arrangements that do not allow the debt to escalate as each new year’s tax becomes due. 11. Summons 11.1 With customers who do not pay when we send a reminder or final notice, it is necessary to issue a summons. We are required to go to Magistrate’s Court and make a complaint stating that the tax remains unpaid. If the Court agrees then the summons is issued. This work costs the Council extra money to administer and we also have to pay the Court a fee for each summons issued. These costs are added to the council tax account. When we send a summons 8 of 12 we enclose information explaining what to do and we ask the customer to contact us to discuss payment if they cannot pay in full. 11.2 We will expect payment of the full balance before the date of the hearing of the summons. In some cases we may make an arrangement for payment as described in section 12. (See Case Example 3, Appendix 1). However this will be on the condition that the arrears are repaid via direct debit. 12. Costs 12.1 As the recovery of a debt progresses to Court, then additional costs will be incurred if a liability order is granted at the Court hearing. As at April 2011, the costs of a summons is £80.00 and a liability order £15.00. Payments made to an account will be posted to clear costs first. Costs will rarely be withdrawn unless we have made a mistake or there is some compelling reason e.g. where we haven't dealt with a customer's letter or complaint that would significantly affect the amount payable, or where it is evident that full payment was received before the issue of the summons. 12.2 The amount of Court costs charged are intended solely to reimburse the overall outlay of taking recovery action in Camden and these costs may vary from time to time in accordance changes to that outlay. 13. Joint And several liability 13.1 Where there is a joint occupation, for example joint tenants or owners, or partnerships for example husband and wife, then we will look to both parties to pay the charge. The law says that each party will be liable for the whole charge (called "joint and several liability"). All our bills and other communications will be addressed to all the liable persons in the property. It is not possible to issue a bill apportioned to each liable person, or divide it into “shares”. 13.2 In the case of a summons, we will send a copy to each person, but only one set of costs will be payable. 13.3 When the tax is not being paid we will take action for recovery of the debt against any or all of the parties. We will make arrangements for payment, but where we cannot make satisfactory arrangements with one party we may continue our action against another party. 14 What happens at Court 14.1 When we issue a summons we tell the taxpayer when the summons will be heard and where. We add on the costs of the summons and we ask for payment in full by the hearing date. A bench (panel) of lay Magistrates or a District Judge will conduct the hearing. 14.2 We have specialist officers who conduct the Court Hearings. They are experienced and have worked consistently hard with the Court staff and officials over a period of time to ensure that the proceedings run as smoothly 9 of 12 as possible and that they conform to the legislative requirements in every respect. 14.3 It is not compulsory for the taxpayer to attend the court hearing, but if he/she wants to dispute the tax or wants to defend their case in the Court then they can and we do not discourage attendance. 14.4 The Court will give an audience to anyone who wishes to appear, however, unless the taxpayer has a valid defence, such as they are not the person who is responsible for the council tax, then the Court is obliged to grant a liability order. Most often the customer is not disputing that the debt is owed, but either cannot afford to pay or wants to make an arrangement to pay. The Court will grant a liability order in these circumstances, but may ask the Council to consider making an arrangement outside of the Court. 14.5 If the taxpayer is disputing a debt and the Court is satisfied that there may be a case to consider then it may grant an Adjournment to a later date to give the Council an opportunity to investigate. 14.6 If the Court is satisfied that the summons was properly served, and the amount remains unpaid then it will grant a liability order. An additional fee is charged for this as described above. 14.7 We will send as many staff as available to the Court to deal with enquiries from anyone who appears at the hearing, and to discuss payment arrangements. Whilst we will try to answer as many enquiries as possible unfortunately, the Court does not have the facilities available for us to conduct in-depth discussions and therefore it is often necessary to arrange to speak to the taxpayer at another time. We usually agree to call the customer on our return to the office. 15 Once we have obtained a liability order 15.1 Once we have a liability order, we will send a letter to the taxpayer advising them of the outcome of the Court hearing and that they have 14 days in which to pay or we will take further action. As the subject of a liability order, a person is legally required to submit employment details under Regulation 56 of the Council Tax (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1992 as amended. Failure to supply the information after a request in writing to do so constitutes a criminal offence with a fine of up to £500.00. Information that we receive is used to establish what appropriate steps to take next, and is not divulged to any other party, except the Court if appropriate. 15.2 We are keen to offer the taxpayer another opportunity to make an arrangement by direct debit and ask them to contact us if they have any enquiries. If this is unsuccessful, the Council has the power to recover the debt using any of the following methods, but the options below are set out in the order that we will usually consider them. 10 of 12  Attachment of Benefits (e.g. Job Seekers Allowance, Pension Credit) If a taxpayer is receiving a welfare benefit then we will usually ask for regular deductions to be made at source. However, we may ask for additional direct payments after considering the amount of debt outstanding and the rate at which it is accruing. When a subsequent liability order is granted we will usually ask for deductions to be made and this attachment will be placed in a "queue" to be started once the current order is paid. Sometimes it is not possible to make an attachment to benefit.  Attachment of Earnings If the taxpayer is in paid employment and we have the employer's details then we will ask the employer to make deductions from salary. The deductions are at a set scale and where there are debts for more than one year the Order will be made on the oldest debt first. The law allows us to make up to 2 Orders at a time.  Bailiff Collection In the absence of any useful information about the taxpayer's circumstances or employment then we will issue the account to external bailiffs contracted to the Council. The bailiff will visit the premises with the aim of obtaining payment. For every visit or action that the bailiff takes a fee will be charged. The bailiff companies are required to follow our "Code of Conduct" guidelines and the terms and conditions of the Council’s contract with them. The bailiff is empowered to make arrangements on our behalf if they think it appropriate. A bailiff may remove goods to be sold at auction or might return the case saying there are no goods to remove ("Nulla Bona"). We will ensure as far as possible that the information the bailiff holds is up-to-date and accurate. The bailiff is expected to operate in a fair and consistent manner and any complaints we receive are treated very seriously and investigated thoroughly. 15.3 The next steps will have a significant impact on the taxpayer and we will consider each case carefully before deciding which is the most appropriate. We will look to see if the taxpayer is on benefit, what type, whether they live alone or there are other family members present in the household. We will look at information about the taxpayers assets and assess whether there is any disability, vulnerability or long term health issues. The vast majority of cases reaching this point will be where the taxpayer has not contacted us at all or where payment arrangements have been made which have been broken. We will proceed with the options below only if, in our judgement, the taxpayer is able to pay but is refusing to do so. .  Charging Order Where a taxpayer owns a property, we will consider taking an action to obtain an order forcing the sale of the property to cover the debt and the costs of the action.  Bankruptcy In some instances, where a charging order is not appropriate, for example where taxpayer does not own the property of there is insufficient equity, we will make a petition for the bankruptcy of the taxpayer. The costs of this type of action can be claimed from the debtor. 11 of 12  Committal to prison If payment is not received then we may decide that the appropriate way forward is to take the case back to Court and ask for an investigation to be made into the debtor's means. This action is only used in cases where bankruptcy or charging orders are not appropriate, and in cases where the bailiff has attempted to collect the debt but has been unsuccessful. Before taking this action we will advise the taxpayer of our intention and again we will give him/her another opportunity to come to some arrangement regarding payment. We will again also ask for information of employer and income. The Court will hold a full investigation into the means and circumstances of the debtor and will decide whether there has been inability, neglect or refusal to pay. The Court can make an arrangement for the repayment of the debt over a certain period, it can remit the debt, or it can impose a prison sentence of up to 90 days. 16. Absconders 16.1 We will use whatever records are legally available to us, from various sources in order to trace and collect from customers who have vacated a property owing council tax without leaving a forwarding address. 17 Complaints 17.1 The Council has an established two stage complaints procedure and complaints about any of the actions taken under this policy will be dealt with through this process. Making a complaint will not usually suspend the recovery process. If the Council has made a mistake then this should be dealt with quickly at the local resolution stage. 18 Conclusion 18.1 The action we take is not meant to punish the individual concerned. Our intention is to secure payment of the council tax in an efficient and cost effective way, whilst still meeting the customer’s needs. We will always act in accordance with the Law. 18.2 We will, as far as possible, ensure that the action we take is reasonable and we will consider what alternatives are available in exceptional or compelling cases. 18.3 We will continue to work towards collecting the maximum amount of Council Tax, whilst aiming to strike a balance between the Council's need to improve the collection rate, our obligations towards all our customers and satisfaction of the Council's policies and Government requirements. Council Tax and Business Rates Division Updated: February 2011 To be reviewed by: February 2013 Contact: Mark Tate, Head of Council Tax and Business Rates 12 of 12 Appendix 1 Case Examples 1. Mr. A receives his annual bill in March and his instalments run from 1 April to 1 January.  He pays his April instalment on 1 April, but does not pay his 1 May instalment.  We send a reminder on 17 May asking for payment by 31 May.  He still does not pay. On 1 June the instalment facility is cancelled and the full amount for the year becomes payable. We send a summons on 3 June. If the full amount on the summons is not paid by the Court hearing date, we will ask for a liability order and if successful, examine the options for further recovery. 2. Ms. B receives her annual bill in March and her instalments run from 1 April to 1 January.  She pays her April instalment on 23 April, after we send out a reminder on 20 April.  She pays May, June and July on time but pays her August instalment on 23 August after we send out another reminder on 20 August.  She does not pay the September instalment. We send a final notice that cancels the instalment arrangement and the full amount for the year becomes due. If we receive the full amount within 7 days, no further action is taken and the instalment arrangement resumes next year. Otherwise a summons is issued. 3. Mr. C has been sent a summons. He does not appear at Court on the hearing date and a liability order is granted.  We send him a letter advising that a liability order has been granted and warning that further recovery action will be taken i
