Document Text: Date: 16/05/2025 Ref: CAM10096 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 15/04/2025 about the death of a young person in supported housing. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested. However, we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below. We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. I am [redacted] the legal father of [redacted] is writing to formally outline my concerns and request clarity regarding historical contact between Camden Council Social Services and **[redacted]**, who tragically died while under the care of Camden Council-supported housing. I understand [redacted] was present during this period, and I seek detailed information about her involvement and the Council’s interactions with [redacted] prior to their death. ###**Key Concerns and Requests** 1. **Circumstances of [redacted] Death** - [redacted] died while residing in Camden-supported housing. I request all records related to their care, including but not limited to: - Risk assessments, care plans, and incident reports. - Notes or logs from staff, including [redacted], regarding [redacted] well-being. 2. **Historical Contact with Social Services** - A full account of all interactions between [redacted] and Camden Social Services, including: - Dates, nature, and outcomes of meetings or communications. - Documentation of any safeguarding concerns raised or actions taken. 3. **Role of [redacted]** - Clarification of [redacted] position and responsibilities during [redacted] time in supported housing. - Records of camden social services and housing support direct involvement with [redacted], including communications, reports, or witness statements. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 4. **Posthumous Rights and Access** - While I understand Freedom of Information (FOI) requests may not apply here, I am prepared to submit a **Subject Access Request (SAR)** under the Data Protection Act 2018 if required. Please confirm: - The process for accessing [redacted] records as their next of kin/legal representative*. - Any documentation needed to validate my authority to act on [redacted] behalf. ### **Final Remarks** [Redacted] death in Camden-supported housing demands transparency. I urge the Council to prioritise this request to ensure accountability and closure. We are withholding this information as we consider the following exemptions apply. Refusal notice: Section 41: Provided in confidence The information for questions 1, 2 and the second part of question 3 are withheld because it is exempt under Section 41. This absolute exemption applies where the information was provided to the public authority in confidence by another person, whereby release would be an actionable breach of confidence. This is an absolute exemption with no public interest test. The information was received by the council from a third party and provided by them under a clear expectation of confidence. The information is about the individual’s life, health, circumstances, and feelings and is clearly information of a private nature that is substantial and not trivial. The information is detailed and not in the public domain. This information is covered by a common law duty of confidence and releasing this information would constitute a breach of confidence owed by the council to the deceased. In other words, if we disclosed the information the third party could take the council to court. The deceased has a living relative who could bring an action for breach of confidence. That person has expressed a clear view that they do not wish to have this information disclosed and so an action from breach of confidence would be realistic. There would be no defence to such an action of overriding public interest given the sensitivity of the information. Section 40 (2): Personal information The information in the first part of question 3 ‘Clarification of [redacted] position and responsibilities during [redacted] time in supported housing’ is the personal data of a junior council officer. The council considers that to disclose the personal data requested would not be in accordance with data protection legislation and therefore we have withheld all of the information under the absolute exemption in Section 40 (2). The exemption states that personal data requested may be withheld when to release it would be a breach of the requirements of data protection law which is the UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018. The information withheld is personal information because it allows living individuals to be identified. The council considers that it would be a breach of the General Data Protection Regulation article 5 requirements of fairness and proportionality to publish this personal information in a FOI request. In doing this we have considered the legitimate public interest in disclosure against the interests of the data subject/s and concluded that in the circumstances disclosure would contravene the data protection requirements of fairness and proportionality particularly considering that Freedom of Information responses are public documents and published to the world and not provided just to the requester. The council’s redaction policy states that junior staff member names, (those below Assistant Director level) unless in public facing positions, would not be released in a FOI response. Therefore, the names of junior staff members have been redacted from the request details as they would have no expectation that their details would be released into the public domain, and especially given the content of the request as we consider that to include them would be a breach of the requirements to act fairly and proportionately. Advice and assistance We are very sorry for your loss and understand that you are seeking answers. Please note that some of the information you have requested - specifically questions 1 to 3 - is likely to be addressed during a future inquest at the Coroner’s Court. For further information, you may wish to contact Poplar Coroner’s Court directly at: coroner.poplar@camden.gov.uk . The matters raised in question 4 has been responded to outside of this FOI request. Document Text: Date: 09/09/2024 Ref: CAM8386 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 21/08//2024 about Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) and related matters. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response Your request was: Dear Camden Council, I am writing to you under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 to request information regarding the qualifications, credentials related to the current position of SEND Tribunal, Disagreement, Mediation, and Resolutions Officer at Camden Council. Specifically, I request the following information: 1. **Qualifications and Credentials**: Please provide details of the qualifications, certifications, and professional credentials required for the role of SEND Tribunal, Disagreement, Mediation, and Resolutions Officer. This should include any relevant degrees, certifications, training, or professional experience related to special educational needs (SEN), mediation, and conflict resolution. 2. **Job Description and Requirements**: Please provide a copy of the official job description for the role of SEND Tribunal, Disagreement, Mediation, and Resolutions Officer, including any required qualifications and experience that are listed as essential or desirable for this position. 3. **Recruitment and Selection Process**: Please provide information on the recruitment and selection process for the role of SEND Tribunal, Disagreement, Mediation, and Resolutions Officer. This should include details of the criteria used to evaluate candidates and any relevant interview or assessment processes. 4. **Conduct and Professional Standards**: I would like to understand the professional standards and codes of conduct that govern the actions of the SEND Tribunal, Disagreement, Mediation, and Resolutions Officer. Specifically, what London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk policies and guidelines are in place at Camden Council regarding appropriate communication and conduct towards parents and families involved in SEND matters? How does the Council address instances where a staff member's actions are alleged to have contravened these standards? 5. **Response to Allegations of Misconduct and Misfeasance in Public Office**: I request information on how Camden Council addresses allegations of misconduct and misfeasance in public office. Specifically, defamatory statements about residents, parents or guardians, or engaging in other actions intended to absolve the Council of its legal obligations, especially regarding EHCP provisions? What steps are taken to investigate and address such conduct, and what justifications, if any, are provided for such actions? 6. **Policies on Misfeasance in Public Office**: Please provide any Camden Council policies or guidelines that pertain to allegations of misfeasance in public office by Council employees, including the procedures for investigation, accountability measures, and potential consequences for those found to have committed such acts. Please provide the requested information in electronic format. If any part of this request is unclear, please contact me for clarification. Additionally, if any of the information requested is exempt from disclosure, please provide a detailed explanation of the exemption(s) applied and the reasons for their application. I look forward to your prompt response within the statutory 20 -working-day period. Thank you for your assistance. The council holds the information requested but is refusing your request under section 14(1). Section 14(1) refusal notice. The council is refusing your request as it considers that it is vexatious. The council has reason to believe that you are acting together with a number of other requesters as part of a campaign to disrupt the council and particularly the SEND service by the volume of FOI requests around this subject. We have noted an increase in requests around SEND in August and early September which is greater than the normal number. We have also noted an unusual number originating from the ‘WhatDoTheyKnow’ website where it is known that requesters may use pseudonyms to hide their actual identity. There are other features in the requests such as content and style that provide evidence that this is not a coincidental increase but a campaign. A number of requests contain allegations about individual named members of staff, with accusations which are unjustifiably personal and abusive. The staff named in requests have been upset and distressed by such allegations and personal attacks. There is evidence that the requester and those acting with them are using the FOI process not to gain information but to undertake a campaign against individual council officers. In doing this, it damages the reputation of the Freedom of Information legislation itself, particularly as they are made on a public website. Handling the requests place a disproportionate burden in terms of work required to locate, collate and extract information, and in disruption to services. The large number of multiple-part requests submitted in a short space of time have the result of putting a disproportionate burden on a small number of staff in the service area who handle such tasks. This disrupts their day-to-day work and has caused anxiety due to the volume and nature of the requests. Those who are part of the campaign have also engaged in frequent emails to the service around these issues as well as complaints. The council has already required the input of senior officers to handle these matters, disrupting normal service delivery for the SEND area, legal services, and the Data Protection Advice Team. Whilst the council acknowledges that there may be some serious purpose in the concerns raised in the requests, the wording, the overlapping nature, the mingling of requests for information with complaints and allegations, show that any such serious purpose is outweighed by the vexatious nature of the requests. The council therefore believes that handling this request would cause a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption and distress that will strain council resources and get in the way of delivering mainstream services and answering legitimate requests. Therefore, the council has refused this request as vexatious. Document Title: Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG)
Document Text: Date: 28/06/2024 Case reference : CAM7920London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 19/06/2024 about Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and/or the Environmental Information Regulations 2004  Response The council does not holds the information requested: Please see the following freedom of information request relating to Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) on new developments. Requested information: For each new development granted planning approval since 2021, please can you provide data on: 1. The total Biodiversity Net Gain percentage included in the proposal, broken down by on-site and off-site gains. 2. Available details of the off-site gain proposed including the local authority and estimated cost of purchase. 3. The actual Biodiversity Net Gain percentage for completed developments, broken down by on-site and off-site gains. 4. The number of statutory credits purchased where applicable. We do not hold this information. This is because: The main piece of legislation behind Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) is the Environment Act 2021, Part 6 adds Schedule 7A to the Town and Country Planning Act and brings BNG into the planning system. Amendments were made to that through LURA 2023. The bit of legislation which sets out the process for considering BNG in planning is set out in The Biodiversity Gain (Town and Country Planning) (Modifications and Amendments) (England) Regulations 2024. So, whilst the legislation to establish BNG dates from 2021 it was only in 2024 that all the necessary secondary legislation came into force to allow/require us to consider it as part of the planning process. BNG applies to all Major Sites from 12th February 2024 and Small Sites from 2nd April 2024, both are defined as set out in the Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) Order 2015. The submission of the Biodiversity Gain Plan (BGP) which sets out how the 10% net gain is to be achieved is a post-planning decision matter, it has to be approved prior to commencement of the development. We have not yet had a BGP submitted for our consideration so there is no data to provide.  As the information not held is environmental, we have to comply with a technicality and tell you that because it is not held it is excepted under Regulation 12 (4)(a) of the EIR 2004.  The Information Commissioner does not require a public interest test where the information is not held. Document Text: Date: 24/01/2024 Ref: CAM6709 Dear Requester, Thank you for your request for information dated 22/12/2024 about the job description, role and duties of a housing officer and disrepair compensation payments. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: What is a housing officer job description 1) What does that cover when it comes to dealing with tenants? A summary of the neighbourhood housing officer’s (NHO’s) job profile is published and publicly available on the Council’s website. Please enter the link below into your web browser: Your Neighbourhood Housing Officer - Camden Council . To avoid delay, council tenants access our repairs service directly but otherwise NHOs are the main point of contact for council tenants and can assist with most housing issues. Other teams may however have responsibility for some decisions, including appl ications for rehousing or adaptations to homes. The Council’s duties to its tenants are set out in our tenancy conditions which you can also find on the website here Council tenant rights and responsibilities - Camden Council . See especially the section headed “Our Duties.” As the information requested is already reasonably accessible elsewhere it is exempt under the absolute exemption in Section 21. 2) Antisocial behaviour? In the tenancy conditions (section B5) we say that we will investigate complaints of antisocial behaviour and give you help and advice if you are affected. The specifics of that vary case by case but section C2 about anti-social behaviour provides examples of situations where the Council may need to step in and take action. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 3) Rent arrears? As a result of an increase in rent arrears following the pandemic and cost of living crisis the Council is piloting specialist teams to work with tenants to prevent and address rent arrears. The Council provides advice and support to tenants who are struggling to pay their rent (including with our own in-house welfare rights team) to help them to keep their tenancies. At the same time, we need to ensure rent is paid to fund the services we have a duty to provide and sometimes that means that enforcement action is necessary and that is part of the NHO role as well. 4) Referrals and which one can they make and if not under housing officer duties who would that be? Working in partnership and helping tenants to access other services that may benefit them is an important part of the NHO role. There are no restrictions that limit the referrals that NHOs, or other housing officers, can make. At the same time, when tenants are able to access services directly, simple signposting can reduce delay and free up time for other work. Most referrals will be to services like Adult Social Care, Children’s Services, Camden Safety Net (for support with domestic abuse) and to our welfare rights and tackling poverty teams. 5) Compensation payments ( during repairs no cooking facilities) The Council’s complaints policy includes a remedies policy and procedure which sets out the approach to compensation. You can find it towards the bottom of the page here: Complaints - Camden Council . 6) Daily rate of compensation when no hot water/ heating Information about compensation for a loss of hot water and or heating (when this is supplied by the Council) is included in the remedies policy , on page 3. 7) Daily rate of compensation when no cooking facilities The remedies policy does not specifically refer to compensation for a loss of gas for cooking but the provision for a loss of gas supply would apply when the Council charge for this. 8) Response times to tenants’ calls, emails policy There is no set response time for telephone calls or emails from tenants. As a matter of courtesy, responses should not of course be unreasonably delayed. You have indicated that you are dissatisfied with the service you have received from your NHO. There is a link to the Council’s complaints policy and procedure above. Alternatively, when you are unhappy about the service you can contact the neighbourhood ma nager. Please do let us know if you would like their contact details. These can also be obtained from Contact Camden on 020 7974 4444. Document Title: Health and safety concerns over G5 masts
Document Text: Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 07 October 2019 about health and safety concerns over G5 masts . We have dealt with this under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 . Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: There was a notice posted in Bacton about the concerns to health and safety with installation of G5 masts on this tower block. On further investigation the notice appears correct and such masts would indeed effect the health of tenants of this block. a. We strongly object to this mast being installed and request removal if this is proven correct, there has been no consultation with tenants or the TRA on this. A report is requested fro m the Landlord on the effects on health to tenants in this block. b. Why is the landlord allowing technology to superceed the health and well being of tenants, who allowed this? c. What is the financial agreement on allowing this technology to be installe d on Bacton Tower? Whilst we will always listen to and consider the views exp ressed by residents, your questions seem to be based on the premise that 5G deployment causes clear detrimental health impacts. Having due regard to an assessment of the availabl e national and international scientific evidence and current national guidance, we do not consider this is the case and we do not commission reports for individual blocks . Also, w e do not enter into contract s or finan caal agrements for installation of 5g masts on specific properties. As a local authority, we cannot disregard guidance and the requirements placed upon us by central Government. Parliament has passed legislation which is designed to facilitate the rollout of telecommunications infrastructure, which the Council is required to comply with and work within. Recent changes to legislation following the introdu ction of the Digital Economy Act 2017 give operators statutory rights to install their equipment to facilitate the creation of individual telecoms sites. Unless a property owner can prove its intention to redevelop the rooftop of a building where access ha s been requested, the operator will simply take the property owner to the Upper Land Tribunal, who will then oblige the owner to grant the operator an agreement within 6 months. Information and Records Management Corporate Services London Borough of Camden Town Hall Judd Street London WC1H 9JE Phone: 020 7974 7857 camden.gov.uk Date: Our reference: Email: 25 November 2019 FOI13534 foi@camden.gov.uk As a property owner, Camden Council has, working within the provisions of the legislation, chosen to work with operators in an effort to reduce the number of sites, through building sharing, and to influence the designs, in order to mitigate the visual impact of an installation. Not only have we had regard to the clear social value benefits of digital connectivity, but also to the currently available scientific evidence, which neither we nor central government consider to demonstrate detrimental health impacts of 4G/ 5G, when the technology is installed and operated within existing guidance. We are seeking to adopt best practice in the implementation of our Digital Rooftops programme. In summary, the management of telecommunications is governed by national and international legislation and guidance, with installations needing to comply with the limitations imposed by the International Commission on Non -Ionising Radiation Protection (ICNIRP). These instruct that the design and placement of sites must ensure that exclusion zones are either in areas that individuals cannot enter (for example in inaccessible clear space adjacent to a rooftop) or be signposted and in a controlled area. This is in line with Table 3.2 in the ‘European Commission's Non -binding guide to go od practice for implementing Directive 2013/35/EU: Electromagnetic Fields’ that you quoted, stating that EMF assessments in respect of common workplace activities, equipment and workplaces are not required for antennas outside operators exclusion zone, not ing that the field strengths usually fall rapidly with distance from the source of the field so that the use of guarding to restrict access to the immediate vicinity will often be a practical option (http://ec.europa.eu/social/BlobServlet?docId=14741&langId=en ). The Council’s position on the health implications of telecom mast installations, is informed by the advice of its Director of Public Health and by guidance from Public Heal th England (PHE), the statutory body responsible for protecting the nation from public health hazards. Radiofrequency electromagnetic field exposures include exposures to radio waves produced by Wi -Fi equipment, smart meters and mobile phone base stations . PHE guidance on this matter was last updated in May 2019. Extensive research has been conducted for many years on the impact of exposure to radio waves on health. This research has been examined by groups of UK and international independent experts, and their conclusions from this accumulated evidence is that adverse health effects are unlikely to occur if exposures are below the levels set in current standards. This link ( https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mobile -phone -base -stations -radio - waves -and-health/mobile -phone -base -stations -radio -waves -and-health ) includes detailed information on exposure guidelines and health -related evidence and reviews. PHE continu es to monitor the latest scientific evidence on this topic and update its advice. Camden will regularly review its position in light of the latest available evidence and national guidance on the health impacts of mobile phone installations. Camden has also commissioned emissions surveys of existing telecommunications installations and has found that the levels of all types of radio frequency transmissions found near to mobile phone base stations amount to less than 0.3% of the current permissible levels set by ICNIRP. We will continue to monitor telecommunications developments in the borough to ensure that they continue to meet existing and future legislation.  A general overview of High Frequency Electro -Magnetic Frequency, 100Khz to 300Ghz (HF EMF), can be found here. With all the telecoms installations in the borough, operators must ensure that all equipment is ICNIRP (International Committee on Non - Ionising Radiat ion Protection) compliant, as stated in the Department for Communities and Local Government’s National Planning Policy Framework (https://www.gov.uk/government/publicat ions/national -planning -policy -framework --2).  Radio base stations and handsets use Electromotive Force (EMF) to transfer information and make mobile phone communications possible. EMFs are used for television and radio transmissions, by the police, fire an d ambulance services, by taxi firms and public utilities. EMFs are also used for a wide range of personal and commercial equipment from electronic car keys, Wi -Fi equipment and baby monitoring devices to shop security tag systems. They are also produced by household electrical appliances like fridges, vacuum cleaners or electric shavers.  In terms of health concerns regarding installations of this type, mobile phones and devices are new but the technology is not, and research has been ongoing in this area for almost 75 years. After a thorough review of the available scientific findings, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported: "To date, the only health effect from radiofrequency (RF) fields identified in scientific reviews has been related to an increase in body temperature (> 1 °C) from exposure at very high field intensity found only in certain industrial facilities, such as RF heaters. The levels of RF exposure from base stations and wireless networks are so low that the temperature increases are insignificant and do not affect human health" [Source: World Health Organisation, Fact Sheet 304, Base stations and wireless technologies, 2006]. In addition, the WHO notes that “Based on a recent in -depth review of the scientific literature, the WHO concluded that current evidence does not confirm the existence of any health consequences from exposure to low level electromagnetic fields” ( http://www.who.int/peh - emf/about/WhatisEMF/en/index 1.html ).  The Advisory Group on Non -ionising Radiation summarised that: “…although a substantial amount of research has been conducted in this area, there is no convincing evidence that RF field exposure below guideline levels causes health effects in adul ts or children.” [Health Effects from Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields – RCE 20, 2012].  In addition, the report ‘Recent Research on EMF and Health Risk – Tenth report from SSM’s Scientific Council on Electromagnetic Fields, 2015’ notes that: “new stud ies on adult and childhood cancer with improved exposure assessment do not indicate any health risks for the general public related to exposure from radiofrequency electromagnetic fields from far -field sources, such as base stations and radio and TV transm itters.  Radio base stations are designed to comply with the stringent, precautionary public exposure guidelines set out by ICNIRP (International Commission on Non -Ionizing Radiation Protection). These guidelines have been developed following a thorough review of the science including both thermal and non -thermal effects. UK radio base station installations have been surveyed by independent bodies and found to be hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of times below these guidelines. When ICNIRP reviewed their g uidelines in 2009 they concluded: “ICNIRP reconfirms the 1998 basic restrictions in the frequency range 100 kHz –300 GHz until further notice.” [Source: ICNIRP statement on the “Guidelines for limiting exposure to time -varying electric, magnetic and electro magnetic fields (up to 300 GHz)”] (As above, these guidelines are currently being revised, with consultation having been undertaken in July to October 2018 and the results being collated at the moment.) I would like to reassure you that the safety of our r esidents, visitors and employees will always be our top priority , and we are committed to improving the health and wellbeing of our residents, and tackling health inequalities. This commitment is set out in our Health and Wellbeing Strategy, overseen by th e Health and Wellbeing Board, chaired by Councillor Georgia Gould, Leader of the Council (see here: https://www.camden.gov.uk/health -decision -making ). With respect to telecoms masts, we are c onfident that, by ensuring these follow and comply with guidance from the appropriate regulatory bodies, we are fulfilling our statutory responsibilities. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds some of the information requested. The answers to your questions are below. We have stated where we do not hold the information requested and why. 1- I would like to see the previous 3 years of receipts for where the council tax funding is being spent. I do not want to see percentages but proof in pounds (£s) as to where the annual council tax is being spent. We do not hold this information.  This is because we do not match specific income (such as council tax) to specific expenditure types. At Camden, Council Tax represents around 14% of the Council’s total annual income. This is combined with our other sources of funding (Fees & Charges, Business Rates, Government Grants etc.) and collectively put towards funding a range of services. 2 - I would like to know if my council tax funds the Police Service, the Ambulance Service, the Waste collection and Schools. If so I would like to know as to what percentage it is distributed? Funding for the Police Service in London is the responsibility of the Greater London Authority (GLA).  The GLA levies an amount of the Council Tax each year to fund its services.  An element of this levy goes towards the cost of the Metropolitan Police Service.  The percentage of Council Tax for Camden taxpayers that was attributable to the Metropolitan Police each year is shown in the table below: Year                 % of Council Tax levied on Camden Council taxpayers that funds the Police Service 2021/22          15.54% 2020/21          15.53% 2019/20          15.50%Details about the Greater London Authorities budgets each year can be found on their website https://www.london.gov.uk/ The Ambulance Service is a nationally funded service and does not receive funding via the Council Tax levy.  Ambulance Trusts receive funding through annual NHS Service Level Agreements made with primary care trusts and clinical commissioning groups in a particular geographic area. Waste Collection is a service provided directly by the Council and as such is partly funded through Council Tax.  Council Tax currently accounts for 13/14% of the Council’s income each year.  The percentage of Council Tax that is attributed to the Waste and Cleaning Services is shown in the table below: Year                 % of Council Tax attributed to Waste and Cleaning Services 2021/22          3.38% 2020/21          4.14% 2019/20          4.14% Schools in England are funded directly by the national government via direct grants to local authorities or directly to the school.  No element of the Council Tax directly funds schools. Details of how schools are funded can be found in the link below. Schools, colleges and children's services: School and college funding and finance - detailed information - GOV.UK ( www.gov.uk ) 3 - Which law, not legislation, states that council tax must be paid? The Local Government Finance Act 1992 is the legislation governing the billing and recovery of Council Tax.  This is primary legislation passed by UK parliament – primary legislation is the term used to describe laws passed by Parliament. 4 - Which law states that it is a criminal offence to not pay council tax? The Local Government Finance Act 1992 allows for a Magistrates Court to issue a prison sentence of up to 90 days if they find someone has not paid through ‘wilful refusal’ to pay or ‘culpable neglect’.  As the Local Government Finance Act 1992 is a legislative act an arrest warrant can be issued should the debtor not appear for the hearing. 5 - Please attach the copy of contract in where I agreed to pay for council tax. Please keep in mind that an ‘assumptuous agreement' does not stand up in court.As this is legislation which requires every liable person, subject to any discounts, exemptions or benefits they may be entitled to, to pay as billed there is no contract. If you are the person liable for the Council Tax charge in line with the hierarchy of liability for paying Council Tax you are automatically required to pay the Council Tax due in line with instalments provided.  As a national charge in line with the Local Government Finance Act 1992 there is no entering into contracts or opting out of paying.  Further Information We do not give our consent for any names and contact details provided in this response to be sent marketing material. Document Text: Date: 24/09/2019 Ref: FOI13206 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 05/09/2019 about sunbeds . Any applicants wishing to offer special treatments (of which ultra -violet tanning is one) must apply to the co uncil for a licence to do so. This can be done either online or via post. The relevant fee must also be paid. Applicants must include numerous documents with the application, which are as follows: • 2 colour passport size photos, taken within the last year - sign the back of each photo • a copy of your passport or drivers licence • original marriage certificate or deed poll documents if applicable • any licensing approval documents from another local authority • original qualification certificates for each of the tre atments you wish to do • a comparability certificate if your qualifications have been obtained from outside the UK, including any official certificate translations • proof of your home address, such as a recent bank statement • your Hepatitis B immunisation card - piercers and tattooists only 1:50 scale floors plans of the premises must also be enclosed, and must include the following details: • the lay -out, including all external and internal walls • all rooms used for treatments - clearly labelled to identify which treatments are carried out in which room • the provision of ventilation, fans, wash hand basins, sinks, sterilization areas, WC’s, etc. • fire exits and escape routes • the provision of any emergency lighting, fire alarm system installed • the location of any win dows and stairs and all entrance or exit doors London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Electrical inspection certificates must also be provided covering the following: • main electrical installation • portable appliances • fire alarm • emergency lighting • fire-fighting equipment Both the Police and Fire Brigade are consulted on the application. If all of the documentation is provided is satisfactory, then an enforcement officer will inspect the premises to check for suitability. If the inspection is satisfactory, and neither the Police or Fire Brigade obj ect, then the licence would be issued at this stage. If the inspection is failed, works will need to be completed as indicated by the enforcement officer, and checked, before any such time as a licence could be issued. Failure to provide the relevant docum ents and / or complete required works can result in the licence application being refused. What process is involved, for a salon to be registered with yourselves. As above How they are checked for compliance. New premises are inspected at time of applicati on to check for suitability. Any works required are identified at the time of inspection, and these works will be checked once complete to ensure they have been completed to the required standard. In addition, if any reports are received indicating there m ay be issues with compliance / suitability while the licence is in force, officers would carry out an additional inspection to investigate. How often they are checked for compliance. Under normal circumstances they would be checked at time of application ( for new licences). However, if issues were indicated / identified with a premises it could be more frequently than this. What are the measurements taken for rays omitted. The Council does not hold this information. We check the paperwork for the machines, but we do not measure, nor do we h ave the facility to measure the UV rays. Who completes the checks. Licensing Enforcement Officers. How do you check that staff are fully trained to advise of the dangers of sunbed use. Officers would check the qualifications provided with the application i nitially. During the inspection of the premises officers would further question staff knowledge / experience and also go through the processes the premises currently operate for the use of the sunbeds. Guidance produced by the Information Commissioner’s Office states that “in assessing whether the cost, or the amount of staff time involved in responding to a request, is sufficient to render a request manifestly unreasonable, the FOIA fees regulations may be a useful starting point.” We are refusing your request on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit". Document Text: Date: 21/10/2022 Case reference : CAM4055 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 10/10/2022 about whistleblowing disclosures. We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: 1. How many whistleblowing disclosures have you received over the last two years? 0 2. Can you provide a breakdown of the whistleblowing concerns received over the last two years? 0 3. The current headcount/total number of staff in your whistleblowing team. 0 4. The amount of expenditure allocated to your whistleblowing team, department or function that deals with disclosures made concerning the bodies, entities or individuals you regulate, supervise or oversee over the last two years. 0 5. Any relevant documents or processes you have in place for dealing with whistleblowing concerns over the last two years. From employee handbook Whistle Blowing Policy Introduction 1.1 Camden Learning will always conduct its business with the highest standards of integrity and honesty. We expect our staff to maintain the same standards. However, all organisations face the risk of things going wrong from time to time, or of unknowingly harbouring illegal or unethical conduct. A culture of openness and accountability is essential in order to prevent such situations occurring and to address them when they do occur. We therefore encourage staff to report suspected wrongdoing as soon as possible, in the knowledge that their concerns will be taken seriously and investigated as appropriate, and that their confidentiality will be respected. 1.2 The law offers protection to those who report wrongdoing within the workplace. 1.3 The company recognises that you may have hesitations about reporting suspected wrongdoing or that you may not always feel comfortable discussing your concerns internally, especially if you believe that the company itself is responsible for the wrongdoing. Therefore, the aims of this policy are: 1.3.1 to ensure that as far as possible you feel able to inform your line manager about any suspected wrongdoing at work which you believe has occurred or is likely to occur; Schedule 6: Whistleblowing Policy 1.3.2 to give guidance on what to do if you have concerns about any wrongdoing; and 1.3.3 to reassure staff that they should be able to raise genuine concerns without fear of reprisals, even if they turn out to be mistaken. 1.4 This policy does not form part of your contract of employment and it may be amended at any time. 2. Scope This policy applies to all employees of Camden Learning. However, the relevant legislation and this policy also covers secondees, contractors, consultants and agency workers. 3. What is Whistleblowing? Whistleblowing is the reporting of suspected wrongdoing or dangers in relation to our activities. This includes bribery, facilitation of tax evasion, fraud or other criminal activity, miscarriages of justice, health and safety risks, damage to the environment and any breach of legal or professional obligations. 4. When should you use this Policy? 4.1 Camden Learning staff and extended workforce are encouraged to use the procedure set out here if you have any concerns at all about suspected wrongdoing at work that has occurred or is likely to occur, relating to: 4.1.1 criminal offences; 4.1.2 a failure to comply with legal obligations; 4.1.3 a miscarriage of justice; 4.1.4 a health and safety danger; 4.1.5 an environmental risk; or 4.1.6 a concealment of any of these. 4.2 Complaints relating to your personal circumstances (such as how you have been treated at work) or which do not fall into the above categories should not generally be made under this policy and should be raised under the Grievance Procedure or the Dignity at Work Policy as appropriate. 5. Procedures Internal Disclosure 5.1 In most cases you should be able to raise any concerns about suspected wrongdoing with your line  manager in the first instance. 5.2 However, where the matter is more serious or you prefer not to raise it with them for any reason, you should raise your concerns to the Chief Executive or a Camden Learning Director in confidence. 5.3 We will arrange a meeting with you as soon as possible to discuss your concerns. You may bring a colleague or union representative to any meetings under this policy. Your companion must respect the confidentiality of your disclosure and any subsequent investigation. 5.4 If the matter requires further investigation, such an investigation will be carried out and you will be informed of the outcome of the investigation and what, if any, action has been taken. 5.5 If you remain unhappy about the speed or conduct of the investigation or the way in which the matter has been resolved, you should refer the matter to the Chief Executive. Where they have investigated your complaint, they will tell you the result of the investigation and what, if any, action has been taken. External Disclosures 5.6 The aim of this policy is to provide an internal mechanism for reporting, investigating and remedying any suspected wrongdoing in the workplace. In most cases you should not find it necessary to alert anyone externally. 5.7 The law recognises that in some circumstances it may be appropriate for you to report your concerns to an external body such as a regulator. We strongly encourage you to seek advice before reporting a concern to anyone external. Protect operates a confidential helpline. Their contact details can be found on their website: https://protect-advice.org.uk/ 6. Confidentiality 6.1 Camden Learning encourages you to raise your concerns openly under this policy. However, if you want to raise your concerns confidentially, every effort will be made to protect your identity and maintain confidentiality as far as possible. 6.2 Camden Learning does not encourage disclosures to be made anonymously. Proper investigation may be more difficult or impossible if it cannot obtain further information from you. It is also more difficult to establish whether any allegations are credible and have been made in good faith. If you are concerned about possible consequences to yourself, you should contact the Managing Director and appropriate measures can then be taken to preserve confidentiality. 7. Protection and Support for Whistleblowers 7.1 The company undertakes that no member of staff who makes a bona fide report under this procedure should be subjected to any detriment as a result, in accordance with section 47B of the Employment Rights Act 1996. 7.2 In the event that you believe you are being subjected to a detriment by any person within the company as a result of your decision to invoke the procedure, you must inform the Chief Executive immediately and appropriate action will be taken to protect you from any reprisals. If the situation is not remedied, you should raise it formally using our Grievance Procedure. 7.3 You must not threaten or retaliate against whistleblowers in any way. If you are involved in such conduct you may be subject to disciplinary action. In some cases, the whistleblower could have a right to sue you personally for compensation in an employment tribunal. 7.4 If it should become clear that the procedure has not been invoked in good faith, for example for malicious reasons, false allegations or to pursue a personal grudge against another member of staff, this will constitute misconduct and will be dealt with in accordance with the terms of the Disciplinary Policy. 7.5 Any staff member who commits a wrongdoing in the process of raising a complaint under this policy (for example by unlawfully accessing computer systems to gather evidence) may be acting in breach of this policy themselves. 7.6 As well as support internally, you can also seek support from Protects confidential helpline or your trade union if you are a union member. 8. Proper Reporting 8.1 Camden Learning is keen to hear of any concerns that members of staff may have about wrongdoing at work and encourages them to use the procedure described above wherever possible. 8.2 Camden Learning recognises there may be matters that cannot be dealt with internally and external authorities will need to become involved. Where this is necessary, the company reserves the right to make such a referral without your consent. The charter has 5 pledges that the council have pledged th eir commitment to achieve: i) Ensure access for Deaf people to information and services ii) Promote learning and high quality teaching of British Sign Language (BSL) iii) Support Deaf children and families iv) Ensure staff working with Deaf people can communicate effec tively in BSL v) Consult with the local Deaf community on a regular basis A new and innovative 2 year pilot programme designed by staff in Camden and Islington, to support families of young deaf children to learn sign language: A Family Sign Language and Communication (FSLC) Skills programme for families of young deaf children. The course will be free and available to families with deaf children in Camden and Islingt on. The course will be run by a sign language tutor who is trained in the FSLC, and by early year’s specialists from Camden and Islington including Advisory Teachers for Deaf children; Speech and London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . Document Text: Date: 14/08/2023 Case reference : CAM5657 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 19/07/2023 about our latest employee survey - copy of questionnaire and copy of the results of the survey .  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However, we are withholding the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained what exemption applies.  Please see the refusal notice which explains how and why it applies. You requested: I would like to request a copy of the latest employee survey at Camden Council (i.e. a copy of the questionnaire that was sent the employees) and also a copy of the results of the said survey. This information is exempt – please see the exemption notice set out below. Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 36 – prejudicial to the effective conduct of public affairs Section 36 of the Act sets out an exemption from the right to know if the disclosure of information, in the reasonable opinion of a qualified person - (b) would be likely to inhibit — (ii) the free and frank exchange of views for the purposes of deliberation, or (c) would otherwise prejudice, or would be likely otherwise to prejudice, the effective conduct of public affairs This exemption applies because: The purpose of the survey (which is something we do often) is to obtain the views of employees in a confidential way. employees are completely free to express their views in a frank and uninhibited manner and they are reported anonymously to senior management.● employees do this with the understanding that their anonymous views would be seen and inform the deliberations and decision making of senior management – but would not be made public.● The results of the survey are then considered carefully by senior management and used to inform future decision making.● In the reasonable opinion of a qualified person, that being the Borough Solicitor, disclosure of the information (survey and the results) under this Act would be likely to inhibit the free and frank exchange of views for the purposes of deliberation and decision making by senior management and prejudice the effective conduct of public affairs. Results of the Survey disclosure of the requested information would inhibit the imparting of views, opinions, or considerations due to the knowledge that they would potentially be made public. While they could not be attributed to anyone individual, they would nonetheless be taken as being the views of the staff. We want our staff to be completely honest in what they say. Our staff however have a loyalty to the organization that could inhibit this if they considered their critical views might be played out in public. The private exchange of views between employer and employee – albeit en masse – should remain private.● disclosure could result also result in views or opinions being self-censored in order to protect the public image of the Council – this would inhibit the purpose of the survey by incorrectly informing senior management of an untrue position.● disclosure would prejudice the effective conduct of public affairs because the council must have a space in which to gain the views or opinions of its workforce. It’s important that this can happen with the employees not worrying or anticipating that this would be made public. Management may be reluctant to begin this dialogue (which should be encouraged) should it then be reported publicly.● further the surveys have been ongoing. Taking one by itself and seeking to interpret it could give a false view of the real situation. In addition, Management is aware of particular internal factors which might influence the results and allow them to understand the results in the proper context. This understanding would not be shared by seeing the results alone and particularly when taken in isolation from previous results and other sources of feedback from staff which are available to management but not to the general public.● being a local authority, such survey results should they potentially become public may for example be impacted by the pre-election publicity rules and otherwise become a matter of●public debate when ideally, they should remain a matter of good employment practice. The questions the questions asked often are as a result of previous results of other surveys and could be sought to be interpreted in order to seek to assess the results of previous surveys.● management wants the option of asking about issues which may be controversial or otherwise matter of public debate without the questions themselves becoming a matter of debate.● discussion in the public arena over what questions are asked or indeed which are not would be distracting and potentially impact the answers given – perhaps with staff amending their answers having seen the debate around the questions.● The public interest arguments for releasing this information are: - Results releasing this information would improve transparency about the way the staff of a publicly funded and democratically accountable organisation feel about that organisation. ● would enable the public to perhaps be able to better judge the effectiveness of the organisation at least with regard to its staff relations.● Questions releasing the information would allow the public to understand the issues management at the Council are interested.● releasing this information would improve transparency about what management ask employees to obtain this information.● The public interest arguments for withholding the information are: - Results the release of such information would harm the frankness and candour of the internal exchange of views in the future and thereby prejudice the Council’s ability to undertake an honest assessment of its employees’ views and opinions. ● the ability to consider and discuss employees’ undiluted views and opinions leads to more effective management decision making.● releasing employees’ views and opinions may give the impression that the views and opinions expressed were intended to be made public rather than being given in confidence to appropriate internal decision makers.● while they are only a snapshot in time to be considered with other surveys and sources of feedback instead, they may be taken as definitive and fixed.● the release of results which suggest the workforce have issues may be used by potential candidates in assessing whether to apply for work when other comparable employers have●not been obliged to release such information. Questions management may be concerned as to the questions they should ask particularly should they cover controversial matters leading to them not being asked despite their utility. ● seeing the questions may lead to speculation as to what prompted them and speculation as to what staff may have thought of the answers to them.● It is considered that the public interest in withholding the information outweighs the public interest in disclosing it. This letter constitutes a refusal notice under the terms of the Act. If internal, which team is delivering this training? If external, are you using an accredited training provider? The Council uses a combination of internal and external training providers to ensure drivers and passenger assistants (PA) working on dedicated school transport have undertaken appropriate training. In house training is organised by our Learning and Development team and Certificate of Professional Competence (CPC) sessions are delivered by some external accredited providers, for example AGVC deliver some PVC training for drivers. 2. London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London . WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk 4. How are meet and greet sessions between transport providers and passengers monitored? We monitor by: • The Travel Options Manager writing to all parents each year to invite them to the depot to meet their driver/PA and type of bus that the child will be transported on. This gives the opportunity for parents to ask questions or raise any concerns they may have. • Welcome packs are issued to all parents, guides, and information on how to contact the service are included. • Spot checks on the service introduced by the Head of Service to ensure service users’ needs are being met. • Staff 1-1s include a discussion point on parent/staff relationships • Bespoke Ras are conducted on pupils which allow parents to raise any concerns or special requests that can be relayed to staff. • Periodic meetings take place with schools where parents are able to attend an d give feedback. • Throughout the year, Service Controllers drive a route and interact with parents, ensuring all feedback is captured. • The service attends Autism Partnership Board meetings where parents are able to feedback to the service. • The service operates an ‘open door policy’ where any matter can be brought forward with the intent of resolution/service improvement. 5. How much budget is allocated to safeguarding training for school transport providers? There is no dedicated budget for training school transport providers. Safeguarding training requirements are included in the corporate safeguarding training. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 26/01/2022 about the impact of high gas and electricity prices on finances and services . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and Environmental Information Regulations 2004. Response The council holds the information requested and the answers to your questions are as follows: I am interested in learning about the impact of high gas and electricity prices on local authorities’ finances and services. Under the Freedom of Information Act, I’d be grateful to know: 1. Have your authority's electricity and gas bills increased since July 2021?  Yes, our electricity and gas bills have increased. 2. If so, by roughly how much? The average price increases are 29-47% for gas and 11-22% for electricity. 3. Is this increase due to a higher rate per unit of gas and electricity charged by your energy provider, or for another reason? The increase is due to wholesale energy price increases. 4. Have you made any reductions to the provision of street lighting in your area since July 2021, or are you planning any reductions? Please specify the changes, if so. Yes, we switched all street lighting to LED.5. If yes, is this because energy bills have risen? No, this is not because energy bills have risen. 6. Have you made any reductions to the provision of lighting or heating in any of your buildings, or are you planning any reductions? Please specify the changes, if so.  There is a reduced heating and lighting requirements as a result of remote working during the pandemic (and in particular during ‘lockdowns’.) 7. If yes, is this because energy bills have risen? No, it is not because energy bills have risen - please see response above. Document Text: Date: 14/11/2022 Case reference : CAM4090 London Borough of Camden Information and Records Management Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk Dear Requester Thank you for your request for information dated 17/10/2022 about No recourse to public funds (NRPF).  We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested.  However we are withholding all of the information because it is exempt as explained below.  We have explained where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply.  Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which explain how and why they apply. 1.         How many requests for support under section 17 of the Children Act 1989 for families with ‘no recourse to public funds’ (NRPF) were made in: a)         2021 b)         2020 c)         2019 2.         How many assessments of families with NRPF seeking support under section 17 of the Children Act 1989 were undertaken by the Council in: a.         2021 b.         2020 c.         2019 3.         In how many cases was accommodation and/or subsistence support provided following assessment? (Please provide breakdown by year) 4.         How many families with NRPF are currently being supported by the local authority under section 17 of the Children Act 1989? 5.         How many dependents in families with NRPF are currently being supported by the local authority under section 17 of the Children Act 1989? We are refusing your request under section 12 on cost grounds because we estimate that compliance with your request will exceed the "appropriate limit".  This is £450 which is equivalent to 18 hours at £25 per hour. The per hour figure is set by Regulations rather than actual salary paid to any officers handling requests. The appropriate limit includes the time it will take the council to discover if it holds the information requested, to locate it, extract it and collate it as well as putting it into any particular format requested by the requester. We are unable to provide a response to your request for the three years you have requested this is because we do not routinely report on NRPF. In order to locate and retrieve the information you are seeking would require an officer to conduct a manual trawl of files for each of the years you are seeking. There are between 1000 – 1500 cases in each of the years you are seeking which would need to examined to determine whether they were classified as NRPF, we estimate on this calculation it would take in excess of 166 hours or 250 hours at 10 minutes per case for 1 year this far exceeds the 18 hour limit. Advice and Assistance We can inform you that for this year – 2022, The number of households living in accommodation provided by the local authority under section 17 of the Children Act 1989 on 30th June 2022 (or closest possible date) was -7 households/ families●  The total number of adults living in these households on 30th June 2022 (or the closest possible date)- the number of adults were 9 –● 5 with one parent 2 with 2 parents The total number of children living in these households on 30th June 2022 (or the closest possible date)- children 7 in total and one expectant parent● All families who are NRPF, by virtue of being destitute and having no recourse, their accommodation, utility bills, council tax are funded and subsistence provided, with additional service often funded like childminding/ nursery fees to enable some to try and gain work to help support their immigration appeal and demonstrate in some circumstance their ability to work and become independent of the state. Documents regarding the infrastructure of the shared boiler system (e.g., what model of boiler is it?/floorplan) We do not hold a clear, electronic copy of the floorplan, however a scan of the boiler room schematic can be shared. While both Hyperoptic and Community Fibre hold bulk wayleave agreements with the Council, Community Fibre has paused its rollout programme for commercial reasons. As the rollout of broadband infrastructure is provider-led, Camden does not have control over the providers’ delivery schedules. Nevertheless, Rowley Way is included in Hyperoptic’s current plans. One of the reasons for the delay is that the estate is a listed building, which can make providers more hesitant to proceed due to the additional costs and requirements involved. We are also in ongoing discussions with other broadband providers who have expressed interest in delivering services, and we hope to have additional providers on board in the near future. To clarify, Camden Council is not withholding permission for FTTP installation at Rowley Way or elsewhere. We continue to work closely with telecommunications providers to encourage investment and support their efforts to bring full fibre broadband to all our residents. Please state the job title and level/banding for the person who is responsible within the council for purchasing these insurance products Information has been withheld because we consider it to be exempt information under Section 31(3) of the Act. The council under se ction 17(4) and section 31(3) neither confirms nor denies whether the information exists or is held. Information and Records Management Corporate Services London Borough of Camden Town Hall Judd Street London WC1H 9JE Phone: 020 7974 7857 camden.gov.uk Date: Our reference: Email: 01 October 2019 FOI13226 foi@camden.gov.uk Refusal Notice The exemption that applies is: section 31: prejudicial to law enforcement It is the council’s view that the confirmation or denial of the p ossession of information relating to the council’s cyber resilience, would be likely to compromise the council's information security strategies by giving cyber criminals insight into vulnerabilities which may, or may not, exist. Section 31(3) is a qualifi ed exemption, as such we have gone on to perform a public interest test in order to assess the public interest arguments for and against declaring whether or not the requested information is held. Public interest arguments for disclosure:  confirmation of p ossession would demonstrate a commitment to transparency with regard to the council’s undertakings, and could provide assurance that the council have robust IT infrastructure in place Public interest arguments for withholding information:  maintaining the i ntegrity and security of the council's systems  preventing cyber -attacks and similar against the council systems.  revealing whether or not the information requested is held or applicable to london borough of camden would be likely to offer cyber criminals insight into not only the strengths of the council’s cyber security, but also any potential weaknesses that may exist. this could ultimately result in a future cyberattack.  one of the reasons that cyber security measures are in place is to protect the int egrity of personal and sensitive personal information.  it is clear to see how the occurrence of a future cyber -attack would prejudice the council’s legal duty to safeguard personal information from loss, theft, inappropriate access or destruction, which i s why Section 31 has been employed in this case On balance the public interest in maintaining the exemption outweighs that in confirming or denying whether information is held and therefore the council neither confirms nor denies whether this information i s held Further Information : Why not check our Portal Open Data Camden before making a new request as your question may already be answered by a previous FOI response or in one of our many useful and interesting datasets. Document Title: Death of a child under Camden YOT supervision
Document Text: FOI12359 - Date: 1st March 2019 Ref: FOI12310 Dear Requester Thank you for your request for informa tion dated the 22nd January 2019 about death of a child under Camden YOT supervision . We have dealt with this under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Response The council holds the information requested , however we are withholding some of the informat ion because it is exempt . The answers to your questions are below w e have stated where we are withholding information and what exemptions apply. Please see the refusal notices at the end of the answers which exp lain how and why the exemptions apply. I und erstand that there was 1 death of a child under Camden YOT supervision during the period April 2013 -May 2018. Please can you provide me with the information contained in the critical learning review and/or extended learning review submitted by the Camden youth offending team following a death of a child under YOT supervision, where the death happened between April 2013 – May 2018. I anticipate that any personal information would need to be omitted from the reviews. I am specifically looking for informatio n contained within the reviews in relation to: - whether a risk of harm had previously been identified - what was in place to manage any potential risk - the learning identified in the report - the good/effective practice identified - the actio ns proposed /enacted following the deaths With regard to your r equest we are withholding this information as we consider that the Absolute Exemption section 40(2) and the Qualified Exemption Section 38 applies to your request. Section 40(2) (Personal Data) The council has withheld this information under the absolute exemption in Section 40 (2). The information withheld is personal information because it allows a living individual to be identified. We have considered the legitimate public interest in disclosure against the interests of the data subject /s and concluded that disclosure would contravene the first principle in the General Data Protection Regulation that personal data is processed fairly and lawfully . In the circumstances of this case disclosure would not be fair to the individuals particular ly considering that F reedom of Information responses are public documents and published to the world and not provided just to Information and Records Management Law and Governance Directorate London Borough of Camden Town Hall Judd Street London. WC1H 9JE e-mail: foi@camden.gov.uk the requester . Information pertaining to the deceased young person has already been reported on and is in the public domai n, were we to release the information requested above into the public domain it would identify the vulnerable livi ng relatives of the deceased. Which would contravene the first principle of GDPR. Section 38 (Health & Safety) We are not obliged to provide information if its release wo uld be likely to endanger the health and safety of an individual. In this case, we believe that releasing the information would be likely to endanger the physical or mental health of individuals related or connected with the deceased young person (sect ion 38 (1) (a) of the Act). We are unable to detail in this response the harm which would be likely to be caused because detailing this would disclose personal information of those affected and would itself lead to harm to their physical or mental health. In line with the terms of this exemption in the Freedom of Information Act, we have also considered whether it would be in the public interest for us to provide you with the information, despite the exemption being applicable. In this case, we have concl uded that the public interest favours withholding the information. When assessing whether or not it was in the public interest to disclose the information to you, we took into account the following factors: Public interest considerations favouring discl osure Full disclosure of the way in which the local authority handled the review . Full disclosure would identify the local authorities learning and actions. Public interest considerations favouring withholding the information The public interest considerations cannot be disclosed as doing so would likely cause harm to those related or connected to the deceased young person.
